          bandhaḥ/ parasparaprāptimātraṃ saṅgaḥ/ tad uktaṃ pūrvaprayogād asaṅgatvād bandhacchedāt
          tathā gatipariṇāmāc ca/ āviddhakulālacakravad vyapagatalepālābuvad eraṇḍabījavad
          agniśikhāvac ca/ ata eva paṭhanti:
children.translated_text: When the causes of bondage such as false view (<s>mithyādarśana</s>) and the like are stopped, due to the absence of new <s>karma</s>, and due to the <s>nirjarā</s> (dissipation) removing accumulated <s>karma</s> through the proximity of its cause, the absolute release from <s>karma</s> is <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). Thus it is stated: the complete release from all <s>karma</s> through the absence of the causes of bondage and through <s>nirjarā</s> is <s>mokṣa</s>. Thereafter, [the soul] goes upward to the end of the universe (<s>lokānta</s>). Just as a potter's wheel set spinning by the impulse of a hand, stick, and the like, even when that [impulse] has ceased, continues spinning by that very force until the impressions are exhausted -- so too, the soul while in worldly existence made many resolutions (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) for the attainment of liberation; for the liberated one, even in their absence, the going to the end of the universe is explicable from prior impressions. Or just as a gourd made heavy by a coating of clay sinks down in water, but when freed from the clay-bond rises upward -- so too, the soul devoid of <s>karma</s>, being unattached, goes upward. From the severing of bondage, like a castor seed; and because of the upward nature of its movement, like a flame of fire. When there is mutual interpenetration of spatial units, the remaining without separation is bondage. Mere mutual contact is association (<s>saṅga</s>). Thus it is stated: from prior momentum, from unattachedness, from the severing of bondage, and from the transformation of movement -- like a spinning potter's wheel, like a gourd freed from clay, like a castor seed, and like a flame of fire. Therefore they read:
The planets such as the moon and sun, having gone forth, return again and again;

children.text: adyāpi na nivartante tv alokākāśam āgatāḥ// iti
children.translated_text: but those who have reached the space beyond the universe (<s>alokākāśa</s>) never return even to this day.
reference marker

children.text:
anye tu gatasamastakleśatadvāsanasyānāvaraṇajñānasya sukhaikatānasyātmana
          uparideśāvasthānaṃ muktir ity āsthiṣata/ evam uktāni sukhaduḥkhasādhanābhyāṃ
          puṇyapāpābhyāṃ sahitāni nava padārthān kecanāṅgīcakruḥ/ tad uktaṃ siddhānte jīvājīvau
          puṇyapāpayutāv āsravaḥ saṃvaro nirjaraṇaṃ bandho mokṣaś ca nava tattvānīti/ saṃgrahe
          pravṛttā vayam uparatāḥ smaḥ/
children.translated_text: Others, however, have maintained: liberation is the abiding of the self in the upper region, for whom all afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>) and their latent impressions (<s>vāsanā</s>) have departed, whose knowledge is unobstructed, and who is of uninterrupted bliss. Thus the stated [categories], together with merit and demerit -- the means of pleasure and pain -- some have accepted as nine categories. As stated in the <s>Siddhānta</s>: <s>jīva</s> (soul), <s>ajīva</s> (non-soul), endowed with merit and demerit, influx (<s>āsrava</s>), restraint (<s>saṃvara</s>), dissipation (<s>nirjaraṇa</s>), bondage (<s>bandha</s>), and liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) -- these are the nine categories. Having engaged in summarization, we have concluded.
reference marker

children.text:
atra sarvatra saptabhaṅginayākhyaṃ nyāyam avatārayanti jaināḥ/ syād asti syān nāsti syād
          asti ca nāsti ca syād avaktavyaḥ syād asti cāvaktavyaḥ syān nāsti cāvaktavyaḥ syād asti ca
          nāsti cāvaktavya iti/
children.translated_text: Everywhere in this [doctrine], the Jainas introduce the method called <s>saptabhaṅgīnaya</s> (the logic of seven-fold predication): (1) 'perhaps it exists' (<s>syād asti</s>), (2) 'perhaps it does not exist' (<s>syān nāsti</s>), (3) 'perhaps it exists and does not exist' (<s>syād asti ca nāsti ca</s>), (4) 'perhaps it is inexpressible' (<s>syād avaktavyaḥ</s>), (5) 'perhaps it exists and is inexpressible' (<s>syād asti cāvaktavyaḥ</s>), (6) 'perhaps it does not exist and is inexpressible' (<s>syān nāsti cāvaktavyaḥ</s>), (7) 'perhaps it exists, does not exist, and is inexpressible' (<s>syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaḥ</s>).
reference marker
<s>Anantavīrya</s> (the one of infinite power) explained all this:
When there is the desire to state that mode, the predication 'perhaps it exists' (<s>syād asti</s>) applies;

children.text: syān nāstīti prayogaḥ syāt tanniṣedhe vivakṣite//
children.translated_text: 'perhaps it does not exist' (<s>syān nāsti</s>) is the formulation when the negation of that is intended.
When both are desired in sequence, the formulation partakes of the aggregate;
when both are desired simultaneously, 'perhaps it is inexpressible' [follows], due to the inability [to express both at once].
When one desires [to express] the first and the inexpressible, the fifth alternative (<s>bhaṅga</s>) is accepted;
when one desires [to express] the last and the inexpressible, the sixth alternative arises.

children.text: samuccayena yuktaś ca saptamo bhaṅga ucyate// iti/
children.translated_text: And connected with the aggregate, the seventh alternative is stated.
This word <s>syāt</s> (perhaps) is indeed an indeclinable, resembling a finite verb, that indicates non-absolutism (<s>anekānta</s>).
reference marker
As stated:
The indeclinable <s>syāt</s>, indicating non-absolutism in sentences, is a qualifier with respect to what is to be understood;
it resembles a finite verb because of its connection with meaning.

children.text:
yadi punar ekāntadyotakaḥ syācchabdo ’yaṃ syāt tadā syād astīti vākye syātpadam
          anarthakaṃ syāt/ anekāntadyotakatve tu syād asti kathaṃcid astīti syātpadāt kathaṃcid ity
          ayam artho labhyata iti nānarthakyam/ tad āha:
children.translated_text: If, however, the word <s>syāt</s> were to indicate absolutism, then in the sentence 'perhaps it exists' (<s>syād asti</s>), the word <s>syāt</s> would be meaningless. But when it indicates non-absolutism, from the word <s>syāt</s>, the meaning 'in some way' (<s>kathaṃcit</s>) is obtained in 'perhaps it exists, i.e., it exists in some way' -- thus it is not meaningless. Therefore it is stated:
The <s>syādvāda</s> (doctrine of conditional predication), by abandoning absolute one-sidedness in every respect, concerned with some particular mode of being,
dependent on the seven-fold predication (<s>saptabhaṅgīnaya</s>), distinguishes what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
reference marker

children.text:
yadi vastv asty ekāntataḥ sarvathā sarvadā sarvatra sarvātmanāstīti nopāditsājihāsābhyāṃ
          kvacit kadācit kenacit pravarteta nivarteta vā/ prāptāprāpaṇīyatvād aheyahānānupapatteś
          ca/ anekāntapakṣe tu kathaṃcit kvacit kenacit sattvena hānopādāne prekṣāvatām upapadyete/
          kiṃ ca vastunaḥ sattvaṃ svabhāvaḥ, asattvaṃ vetyādi praṣṭavyam/ na tāvad astitvaṃ vastunaḥ
          svabhāva iti samasti/ ghaṭo ’stīty anayoḥ paryāyatayā yugapat prayogāyogāt/ nāstīti
          prayogavirodhāc ca/ evam anyatrāpi yojyam/ yathoktam:
children.translated_text: If a thing exists absolutely, in every way, at all times, everywhere, and in all respects, then one would never engage or desist with respect to anything, at any time, by any means, through the [impulses of] desire to acquire and desire to abandon. Because of what is already attained being non-obtainable, and the impossibility of abandoning what cannot be abandoned. But in the non-absolutist position, through being existent in some way, somewhere, and by something, both abandonment and acquisition are explicable for the discerning. Moreover, is the existence of a thing its own-nature, or its non-existence? -- and so on, must be asked. It is not consistent that existence is the own-nature of a thing. Because 'a pot exists' -- these two [the pot and existence] cannot be used simultaneously as synonyms. And because of contradiction with the usage 'does not exist.' The same should be applied elsewhere. As stated:

children.text: ghaṭo ’stīti na vaktavyaṃ sann eva hi yato ghaṭaḥ/
children.translated_text: One should not say 'a pot exists,' for the pot is already existent;

children.text: nāstīty api na vaktavyaṃ virodhāt sadasattvayoḥ// ityādi/
children.translated_text: nor should one say 'does not exist,' because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence. And so on.

children.text:
sadasatsadasadanirvacanīyavādabhedena prativādinaś caturvidhāḥ/ punar apy
          anirvacanīyamatena miśritāni sadasadādimatānīti trividhāḥ/ tān prati kiṃ vastv
          astītyādiparyanuyoge kathaṃcid astītyādiprativacanasaṃbhavena te vādinaḥ sarve nirviṇṇāḥ
          santas tūṣṇīm āsata iti saṃpūrṇārthaviniścāyinaḥ syādvādam aṅgīkurvatas tatra tatra vijaya
          iti sarvam upapannam/ yad avocad ācāryaḥ syādvādamañjaryām:
children.translated_text: Opponents are of four kinds, by the distinction of the doctrines of being, non-being, both being and non-being, and the inexpressible. Again, mixed with the inexpressible doctrine, the doctrines of being, non-being, and the rest are [reduced to] three kinds. Against them, in the inquiry 'does a thing exist?' and the like, since the response 'it exists in some way' and the like is possible, all those disputants, being confounded, sit silently -- thus the adherents of <s>syādvāda</s>, who ascertain the complete meaning, achieve victory in every case. Everything is well-established. As the teacher stated in the <s>Syādvādamañjarī</s>:
Therefore, one should speak thus [i.e., conditionally].
reference marker
A thing, having the nature of non-absolutism (<s>anekānta</s>), is the object of all cognitions;
a meaning qualified by one aspect is considered the domain of a viewpoint (<s>naya</s>).
When reasoning, each having a single focus, operates on the path of scripture,
the <s>syādvāda</s> (conditional predication) that ascertains the complete meaning is called scripture (<s>śruta</s>).
Since other doctrines are mutually opposing in thesis and counter-thesis,
they are, as it were, quarrelsome discourses;
desiring all viewpoints without distinction,
the doctrine of the <s>Arhat</s> is not partisan.
reference marker
<s>Jinadattasūri</s> stated the Jaina doctrine thus:
Obstruction (<s>antarāya</s>) of strength, enjoyment, and possessions, of both giving and receiving,
likewise sleep, fear, and [wrong] knowledge are reprehensible. //1//
Violence, pleasure and displeasure, attachment and aversion, non-restraint, desire,

children.text: śoko mithyātvam ete ’ṣṭādaśa doṣā na yasya saḥ //2//
children.translated_text: grief, and false view -- he who is free from these eighteen defects -- //2//
the <s>Jina</s> (Conqueror) is the deity; the proper guru is the teacher of true knowledge of categories;
knowledge, vision, and conduct are the path to liberation. //3//

children.text: syādvādasya pramāṇe dve pratyakṣam anumāpi ca/
children.translated_text: The <s>syādvāda</s> has two <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge): perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>);

children.text: nityānityātmakaṃ sarvaṃ nava tattvāni sapta vā //4//
children.translated_text: everything has both permanent and impermanent nature; the categories are nine or seven. //4//
<s>Jīva</s> (soul) and <s>ajīva</s> (non-soul), merit and demerit, influx (<s>āsrava</s>) and restraint (<s>saṃvara</s>) as well,
bondage (<s>bandha</s>), dissipation (<s>nirjaraṇa</s>), and liberation (<s>mukti</s>) -- the explanation of these is now stated. //5//
<s>Jīva</s> has consciousness as its mark; <s>ajīva</s> is what is other than that;
meritorious <s>karma</s>-particles (<s>pudgala</s>) are merit (<s>puṇya</s>); demerit (<s>pāpa</s>) is the opposite of that. //6//
<s>Saṃvara</s> (restraint) closes the door of the stream [of influx];
the entry of <s>karmas</s> is bondage (<s>bandha</s>); <s>nirjara</s> (dissipation) is their separation. //7//
Liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>) is from the destruction of the eight <s>karmas</s>; and some [include] subsumption [of categories],
merit [being subsumed] in restraint, and demerit in influx. //8//
For the self who has attained the infinite tetrad [of knowledge, vision, bliss, and power], who transcends the universe (<s>lokāgūḍha</s>),
whose eight <s>karmas</s> are destroyed -- liberation is the irreversible departure, as taught by the <s>Jina</s>. //9//
Carrying a broom to sweep [insects from the path], eating alms-food, with plucked hair,
wearing white garments, patient in nature, unattached -- such are the Jaina monks. //10//
With plucked hair, peacock-feather broom in hand, eating from the hand alone, sky-clad (<s>digambara</s>),

children.text: ūrdhvāśino gṛhe dātur dvitīyāḥ syur jinarṣayah //11//
children.translated_text: eating while standing, in the house of the donor -- the second [type] are the Jaina sages. //11//

children.text: bhuṅkte na kevalī na strī mokṣam eti digambaraḥ/
children.translated_text: A <s>kevalin</s> (omniscient) does not eat; a woman does not attain liberation; the <s>Digambara</s> [holds];

children.text: prāhur eṣām ayaṃ bhedo mahāñ śvetāmbaraiḥ saha //12// iti/
children.translated_text: they declare this is the great difference between them and the <s>Śvetāmbaras</s>. //12//
Thus concludes the <s>Ārhatadarśana</s> (Jaina philosophy) in the <s>Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha</s>.
Now the <s>Rāmānuja</s> philosophy //4//
reference marker

children.text:
tad etad ārhatamataṃ prāmāṇikagarhaṇam arhati/ na hy ekasmin vastuni paramārthe sati
          paramārthasatāṃ yugapat sadasattvādidharmāṇāṃ samāveśo saṃbhavati/ na ca sadasattvayoḥ
          parasparaviruddhayoḥ samuccayāsaṃbhave vikalpaḥ kiṃ na syād iti vaditavyam/ kriyā hi
          vikalpyate na vastv iti nyāyāt/ na ca
children.translated_text: Now this <s>Ārhata</s> (Jaina) doctrine deserves censure by those who follow valid authority. For in a single thing that is ultimately real, the coexistence of mutually [contradictory] properties such as existence and non-existence is not possible in the ultimate sense. Nor should it be said 'why should there not be an alternative?' when the aggregate of existence and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory, is impossible -- for the principle is: action is subject to alternatives, not a thing.
The whole world is of non-absolute nature, like <s>Heramba-Narasiṃha</s> (Gaṇeśa-Man-Lion) --

children.text:
iti dṛṣṭāntāvaṣṭambhavaśād eṣṭavyam/ ekasmin deśe gajatvaṃ siṃhatvaṃ vāparasmin naratvam
          iti deśabhedena virodhābhāvena tasyaikasmin deśa eva sattvāsattvādinānekāntatvābhidhāne
          dṛṣṭāntānupapatteḥ/
children.translated_text: this should not be maintained on the strength of such an example. Because elephantness in one part and lion-or-humanness in another part -- since by the difference of location there is no contradiction -- when asserting non-absolutism of existence and non-existence in one and the same location, the example is inapplicable.
reference marker

children.text:
nanu dravyātmanā sattvaṃ paryāyātmanā tadabhāva ity ubhayam apy upapannam iti cen maivam/
          kālabhedena hi kasyacit sattvam asattvaṃ ca svabhāva iti na kaścid doṣaḥ/ na caikasya
          hrasvadīrghatvavad anekāntatvaṃ jagataḥ syād iti vācyam/ pratiyogibhedena virodhābhāvāt/
          tasmāt pramāṇābhāvād yugapat sattvāsattve parasparaviruddhe naikasmin vastuni vastuṃ
          yukte/ evam anyāsām api bhaṅgīnāṃ bhaṅgo ’vagantavyaḥ/ kiṃ ca sarvasyāsya mūlabhūtaḥ
          saptabhaṅginayaḥ svayam ekānto ’nekānto vā/ ādye sarvam anekāntam iti pratijñāvyāghātaḥ/
          dvitīye vivakṣitārthāsiddhiḥ/ anekāntatvenāsādhakatvāt/ tathā ceyam ubhayataḥpāśā rajjuḥ
          syādvādinaḥ syāt/ api ca navatvasaptatvādinirdhāraṇasya phalasya tannirdhārayituḥ pramātuś
          ca tatkaraṇasya pramāṇasya prameyasya ca navatvāder aniyame sādhu samarthitam ātmanas
          tīrthakaratvaṃ devānāṃpriyeṇārhatamatapravartakena/ tathā jīvasya
          dehānurūpaparimāṇatvāṅgīkāre yogabalād anekadehaparigrāhakayogiśarīreṣu pratiśarīraṃ
          jīvavicchedaḥ prasajyeta/ manujaśarīraparimāṇo jīvo mataṅgajadehaṃ kṛtsnaṃ praveṣṭuṃ na
          prabhavet/ kiṃ ca gajādiśarīraṃ parityajya pipīlikāśarīraṃ viśataḥ
          prācīnaśarīrasaṃniveśavināśo ’pi prāpnuyāt/ na ca yathā pradīpaprabhāviśeṣaḥ
          prapāprāsādādyudaravartisaṃkocavikāśavāṃs tathā jīvo ’pi manujamataṅgajādiśarīreṣu syād
          ity eṣitavyam/ pradīpavad eva savikāratvenānityatvaprāptau
          kṛtapraṇāśākṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅgāt/ evaṃ pradhānamallanirbarhaṇanyāyena
          jīvapadārthadūṣaṇābhidhānadiśānyatrāpi dūṣaṇam utprekṣaṇīyam/ tasmān
          nityanirdoṣaśrutiviruddhatvād idam upādeyaṃ na bhavati/ tad uktaṃ bhagavatā vyāsena
          naikasminn asaṃbhavāt iti/ rāmānujena ca jainamatanirākaraṇaparatvena tad idaṃ sūtraṃ
          vyākāri/
children.translated_text: Objection: 'Both [propositions] are tenable — existence in the mode of substance, and non-existence in the mode of modification.' Not so! For the existence and non-existence of something at different times is [its] own nature, so there is no fault. Nor should it be said that, like shortness and tallness, the world would have non-absoluteness (<s>anekāntatva</s>) — because there is no contradiction when the counter-correlates are different. Therefore, since there is no means of valid knowledge [to establish it], simultaneous existence and non-existence, being mutually contradictory, cannot reasonably reside in a single entity. In the same way, the refutation of the other formulations [of the <s>syādvāda</s>] should also be understood. Moreover, is this <s>saptabhaṅgīnaya</s> (sevenfold predication), which is the root of all this, itself absolute or non-absolute? In the first case, the thesis 'everything is non-absolute' would be self-contradictory. In the second case, the intended meaning would remain unestablished — because, being non-absolute, it would be non-probative. And thus this would be a rope binding from both sides for the <s>syādvādin</s> (proponent of conditional predication). Furthermore, when [there is] no fixity regarding the result — such as the determination of nine-ness or seventy-ness — nor regarding the knower who determines it, nor regarding the instrument of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), nor regarding the object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) such as nine-ness and the like — then the claim of <s>Tīrthaṅkara</s>-hood for one's own [teacher] has been well established by the one dear to the gods, the proponent of the <s>Ārhat</s> doctrine! Furthermore, if it is accepted that the soul has a size conforming to the body, then by the force of <s>yoga</s>, in the bodies of <s>yogins</s> who occupy multiple bodies, a splitting of the soul in each body would follow. A soul of human-body size would not be able to enter the entire body of an elephant. Moreover, when [the soul], leaving an elephant-body and entering an ant-body, the destruction of the configuration of the previous body would also follow. Nor should it be maintained that, just as the light of a lamp expands and contracts within the interiors of wells, palaces, and the like, so too the soul [expands and contracts] in human, elephant, and other bodies — because, if it were subject to change like a lamp, impermanence would follow, and the undesirable consequences of the destruction of what has been done and the arrival of what has not been done would arise. Thus, by the method of defeating the chief wrestler, from the indication of the refutation of the category of <s>jīva</s> (soul), refutation elsewhere too should be imagined. Therefore, since it contradicts the eternal, faultless <s>Śruti</s> (Vedic revelation), this [Jaina doctrine] is not to be accepted. As the blessed <s>Vyāsa</s> has stated: '[It is] not [possible] in a single [entity], because of impossibility.' And <s>Rāmānuja</s> has commented on this <s>sūtra</s> with the intent of refuting the Jaina doctrine.

children.text:
eṣa hi tasya siddhāntaḥ: cidacidīśvarabhedena bhoktṛbhogyaniyāmakabhedena ca vyavasthitās
          trayaḥ padārthā iti/ taduktam:
children.translated_text: For this is his (<s>Rāmānuja</s>'s) established doctrine: three categories (<s>padārthas</s>) are established, distinguished as <s>cit</s> (consciousness), <s>acit</s> (non-consciousness), and <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), and [distinguished] as the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller. As stated:

children.text: īśvaraś cid acic ceti padārthatritayaṃ hariḥ/
children.translated_text: '<s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), <s>cit</s> (consciousness), and <s>acit</s> (non-consciousness) — this is the triad of categories; <s>Hari</s> is the Lord;

children.text: īśvaraś cid iti prokto jīvo dṛśyaṃ acit punaḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) is called <s>cit</s>, and the visible [world] is <s>acit</s>.' Thus.

children.text:
apare punar aśeṣaviśeṣapratyanīkaṃ cinmātraṃ brahmaiva paramārthaḥ/ tac ca
          nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvam api tat tvam asi ityādisāmānādhikaraṇyādhigatajīvaikyaṃ
          badhyate mucyate ca/ tadatiriktanānāvidhabhoktṛbhoktavyādibhedaprapañcaḥ sarvo ’pi tasminn
          avidyayā parikalpitaḥ sad eva somyedam agra āsīd ekam evādvitīyam
          ityādivacananicayaprāmāṇyād iti bruvāṇās tarati śokam ātmavit ityādiśrutiśiraḥśatavaśena
          nirviśeṣabrahmātmaikatvavidyayānādyavidyānivṛttim aṅgīkurvāṇāḥ
children.translated_text: Others, however, [maintain that] <s>Brahman</s> — which is pure consciousness (<s>cinmātra</s>), opposed to all distinctions — is alone the ultimate reality. And that [<s>Brahman</s>], though by nature eternally pure, awakened, and free, is known to be one with the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) through the co-referentiality [established by] statements such as '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' ('That thou art') and the like, and [yet] is bound and liberated. The entire manifold of diverse enjoyers, enjoyed, and the like, which is other than that [<s>Brahman</s>], is superimposed upon it through <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — on the authority of the collection of statements such as 'Being alone, O dear one, this was in the beginning, one only, without a second.' Those who speak thus,

children.text: mṛtyoḥ sa mṛtyum āpnoti ya iha nāneva paśyati/
children.translated_text: 'He who sees as if there is diversity here attains death after death' —

children.text:
iti bhedanindāśravaṇena pāramārthikaṃ bhedaṃ nirācakṣāṇā vicakṣaṇaṃmanyās tam imaṃ
          vibhāgaṃ na sahante/
children.translated_text: who, by hearing the censure of difference [in such passages], deny ultimate difference — those self-styled discerning ones do not tolerate this distinction [maintained by the <s>Viśiṣṭādvaitin</s>].

children.text:
tatrāyaṃ samādhir abhidhīyate/ bhaved etad evaṃ yady avidyāyāṃ pramāṇaṃ vidyeta/ nanv
          idam anādi bhāvarūpaṃ jñānanivartyam ajñānam aham ajño mām anyaṃ ca na jānāmīti
          pratyakṣapramāṇasiddham/ tad uktam:
children.translated_text: Therein, this resolution is stated. This would be so if there were a means of valid knowledge for <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). Objection: 'This beginningless, positive (<s>bhāvarūpa</s>), ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), removable by knowledge — "I am ignorant, I do not know myself or anything else" — is established by the direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) as a means of knowledge.' As stated:
'That which is beginningless, positive in nature, and dissolved by knowledge —

children.text: tad ajñānam iti prājñā lakṣaṇaṃ saṃpracakṣate// iti/
children.translated_text: that, the wise declare, is the definition of <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance).' Thus.

children.text:
na caitaj jñānābhāvaviṣayam ity āśaṅkanīyam/ ko hy evaṃ brūyāt prabhākarakarāvalambī
          bhaṭṭadattahasto vā/
children.translated_text: Nor should it be suspected that this [ignorance] pertains to the absence of knowledge. For who would say so — whether one following <s>Prabhākara</s> and supported by his hand, or one holding the hand of <s>Bhaṭṭa</s>'s tradition?
Not the first [<s>Prabhākara</s>] —
'Of a thing that by its own form and another's form is always of the nature of both existent and non-existent,

children.text: vastuni jñāyate kiṃcit kaiścid rūpaṃ kadācana/ /
children.translated_text: some form is known by some [knower] at some time.'

children.text: bhāvāntaram abhāvo hi kayācit tu vyapekṣayā/
children.translated_text: 'Absence is indeed another positive entity from a certain perspective;
absence that is other than a positive entity — no such [thing exists], because it cannot be characterized' —
thus, since [<s>Prabhākara</s>], by saying so, does not accept absence (<s>abhāva</s>) as distinct from positive entities.

children.text:
na dvitīyaḥ/ abhāvasya ṣaṣṭhapramāṇagocaratvena jñānasya nityānumeyatvena ca tadabhāvasya
          pratyakṣaviṣayatvānupapatteḥ/ yadi punaḥ pratyakṣābhāvavādī kaścid evam ācakṣīta taṃ
          pratyācakṣīta/ aham ajña ity asminn anubhave ’ham ity ātmano ’bhāvadharmitayā jñānasya
          pratiyogitayā cāvagatir asti na vā/ asti ced virodhād eva na jñānābhāvānubhavaḥ/ na ced
          dharmipratiyogijñānasāpekṣo jñānābhāvānubhavaḥ sutarāṃ na saṃbhavati/ tasyājñānasya
          bhāvarūpatve prāguktadūṣaṇābhāvād ayam anubhavo bhāvarūpājñānagocara evābhyupagantavya
          iti/
children.translated_text: Not the second [<s>Bhaṭṭa</s>] — because, since absence is the object of the sixth means of knowledge (<s>anupalabdhi</s>), and knowledge is always to be inferred, the absence of that [knowledge] cannot be the object of perception. But if some proponent of perception-as-absence were to state this, one should reply to him: In the experience 'I am ignorant,' is there or is there not an apprehension of the self as the substratum of absence and of knowledge as the counter-correlate? If there is, then, precisely because of the contradiction, there is no experience of the absence of knowledge. If there is not, then the experience of the absence of knowledge, being dependent on the knowledge of substratum and counter-correlate, is all the more impossible. Since there are no such objections when ignorance is of a positive nature (<s>bhāvarūpa</s>), this experience should be accepted as having positive ignorance as its object.

children.text:
tad etad gaganaromanthāyitam/ bhāvarūpasyājñānasya jñānābhāvena samānayogakṣematvāt/
          tathā hi: viṣayatvenāśrayatvena cājñānasya vyāvartakatayā pratyagarthaḥ pratipanno na vā/
          pratipannaś cet svarūpajñānanivartyaṃ tad ajñānam iti tasmin pratipanne kathaṃkāram
          avatiṣṭhate/ apratipannaś ced vyāvartakāśrayaviṣayaśūnyam ajñānaṃ katham anubhūyeta/ atha
          viśadaḥ svarūpāvabhāsa evājñānavirodhī nājñānena saha bhāsata ity āśrayaviṣayajñāne saty
          api nājñānānubhavavirodha iti hanta tarhi jñānābhāve ’pi samānam etad anyatrābhiniveśāt/
          tasmād ubhayābhyupagatajñānābhāva evāham ajño mām anyaṃ ca na jānāmīty anubhavagocara ity
          abhyupagantavyam/
children.translated_text: This is [mere] rumination on the sky! Because positive ignorance shares the same fate as the absence of knowledge. For consider: has the inner self (<s>pratyagātman</s>) been cognized as that which differentiates ignorance — as its object and substratum — or not? If cognized, then when that [self] is cognized, how can ignorance — which is removable by the knowledge of one's own nature — persist? If not cognized, how can ignorance — devoid of its differentiating substratum and object — be experienced? Now, if [it is argued that] it is precisely the vivid manifestation of one's own nature that is opposed to ignorance, and [therefore ignorance] does not manifest together with [self-knowledge] — then, even when the knowledge of substratum and object is present, there is no contradiction with the experience of ignorance — well then, the same holds good even for the absence of knowledge! Because of attachment to another [theory], there is the same [problem]. Therefore, what must be accepted is that the mutually acknowledged absence of knowledge alone is the object of the experience 'I am ignorant, I do not know myself or anything else.'

children.text:
astu tarhy anumānaṃ mānaṃ — vivādāspadaṃ pramāṇajñānaṃ
          svaprāgabhāvavyatiriktasvaviṣayāvaraṇasvanivartyasvadeśagatavastvantara-pūrvakam
          aprakāśitārthaprakāśakatvād andhakāre prathamotpannapradīpaprabhāvad iti/
children.translated_text: Objection: 'Let inference then be the means of valid knowledge [for establishing positive ignorance] — the subject of dispute: the cognition that is a means of knowledge presupposes a real entity other than its own prior-absence, located at its own locus, concealing its own object, and removable by itself — because it illuminates a previously unilluminated object — like the light of a lamp first produced in darkness.'

children.text:
tad api kṣodakṣamam/ ajñāne’ py anabhimatājñānāntarasādhane ’pasiddhāntāpātāt/
          tadasādhane ’naikāntikatvāt/ dṛṣṭāntasya sādhanavikalatvāc ca/ na hi pradīpaprabhāyā
          aprakāśitārthaprakāśakatvaṃ saṃbhavati/ jñānasyaiva prakāśakatvāt/ saty api pradīpe
          jñānena viṣayaprakāśasaṃbhavāt/ pradīpaprabhāyās tu cakṣurindriyasya jñānaṃ samutpādayato
          virodhisaṃtamasanirasanadvāreṇopakārakatvamātram evety alam ativistareṇa/
children.translated_text: That too is susceptible to refutation. Because, if [the inference is intended] to prove ignorance, but [actually] proves another unintended [kind of] ignorance, the fallacy of <s>apasiddhānta</s> (deviation from one's own doctrine) would arise. If it does not prove that [other ignorance], then the fallacy of <s>anaikāntikatva</s> (inconclusiveness) would arise. And because the example is deficient in the probans. For the light of a lamp cannot possibly illuminate a previously unilluminated object — because it is knowledge alone that illuminates. Even in the presence of a lamp, the illumination of an object is possible [only] through knowledge. The light of a lamp merely assists by removing the obstructing darkness for the eye-organ that produces knowledge — but enough of excessive elaboration!

children.text:
pratiprayogaś ca vivādādhyāsitam ajñānaṃ na jñānamātrabrahmāśritam ajñānatvāc
          chuktikādyajñānavad iti/ nanu śuktikādyajñānasyāśrayasya pratyagarthasya
          jñānamātrasvabhāvatvam eveti cen maivaṃ śaṅkiṣthāḥ/ anubhūtir hi svasadbhāvenaiva kasyacid
          vastuno vyavahārānuguṇatvāpādanasvabhāvo jñānāvagatisaṃvidādyaparanāmā sakarmako
          ’nubhavitur ātmano dharmaviśeṣaḥ/ anubhavitur ātmatvam ātmavṛttiguṇaviśeṣasya jñānatvam
          ity āśrayaṇāt/ nanu jñānarūpasyātmanaḥ kathaṃ jñānaguṇakatvam iti cet tad asāram/ yathā hi
          maṇidyumaṇiprabhṛti tejodravyaṃ prabhāvadrūpeṇāvatiṣṭhamānaṃ prabhārūpaguṇāśrayaḥ/
          svāśrayād anyatrāpi vartamānatvena rūpavattvena ca prabhā dravyarūpāpi
          taccheṣatvanibandhanaguṇavyavahārā/ evam ayam ātmā svaprakāśacidrūpa eva caitanyaguṇaḥ/
          tathā ca śrutiḥ: sa yathā saindhavaghano ’nantaro ’bāhyaḥ kṛtsno rasaghana evaivaṃ vā are
          ’yam ātmānantaro ’bāhyaḥ kṛtsnaḥ prajñānaghana eva/ atrāyaṃ puruṣaḥ svayaṃjyotir bhavati/
          na hi vijñātur vijñāter viparilopo vidyate atha yo vededaṃ jighrāṇīti sa ātmā yo ’yaṃ
          vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdy antarjyotiḥ puruṣaḥ/ eṣa hi draṣṭā spraṣṭā śrotā ghrātā rasayitā
          mantā boddhā kartā vijñānātmā puruṣaḥ ityādikā/
children.translated_text: And the counter-argument [is this]: the <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance) that is the subject of dispute does not reside in <s>Brahman</s> whose nature is mere knowledge — because it is ignorance — like the ignorance of nacre and the like. Objection: 'But the substratum of the ignorance of nacre and the like — the inner self — is indeed of the nature of mere knowledge!' Do not entertain such doubt! For <s>anubhūti</s> (experience) is a particular attribute of the self that is the experiencer — having the nature of rendering some entity amenable to practical activity by its own existence, [and] designated by the alternative names knowledge, cognition, awareness, and the like — [it is] transitive, [directed at an object]. The selfhood of the experiencer [is one thing], and the knowledge-hood of the quality (<s>guṇa</s>) residing in the self [is another] — because of the distinction [between substance and attribute]. Objection: 'But how can the self, whose nature is knowledge, have knowledge as a quality?' That is groundless. For just as a gem, a luminous jewel, and the like — being luminous substances that exist in the form of radiance — are nonetheless the substrata of the quality of radiance; since radiance, by existing even elsewhere than its own substratum and by possessing color, though of the nature of a substance, is conventionally treated as a quality due to its being subordinate to that [substance] — so too this self, though of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, has consciousness (<s>caitanya</s>) as a quality. And thus the <s>Śruti</s> (Vedic revelation): 'Just as a lump of salt — without interior, without exterior — is entirely a mass of taste, so too this self — without interior, without exterior — is entirely a mass of consciousness.' 'Herein, this <s>Puruṣa</s> (person) is self-luminous.' 'For there is no cessation of the knowing of the knower.' 'And he who knows "I shall smell this" — that is the self; that which is this <s>Puruṣa</s> made of <s>vijñāna</s> (knowledge), the inner light among the vital breaths.' 'He is the seer, toucher, hearer, smeller, taster, thinker, knower, doer — the <s>Puruṣa</s> whose self is <s>vijñāna</s> (knowledge)' — and so forth.

children.text:
na ca anṛtena hi pratyūḍhāḥ iti śrutir avidyāyāṃ pramāṇam ity āśrayituṃ śakyam/
          ṛtetaraviṣayo hy anṛtaśabdaḥ/ ṛtaśabdaś ca karmavacanaḥ/ ṛtaṃ pibantau iti vacanāt/ ṛtaṃ
          karma phalābhisaṃdhirahitaṃ paramapuruṣārādhanaveṣaṃ tatprāptiphalam/ atra tadvyatiriktaṃ
          sāṃsārikālpaphalaṃ karmānṛtaṃ brahmaprāptivirodhi/ ya etaṃ brahmalokaṃ na vindanti anṛtena
          hi pratyūḍhāḥ iti vacanāt/ māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyāt ityādau māyāśabdo
          vicitrārthasargakaratriguṇātmakaprakṛtyabhidhāyako nānirvacanīyājñānavacanaḥ/
children.translated_text: Nor can it be relied upon that the <s>Śruti</s> 'For they are obstructed by the unreal (<s>anṛta</s>)' is a means of knowledge for <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance). For the word '<s>anṛta</s>' has as its scope that which is other than <s>ṛta</s>. And the word '<s>ṛta</s>' denotes action (<s>karma</s>) — from the statement '<s>ṛtaṃ pibantau</s>' ('the two who drink <s>ṛta</s>'). <s>Ṛta</s> is action (<s>karma</s>) that is free from desire for results, having the form of worship of the Supreme Person (<s>paramapuruṣa</s>), and bearing the fruit of attaining Him. Here, what is other than that — the worldly action of meager fruit — is <s>anṛta</s>, opposed to the attainment of <s>Brahman</s> — from the statement 'Those who do not find this world of <s>Brahman</s> — for they are obstructed by the unreal.' And in [the passage] 'Know <s>māyā</s> to be <s>prakṛti</s>' and the like, the word '<s>māyā</s>' designates <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), which is constituted by the three <s>guṇas</s> and capable of producing a variegated creation — it does not denote the indeterminable (<s>anirvacanīya</s>) ignorance [of the Advaitin].
'The thousand <s>māyās</s> (magical weapons) of <s>Śambara</s>, the swift one,
were destroyed one by one by [<s>Indra</s>] who protected the body of the child (<s>bāla</s>).'

children.text:
ityādau vicitrārthasargasamarthasya pāramārthikasyaivāsurādyastraviśeṣasyaiva
          māyāśabdābhidheyatvopalambhāt/ ato na kadācid api śrutyā
          anirvacanīyājñānapratipādanam/
children.translated_text: In [passages] such as these, since it is observed that the word '<s>māyā</s>' denotes a real, supreme magical weapon of the <s>Asuras</s> and the like — one that is capable of producing a variegated creation — therefore, never is indeterminable ignorance taught by the <s>Śruti</s>.

children.text:
nāpy aikyopadeśānyathānupapattyā/ tattvaṃpadayoḥ saviśeṣabrahmābhidhāyitvena niruddhayor
          jīvaparayoḥ svarūpaikyasya pratipattum aśakyatayārthāpatter anudayadoṣadūṣitatvāt/ tathā
          hi: tatpadaṃ nirastasamastadoṣam anavadhikātiśayāsaṃkhyeyakalyāṇaguṇāspadaṃ
          jagadudayavibhavalayalīlaṃ brahma pratipādayati/ tad aikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya ityādiṣu
          tasyaiva prakṛtatvāt/ tatsamānādhikaraṇaṃ tvaṃpadaṃ ca

children.translated_text: denotes <s>Brahman</s> as having the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) qualified by consciousness as its body. Because co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) has the purport of [denoting] a single entity qualified by two modes.

Nor [is it established] through the impossibility of explaining [things] otherwise by means of the identity-statements. Because, since the words '<s>tat</s>' (That) and '<s>tvam</s>' (thou) are denotative of <s>Brahman</s> qualified by attributes, the <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) [by which one would arrive at] the essential identity of <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) and <s>para</s> (Supreme) — which are [thereby] precluded [from denoting a qualityless Brahman] — is vitiated by the fault of non-arising, since [such identity] cannot be apprehended. For, the word '<s>tat</s>' denotes <s>Brahman</s>, which is free from all defects, the abode of innumerable auspicious qualities of unsurpassable excellence, and whose sport is the origination, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe — because that very [<s>Brahman</s>] is the subject in passages such as '<s>tad aikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya</s>' ('It willed: may I become many, may I be born') and the like. And the word '<s>tvam</s>' (thou), being co-referential with '<s>tat</s>',

children.text:
nanu so ’yaṃ devadatta itivat tat tvam iti padayor viruddhabhāgatyāgalakṣaṇayā
          nirviśeṣasvarūpam ātmaikyaṃ sāmānādhikaraṇyārthaḥ kiṃ na syāt/ yathā so ’yam ity atra
          tacchabdena deśāntarakālāntarasaṃbandhī puruṣaḥ pratīyate/ idaṃśabdena ca
          saṃnihitadeśavartamānakālasaṃbandhī/ tayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyenaikyam avagamyate/ tatraikasya
          yugapad viruddhadeśakālapratītir na saṃbhavatīti dvayor api padayoḥ svarūpaparatve
          svarūpasya caikyaṃ pratipattuṃ śakyam/ evam atrāpi
          kiṃcijjñatvasarvajñatvādiviruddhāṃśaprahāṇenākhaṇḍasvarūpaṃ lakṣyata iti cet
children.translated_text: (Objection:) Just as in '<s>so 'yaṃ Devadattaḥ</s>' ('This is that <s>Devadatta</s>'), could not the co-referential meaning of the words '<s>tat</s>' and '<s>tvam</s>' be the identity of the self in its unqualified essential nature, through <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) by the abandonment of contradictory aspects? Just as in 'this is that [<s>Devadatta</s>],' the word '<s>tat</s>' (that) gives rise to the apprehension of a person connected with another place and another time, and the word '<s>idam</s>' (this) [gives rise to the apprehension of one] connected with the proximate place and the present time — through their co-reference, identity is understood. Therein, since the apprehension of contradictory place and time for one [person] simultaneously is impossible, when both words have the essential nature as their referent, the identity of the essential nature can be apprehended. Likewise here too, if [one says that] through the abandonment of contradictory aspects such as limited knowledge and omniscience, the undivided essential nature is indicated —

children.text:
viṣamo ’yam upanyāsaḥ/ dṛṣṭānte ’pi virodhavaidhuryeṇa lakṣaṇāgandhāsaṃbhavāt/ ekasya
          tāvad bhūtavartamānakāladvayasaṃbandho na viruddhaḥ/ deśāntarastitir bhūtā
          saṃnihitadeśasthitir vartata iti deśabhedasaṃbandhavirodhaś ca kālabhedena pariharaṇīyaḥ/
          lakṣaṇāpakṣe ’py ekasyaiva padasya lakṣakatvāśrayaṇena virodhaparihāre padadvayasya
          lākṣaṇikatvasvīkāro na saṃgacchate/ itarathaikasya vastunas tattedaṃtāviśiṣṭatvāvagāhanena
          pratyabhijñāyāḥ prāmāṇyānaṅgīkāre sthāyitvāsiddhau kṣaṇabhaṅgavādī bauddho vijayeta/ evam
          atrāpi jīvaparamātmanoḥ śarīrātmabhāvena tādātmyaṃ na viruddham iti pratipāditam/ jīvātmā
          hi brahmaṇaḥ śarīratayā prakāratvād brahmātmakaḥ/ ya ātmani tiṣṭhann ātmano ’ntaro yam
          ātmā na veda yasyātmā śarīram iti śrutyantarāt/
children.translated_text: (Reply:) This analogy is inappropriate. Because even in the illustration, secondary signification (<s>lakṣaṇā</s>) cannot apply at all, since [there is] no real contradiction to be circumvented. For a single [person], connection with two times — past and present — is not contradictory. And the contradiction of connection with different places must be resolved through the difference of times: 'his stay in another place was past; his stay in the proximate place is present.' Even on the view of secondary signification, when one resorts to the secondary signifying function of a single word to resolve the contradiction, the acceptance that both words are secondary is not coherent. Otherwise, if one does not accept the validity of recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) — which apprehends a single entity as qualified by 'that-ness' and 'this-ness' — then, since the permanence [of the subject] would be unestablished, the Buddhist advocate of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅgavādī</s>) would triumph. Likewise here too, it has been demonstrated that the identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) of the <s>jīva</s> and <s>Paramātman</s> through the body-soul relationship is not contradictory. For the <s>jīvātman</s>, being a mode (<s>prakāra</s>) of <s>Brahman</s> by virtue of being its body, is of the nature of <s>Brahman</s>. As stated in another <s>śruti</s>: 'He who dwells in the <s>ātman</s>, who is within the <s>ātman</s>, whom the <s>ātman</s> does not know, whose body is the <s>ātman</s>.'

children.text:
atyalpam idam ucyate/ sarve śabdāḥ paramātmana eva vācakāḥ/ na ca paryāyatvam/
          dvārabhedasaṃbhavāt/ tathā hi jīvasya śarīratayā prakārabhūtāni devamanuṣyādisaṃsthānānīva
          sarvāṇi vastūnīti brahmātmakāni tāni sarvāṇi/ ataḥ
children.translated_text: What has been said is too little. All words are denotative of the <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self) alone. And there is no synonymy, because of the possibility of different modes of access (<s>dvāra</s>). For, just as the configurations such as god, human being, and so on — which are modes (<s>prakāra</s>) by virtue of being the body of the <s>jīva</s> — so too all entities are of the nature of <s>Brahman</s> by virtue of being its body. Therefore:
A god, a human being, a <s>yakṣa</s>, a <s>piśāca</s>, a serpent, a <s>rākṣasa</s>,

children.text: pakṣī vṛkṣo latā kāṣṭhaṃ śilā tṛṇaṃ ghaṭaḥ pataḥ//
children.translated_text: a bird, a tree, a creeper, a piece of wood, a stone, a blade of grass, a pot, a cloth —

children.text:
ityādayaḥ sarve śabdāḥ prakṛtipratyayayogenābhidhāyakatayā prasiddhā loke tadvācyatayā
          pratīyamānatattatsaṃsthānavadvastumukhena
          tadabhimānijīvatadantaryāmiparamātmaparyantasaṃghātasya vācakāḥ/ devādiśabdānāṃ
          paramātmaparyantatvam uktaṃ tattvamuktāvalyāṃ caturthasare:
children.translated_text: all such words, known in the world as denotative through the combination of root and suffix, denote — by means of the entity possessing the particular configuration that is understood as their referent — the aggregate extending up to the <s>jīva</s> who identifies with it and the <s>Paramātman</s> who is the inner controller of that [<s>jīva</s>]. That the words such as '<s>deva</s>' etc. extend up to the <s>Paramātman</s> has been stated in the <s>Tattvamuktāvalī</s>, in the fourth chapter:
The word '<s>deva</s>' etc. denotes the <s>jīva</s> because of denoting what is inseparably established from it (<s>apṛthaksiddhabhāva</s>);
and the usage in common life and <s>Veda</s> to this effect is abundant and firm here.
this is free from the need for extraction (<s>niṣkarṣa</s>),
The subsistence of the configuration of god, mortal, etc. in the absence of connection with the <s>ātman</s> is not observed;

children.text: jīvātmānupraveśāj jagati vibhur api vyākaron nāmarūpe// iti/
children.translated_text: because of the entry of the <s>jīvātman</s> into the world, the all-pervading one [<s>Brahman</s>] also differentiated name and form. Thus.

children.text:
anena devādiśabdānāṃ śarīraviśiṣṭajīvaparyantatvaṃ pratipādya saṃsthānaikyādyabhāve
          ityādinā śarīralakṣaṇaṃ darśayitvā śabdais tanvaṃśarūpaprabhṛtibhiḥ ityādinā
          viśvasyeśvarād apṛthaksiddhatvam upapādya niṣkarṣākūta ityādinā padyena sarveṣāṃ śabdānāṃ
          paramātmaparyantatvaṃ pratipāditaṃ tat sarvaṃ tata evāvadhāryam/ ayam evārthaḥ samarthito
          vedārthasaṃgrahe nāmarūpaśrutivyākaraṇasamaye rāmānujena/
children.translated_text: By this [verse], having established that the words such as '<s>deva</s>' etc. extend up to the <s>jīva</s> qualified by the body, and having shown the definition of body by [the words] beginning with 'in the absence of identity of configuration' etc., and having demonstrated the inseparability (<s>apṛthaksiddhatva</s>) of the universe from <s>Īśvara</s> by [the words] beginning with 'by the words such as body, form, luster, etc.,' and having established the extension of all words up to the <s>Paramātman</s> by [another] verse beginning with 'the intention of extraction' — all that should be ascertained from that very [text]. This same meaning has been established by <s>Rāmānuja</s> in the <s>Vedārthasaṃgraha</s>, in the section on the explanation of the <s>nāmarūpa-śruti</s> (scripture on name and form).

children.text:
kiṃ ca sarvapramāṇasya saviśeṣaviṣayatayā nirviśeṣavastuni na kim api pramāṇaṃ samasti/
          nirvikalpakapratyakṣe ’pi saviśeṣam eva vastu pratīyate/ anyathā savikalpake so ’yam iti
          pūrvapratipannaprakāraviśiṣṭapratītyanupapatteḥ/
children.translated_text: Moreover, since all means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>) have as their object [entities] qualified by attributes, there is no <s>pramāṇa</s> whatsoever for an attributeless (<s>nirviśeṣa</s>) reality. Even in non-conceptual perception (<s>nirvikalpaka pratyakṣa</s>), it is only a reality qualified by attributes that is apprehended. Otherwise, the re-cognition in determinate perception (<s>savikalpaka</s>) — 'this is that same [thing]' — which has as its content the [object] qualified by the mode previously apprehended, would be inexplicable.

children.text:
kiṃ ca tattvamasyādivākyaṃ na prapañcasya bādhakam/ bhrāntimūlakatvāt
          bhrāntiprayuktarajjusarpavākyavat/ nāpi brahmātmaikyajñānaṃ nivartakam/ tatra
          pramāṇābhāvasya prāg evopapādanāt/ na ca prapañcasya satyatvapratiṣṭhāpanapakṣa
          ekavijñānena sarvavijñānapratijñāvyākopaḥ/
          prakṛtipuruṣamahadahaṃkāratanmātrabhūtendriyacaturdaśabhuvanātmaka-brahmāṇḍatadantarvartidevatiryaṅmanuṣyasthāvarādisarvaprakārasaṃsthāna-saṃsthitaṃ
          kāryam api sarvaṃ brahmaiveti kāraṇabhūtabrahmātmajñānād

eva sarvavijñānaṃ bhavatīty ekavijñānena sarvavijñānasyopapannataratvāt/ api ca
          brahmavyatiriktasya sarvasya mithyātve sarvasyāsattvād evaikavijñānena
          sarvavijñānapratijñā bādhyeta/ nāmarūpavibhāgānarhasūkṣmadaśāvat prakṛtipuruṣaśarīraṃ
          brahma kāraṇāvastham/ jagatas tadāpattir eva pralayaḥ/
          nāmarūpavibhāgavibhaktasthūlacidacidvastuśarīraṃ brahma kāryāvastham/ brahmaṇas
          tathāvidhasthūlabhāvaś ca sṛṣṭir ity abhidhīyate evaṃ ca kāryakāraṇayor ananyatvam apy
          ārambhaṇādhikaraṇe pratipāditam upapannataraṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: the knowledge of everything arises — thus, through the knowledge of one, the knowledge of everything is well-established. Moreover, if everything other than <s>Brahman</s> were false, then precisely because of the non-existence of everything, the promise 'by knowing one thing, everything is known' would be contradicted. <s>Brahman</s> in its causal state has <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> as its body in a subtle condition not amenable to the differentiation of name and form. The reabsorption (<s>pralaya</s>) of the world is precisely its return to that [state]. <s>Brahman</s> in its effectual state has as its body the gross conscious and non-conscious entities differentiated by the differentiation of name and form. And the transformation of <s>Brahman</s> into such a gross condition is called creation (<s>sṛṣṭi</s>). And thus, the non-difference of cause and effect, which was demonstrated in the <s>Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa</s> (the section beginning with the topic of origination), is well-established.

Moreover, the sentence '<s>tat tvam asi</s>' ('That thou art') and the like does not sublate the phenomenal world. Because it [i.e., the sublation of the world] would be rooted in delusion, like the statement about a rope-snake based on error. Nor is the knowledge of the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>ātman</s> the remover [of the world], because the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> for that [identity-knowledge as a remover] has already been demonstrated above. Nor, on the position that establishes the reality of the phenomenal world, is there any contradiction with the promise 'by knowing one thing, everything is known.' Because the effect — which is constituted by the cosmic egg (<s>brahmāṇḍa</s>) composed of <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), <s>Puruṣa</s> (soul), <s>Mahat</s> (the Great Principle), <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> (ego), <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements), elements, sense-organs, and the fourteen worlds, together with all types of configurations within it — gods, animals, humans, immovable beings, etc. — all this too is nothing but <s>Brahman</s>; therefore, from the knowledge of the self that is <s>Brahman</s>, which is the cause,

children.text:
nirguṇavādāś ca prākṛtaheyaguṇaniṣedhaviṣayatayā vyavasthitāḥ/ nānātvaniṣedhavādāś
          caikasyaiva brahmaṇaḥ śarīratayā prakārabhūtaṃ sarvaṃ cetanācetanātmakaṃ vastv iti
          sarvasyātmatayā sarvaprakāraṃ brahmaivāvasthitam iti
          sarvātmakabrahmapṛthagbhūtavastusadbhāvaniṣedhaparatvābhyupagamena pratipāditāḥ/
children.translated_text: And the passages asserting the absence of qualities (<s>nirguṇavāda</s>) are explained as having their purport in the negation of base, reprehensible qualities. And the passages negating plurality (<s>nānātvaniṣedha</s>) are explained by accepting [their purport] as the negation of the existence of any entity separate from <s>Brahman</s>, which, as the self of all, is <s>Brahman</s> alone abiding in all modes — since all conscious and non-conscious reality, being a mode (<s>prakāra</s>) of the one <s>Brahman</s> by virtue of being its body, [means that] <s>Brahman</s> as the self of all abides as all modes.

children.text:
kim atra tattvaṃ bhedo ’bheda ubhayātmakaṃ vā/ sarvaṃ tattvam/ tatra sarvaśarīratayā
          sarvaprakāraṃ brahmaivāvasthitam ity abhedo ’bhyupeyate/ ekam eva brahma
          nānābhūtacidacitprakārān nānātvenāvasthitam iti bhedābhedau/ cidacidīśvarāṇāṃ
          svarūpasvabhāvavailakṣaṇyād asaṃkarāc ca bhedaḥ/ tatra cidrūpāṇāṃ jīvātmanām
          asaṃkucitāparicchinnanirmalajñānarūpāṇām anādikarmarūpāvidyāveṣṭitānāṃ
          tattatkarmānurūpajñānasaṃkocavikāsau bhogyabhūtācitsaṃsargas
          tadanuguṇasukhaduḥkhopabhogadvayarūpā bhoktṛtā bhagavatpratipattir bhagavatpadaprāptir
          ityādayaḥ svabhāvāḥ/ acidvastūnāṃ tu bhogyabhūtānām acetanatvam apuruṣārthatvaṃ
          vikārāspadatvam ityādayaḥ/ parasyeśvarasya bhoktṛbhogyayor antaryāmirūpeṇāvasthānam
          aparicchedyajñānaiśvaryavīryaśaktitejaḥprabhṛtyanavadhikātiśayāsaṃkhyeya-kalyāṇaguṇagaṇatā
          svasaṃkalpapravṛttasvetarasamastacidacidvastujātatā
          svābhimatasvānurūpaikarūpadivyarūpaniratiśayavividhānantabhūṣaṇa-tetyādayaḥ/
children.translated_text: What is the ultimate truth here — difference, non-difference, or a combination of both? Everything is the truth. Therein, since <s>Brahman</s> alone abides as all modes through being the body of all, non-difference is accepted. One and the same <s>Brahman</s> abides as many, having as its modes the diverse conscious and non-conscious [entities] — thus both difference and non-difference [are maintained]. Because of the distinctness of the essential nature and attributes of the conscious (<s>cit</s>), the non-conscious (<s>acit</s>), and <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), and because of their non-confusion, [there is] difference. Therein, the attributes of the <s>jīvātmans</s> (individual souls), who are denoted by the word '<s>cit</s>' (consciousness), who are distinct from the <s>Paramātman</s> and eternal, whose nature is consciousness — uncontracted, unlimited, and pure — but who are enveloped by beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) in the form of <s>karma</s>: the contraction and expansion of knowledge in accordance with their respective <s>karmas</s>, contact with non-conscious [matter] that is the object of enjoyment, the status of being an enjoyer (<s>bhoktṛtā</s>) in the form of the two [experiences] — happiness and suffering — corresponding to that [contact], devotion to the Lord (<s>bhagavatpratipatti</s>), attainment of the Lord's abode (<s>bhagavatpadaprāpti</s>), and the like. The attributes of non-conscious entities (<s>acit</s>), which are the objects of enjoyment: unconsciousness, the nature of not being a human goal in themselves, being the locus of transformation, and the like. Of the Supreme <s>Īśvara</s>: abiding in the form of the inner controller (<s>antaryāmin</s>) of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the host of innumerable auspicious qualities of unsurpassable excellence beginning with knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, radiance, and the like, being the source of all conscious and non-conscious entities that proceed by His own will, and having a divine form that is singular, of a nature conforming to and desired by Himself, of unsurpassable and manifold infinite ornamentation — and so forth.
But <s>Veṅkaṭanātha</s> has set forth the classification of categories thus without ambiguity:

children.text: dravyādravyaprabhedān mitam ubhayavidhaṃ tadvidas tattvam āhuḥ
children.translated_text: Those who know it declare that reality (<s>tattva</s>) is of two kinds, measured by the division into substance (<s>dravya</s>) and non-substance (<s>adravya</s>).

children.text: dravyaṃ dvedhā vibhaktaṃ jaḍam ajaḍam iti prācyam avyaktakālau/
children.translated_text: <s>Dravya</s> (substance) is divided into two: non-conscious (<s>jaḍa</s>) and conscious (<s>ajaḍa</s>). The former [includes] the Unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>) and Time (<s>kāla</s>).

children.text: antyaṃ pratyak parāk ca prathamam ubhayathā tatra jīveśabhedāt
children.translated_text: The latter [is divided] into the inner (<s>pratyak</s>) and the outer (<s>parāk</s>); the first [inner] is of two kinds, by the distinction of <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) and <s>Īśa</s> (Lord).

children.text: nityā bhūtir matiś cety aparam iha jaḍām ādimāṃ kecid āhuḥ//
children.translated_text: Eternal glory (<s>nityā bhūti</s>) and knowledge (<s>mati</s>) [are also substances] — thus some call the first [i.e., the non-conscious] also as non-conscious (<s>jaḍa</s>).

children.text: tatra dravyaṃ daśāvat prakṛtir iha guṇaiḥ sattvapūrvair upetā
children.translated_text: Therein, substance has [various] states: <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) here is endowed with the <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) beginning with <s>sattva</s>.

children.text: kālo 'bdādyākṛtiḥ syād aṇur avagatimāñ jīva īśo ’nya ātmā/
children.translated_text: Time (<s>kāla</s>) would have the form of years and the like; the atom (<s>aṇu</s>) possessing cognition is the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul); the other self (<s>ātmā</s>) is <s>Īśa</s> (the Lord).
Eternal glory (<s>nityabhūti</s>) is declared to be beyond the three <s>guṇas</s>, endowed with <s>sattva</s>; likewise,

children.text: jñātur jñeyāvabhāso matir iti kathitaṃ saṃgrahād dravyalakṣma//
children.translated_text: knowledge (<s>mati</s>) is said to be the manifestation of the knowable to the knower — thus the definition of substance has been stated in summary.
And so on.

children.text:
tatra cicchabdavācyā jīvātmānaḥ paramātmanaḥ sakāśād bhinnā nityāś ca/ tathā ca śrutiḥ:
          dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā ityādikā/ ata evoktaṃ nānātmāno vyavasthātaḥ iti/ tannityatvam
          api śrutiprasiddham/
children.translated_text: Therein, the <s>jīvātmans</s> (individual souls), denoted by the word '<s>cit</s>' (consciousness), are distinct from the <s>Paramātman</s> (Supreme Self) and eternal. And thus the <s>śruti</s>: '<s>dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā</s>' ('Two birds, companions, always united') and the like. Hence it was said: '<s>nānātmāno vyavasthātaḥ</s>' ('The selves are many, from [their] distinct establishment'). Their eternality too is well-known from <s>śruti</s>:

children.text: na jāyate mriyate vā vipaścin nāyaṃ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ/
children.translated_text: He is not born, nor does he die, this wise one; he did not come into being, nor will he come to be again.

children.text: ajo nityaḥ śāśvato ’yaṃ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre// iti
children.translated_text: Unborn, eternal, everlasting, primeval — he is not slain when the body is slain. Thus.

children.text:
aparathā kṛtapraṇāśākṛtābhyāgamaprasaṅgaḥ/ ata evoktaṃ vītarāgajanmādarśanāt iti/
          tadaṇutvam api śrutiprasiddham:
children.translated_text: Otherwise, the absurd consequence of the destruction of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done [would follow]. Hence it was said: '<s>vītarāgajanmādarśanāt</s>' ('Because the birth of one free from attachment is observed'). Their atomic nature (<s>aṇutva</s>) too is well-known from <s>śruti</s>:
Of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, again imagined as hundredfold —

children.text: bhāgo jīvaḥ sa vijñeyaḥ sa cānantyāya kalpate//
children.translated_text: that is to be known as the <s>jīva</s> (individual soul), and it is fit for infinity.

children.text: iti/ ārāgramātraḥ puruṣaḥ aṇur ātmā cetasā veditavyaḥ iti ca/
children.translated_text: Thus. 'The <s>Puruṣa</s> (soul) is of the measure of a thumb-tip.' 'The atomic <s>ātman</s> is to be known by the mind.' Thus.

children.text: acicchabdavācyaṃ dṛśyaṃ jaḍaṃ jagat trividhaṃ bhogyabhogopakaraṇabhogāyatanabhedāt/
children.translated_text: The visible, non-conscious (<s>jaḍa</s>) world, denoted by the word '<s>acit</s>' (non-consciousness), is threefold: by the distinction of the object of enjoyment (<s>bhogya</s>), the instrument of enjoyment (<s>bhogopakaraṇa</s>), and the locus of enjoyment (<s>bhogāyatana</s>).

children.text:
tasya jagataḥ kartopādānaṃ ceśvarapadārthaḥ puruṣottamo vāsudevādipadavedanīyaḥ/ tad apy
          uktam:
children.translated_text: Of that world, <s>Puruṣottama</s> (the Supreme Person), who is the category denoted by the word '<s>Īśvara</s>' (Lord), knowable by the words '<s>Vāsudeva</s>' and the like, is both the efficient cause (<s>kartṛ</s>) and the material cause (<s>upādāna</s>). As stated:
<s>Vāsudeva</s> is the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>, endowed with auspicious qualities,
the material cause of the worlds, the creator, and the controller of souls. Thus.

children.text:
sa eva vāsudevaḥ paramakāruṇiko bhaktavatsalaḥ paramapuruṣas
          tadupāsakānuguṇatattatphalapradānāya svalīlāvaśād arcāvibhavavyūhasūkṣmāntaryāmibhedena
          pañcadhāvatiṣṭhate/ tatrārcā nāma pratimādayaḥ/ rāmādyavatāro vibhavaḥ/ vyūhaś caturvidho
          vāsudevasaṃkarṣaṇapradyumnātiruddhasaṃjñakaḥ/ sūkṣmaṃ saṃpūrṇaṣaḍguṇaṃ vāsudevākhyaṃ paraṃ
          brahma/ guṇā apahatapāpmatvādayaḥ/ so 'pahatapāpmā vijaro vimṛtyur viśoko vijighatso
          ’pipāsaḥ satyakāmaḥ satyasaṃkalpaḥ iti śruteḥ/ antaryāmī sakalajīvaniyāmakaḥ/ ya ātmani
          tiṣṭhann ātmānam antaro yamayati iti śruteḥ/
children.translated_text: That very <s>Vāsudeva</s>, supremely compassionate, affectionate toward his devotees, the Supreme Person (<s>Puruṣottama</s>), for the purpose of granting appropriate fruits to his worshippers, through his own play (<s>līlā</s>), abides in fivefold form: as <s>arcā</s> (image), <s>vibhava</s> (incarnation), <s>vyūha</s> (emanation), <s>sūkṣma</s> (subtle), and <s>antaryāmin</s> (inner controller). Therein, <s>arcā</s> refers to images (<s>pratimā</s>) and the like. <s>Vibhava</s> is the incarnation such as <s>Rāma</s> and others. <s>Vyūha</s> is fourfold, designated as <s>Vāsudeva</s>, <s>Saṃkarṣaṇa</s>, <s>Pradyumna</s>, and <s>Aniruddha</s>. <s>Sūkṣma</s> is the Supreme <s>Brahman</s> called <s>Vāsudeva</s>, possessing the complete six qualities. The qualities are: being free from evil, and so forth. From the <s>śruti</s>: "He is free from evil, free from old age, free from death, free from sorrow, free from hunger, free from thirst; his desires are true, his resolves are true." The <s>antaryāmin</s> is the controller of all souls. From the <s>śruti</s>: "He who, dwelling in the Self, controls the Self from within."
Section 4.244

children.text:
tatra pūrvapūrvamūrtyupāsanayā puruṣārthaparipanthiduritanicayakṣaye saty
          uttarottaramūrtyupāstyadhikāraḥ/ tad uktam:
children.translated_text: Therein, through the worship of each successive prior form, when the accumulation of sins that obstruct the supreme goal has been destroyed, one becomes qualified for the worship of each successive later form. As stated:
"<s>Vāsudeva</s>, out of affection for his devotees, grants abundant fruit
corresponding to their respective desires, in accordance with [their] qualification.

children.text: tadarthaṃ līlayā svīyāḥ pañca mūrtīḥ karoti vai/
children.translated_text: For that purpose, through his play, he indeed creates his own five forms.

children.text: pratimādikam arcā syād avatārās tu vaibhavāḥ//
children.translated_text: Images and the like constitute the <s>arcā</s>; incarnations are the <s>vibhavas</s>.
<s>Saṃkarṣaṇa</s>, <s>Vāsudeva</s>, <s>Pradyumna</s>, and <s>Aniruddha</s> —
the fourfold <s>vyūha</s> should be known. The <s>sūkṣma</s> possesses the complete six qualities.

children.text: tad eva vāsudevākhyaṃ paraṃ brahma nigadyate/
children.translated_text: That very one, called <s>Vāsudeva</s>, is declared to be the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>.
The <s>antaryāmin</s>, dwelling within the <s>jīva</s> (soul), is said to be the impeller of the <s>jīva</s>,
described by the web of Vedāntic statements beginning with 'He who [dwells] in the Self.'
When sins have been dispelled through the worship of the <s>arcā</s>, one becomes qualified
for the worship of the <s>vibhava</s>; after that, for the worship of the <s>vyūha</s>; then beyond that,

children.text: sūkṣme tadanu śaktaḥ syād antaryāmiṇam īkṣitum// iti/
children.translated_text: one becomes capable of the <s>sūkṣma</s>, and thereafter of beholding the <s>antaryāmin</s>."
Section 4.258

children.text:
tadupāsanaṃ ca pañcavidham abhigamanam upādānam ijyā svādhyāyo yoga iti śrīpañcarātre
          ’bhihitam/ tatrābhigamanaṃ nāma devatāsthānamārgasya saṃmārjanopalepanādi/ upādānaṃ
          gandhapuṣpādipūjāsādhanasaṃpādanam/ ijyā nāma devatāpūjanam/ svādhyāyo nāma
          arthānusaṃdhānapūrvako mantrajapo vaiṣṇavasūktastotrapāṭho nāmasaṃkīrtanaṃ
          tattvapratipādakaśāstrābhyāsaś ca/ yogo nāma devatānusaṃdhānam/
children.translated_text: And that worship is fivefold, as stated in the glorious <s>Pañcarātra</s>: approaching (<s>abhigamana</s>), gathering [of materials] (<s>upādāna</s>), offering (<s>ijyā</s>), self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>), and meditation (<s>yoga</s>). Therein, approaching (<s>abhigamana</s>) means sweeping, plastering, and the like of the path to the deity's abode. Gathering (<s>upādāna</s>) is the procuring of worship materials such as sandal paste, flowers, and the like. Offering (<s>ijyā</s>) means the worship of the deity. Self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>) means the recitation of <s>mantras</s> preceded by reflection on their meaning, the recitation of <s>Vaiṣṇava</s> hymns and praises, the chanting of divine names, and the study of scriptures that expound the truth. Meditation (<s>yoga</s>) means contemplation of the deity.
Section 4.264

children.text:
evam upāsanākarmasamuccitena vijñānena draṣṭṛdarśane naṣṭe bhagavadbhaktasya tanniṣṭhasya
          bhaktavatsalaḥ paramakāruṇikaḥ puruṣottamaḥ svayāthātmyānubhavānugūṇaniravadhikānandarūpaṃ
          punarāvṛttirahitaṃ svapadaṃ prayacchati/ tathā ca smṛtiḥ:
children.translated_text: Thus, through knowledge combined with the practice of worship, when the distinction between seer and seen has been dissolved, to his devotee who is thus established, the Supreme Person (<s>Puruṣottama</s>), affectionate toward devotees, supremely compassionate, grants his own abode — which has the form of limitless bliss corresponding to the experience of his true nature, and which is free from return [to <s>saṃsāra</s>]. And thus the <s>smṛti</s> (remembered scripture):
"Having attained Me, the great souls who have reached supreme perfection

children.text: nāpnuvanti mahātmānaḥ saṃsiddhiṃ paramāṃ gatāḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: do not again take birth, which is the abode of suffering and impermanent."
"<s>Vāsudeva</s> too, having received his devotee, grants imperishable bliss

children.text: punarāvṛttirahitaṃ svīyaṃ dhāma prayacchati// iti ca/
children.translated_text: and his own abode, free from return."

children.text:
tad etat sarvaṃ hṛdi nidhāya mahopaniṣanmatāvalambanena bhagavadbaudhāyanācāryakṛtāṃ
          brahmasūtravṛttiṃ vistīrṇām ālakṣya rāmānujaḥ śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣyam akārṣīt/ tatrāthāto
          brahmajijñāsā iti prathamasūtrasyāyam arthaḥ:
children.translated_text: Keeping all this in his heart, relying upon the views of the great <s>Upaniṣads</s>, and having surveyed the extensive commentary on the <s>Brahmasūtras</s> composed by the venerable teacher <s>Bodhāyana</s>, <s>Rāmānuja</s> composed the commentary on the <s>Śārīrakamīmāṃsā</s> (embodied inquiry). Therein, the meaning of the first <s>sūtra</s>, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>," is as follows:

children.text:
atrāthaśabdaḥ pūrvavṛttakarmādhigamanānantaryārthaḥ/ tad uktaṃ vṛttikāreṇa: vṛttāt
          karmādhigamād anantaraṃ brahma vividiṣatīti/ ataḥśabdo hetvarthaḥ/
          adhītasāṅgavedasyādhigatatadarthasya vinaśvaraphalāt karmaṇo viraktatvād dhetoḥ
          sthiramokṣābhilāṣukasya tadupāyabhūtabrahmajijñāsā bhavati/ brahmaśabdena svabhāvato
          nirastasamastadoṣānavadhikātiśayāsaṃkhyeyakalyāṇaguṇaḥ puruṣottamo ’bhidhīyate/ evaṃ ca
          karmajñānasya tadanuṣṭḥānasya ca vairāgyotpādanadvārā cittakalmaṣāpanayadvārā ca
          brahmajñānaṃ prati sādhanatvena tayoḥ kāryakāraṇatvena pūrvottaramīmāṃsayor ekaśāstratvam/
          ata eva vṛttikārā ekam evedaṃ śāstraṃ jaiminīyena ṣoḍaśalakṣaṇenety āhuḥ/
children.translated_text: Here the word "now" (<s>atha</s>) means "immediately after the previous attainment of the knowledge of <s>karma</s> (ritual action)." Thus the commentator (<s>vṛttikāra</s>) has stated: "Immediately after the attainment of the knowledge of <s>karma</s>, one desires to know <s>Brahman</s>." The word "therefore" (<s>ataḥ</s>) indicates a reason. For one who has studied the <s>Vedas</s> with their auxiliaries and has understood their meaning, who is disenchanted with <s>karma</s> because of its perishable fruit — for such a one desiring stable liberation, the inquiry into <s>Brahman</s>, which is the means thereto, arises. By the word "<s>Brahman</s>" is meant <s>Puruṣottama</s> (the Supreme Person), who by nature is free from all defects and possesses infinite, surpassing, innumerable auspicious qualities. And thus, since the knowledge of <s>karma</s> and its performance serve as means to the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> — through the door of producing dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>) and through the door of removing the impurities of the mind — the <s>Pūrvamīmāṃsā</s> (Prior Inquiry) and the <s>Uttaramīmāṃsā</s> (Later Inquiry) form one single science, as cause and effect. Therefore, the commentators say: "This is indeed one science, together with the <s>Jaiminīya</s> [portion] of sixteen topics."
Section 4.286

children.text:
karmaphalasya kṣayitvaṃ brahmajñānaphalasya cākṣayitvaṃ "parīkṣya lokān karmacitān
          brāhmaṇo nirvedam āyān nāsty akṛtaḥ kṛtena" ityādiśrutibhir
          anumānārthāpattyupabṛṃhitābhiḥ pratyapādi/ ekaikanindayā karmaviśiṣṭasya jñānasya
          mokṣasādhanatvaṃ darśayati śrutiḥ:
children.translated_text: The perishability of the fruit of <s>karma</s> and the imperishability of the fruit of the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> have been established by <s>śruti</s> passages such as "Having examined the worlds produced by <s>karma</s>, a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> should arrive at dispassion: what is not made cannot be [attained] by what is made" — supported by inference and presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>). The <s>śruti</s>, by censuring each [karma and knowledge] individually, shows that knowledge combined with <s>karma</s> is the means to liberation:
"Those who worship ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>) enter into blind darkness;

children.text: tato bhūya iva te tamo ya u vidyāyāṃ ratāḥ//
children.translated_text: and those who delight in knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) enter into even greater darkness, as it were.

children.text: vidyāṃ cāvidyāṃ ca yas tad vedobhayaṃ saha/
children.translated_text: But he who knows both knowledge and ignorance together —
crossing death through ignorance, he attains immortality through knowledge."
And so forth. Thus it is stated in the <s>Pāñcarātrarahasya</s> (Secret of the <s>Pañcarātra</s>):
"That very ocean of compassion, the Blessed Lord, affectionate toward devotees,
in accordance with his worshippers, assumes the fivefold form.
That [fivefold form], designated as <s>arcā</s>, <s>vibhava</s>, <s>vyūha</s>, <s>sūkṣma</s>, and <s>antaryāmin</s> —

children.text: yad āśrityaiva cidvargas tat taj jñeyaṃ prapadyate//
children.translated_text: relying upon which alone, the group of conscious beings attains the respective object to be known.
One whose sins have been destroyed through the particular worship of each preceding [form]
becomes qualified for the worship of each succeeding form.
Thus, day after day, in accordance with <s>Śrauta</s> (Vedic) and <s>Smārta</s> (traditional) duties,
through the worship described, <s>Vāsudeva</s> becomes pleased with men.
When <s>Hari</s> is pleased in his soul, through devotion (<s>bhakti</s>) in the form of sustained meditation (<s>nididhyāsana</s>),
he immediately removes <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), which has the form of the aggregate of <s>karma</s>.
Then, for those men, [the qualities] hidden by <s>saṃsāra</s>, which are natural —
the auspicious qualities such as omniscience and the like — become manifest.

children.text: evaṃ guṇāḥ samānāḥ syur muktānām īśvarasya ca/
children.translated_text: Thus the qualities of the liberated become equal to those of the Lord,
except that the sole quality of being the creator of all belongs to the Lord distinctively beyond them.

children.text: muktās tu śeṣiṇi brahmaṇy aśeṣe śeṣarūpiṇaḥ/
children.translated_text: But the liberated, in the form of servants (<s>śeṣa</s>) to <s>Brahman</s> who is the complete master (<s>śeṣin</s>),

children.text: sarvān aśnuvate kāmān saha tena vipaścitā// iti/
children.translated_text: enjoy all desires together with that wise one."
Section 4.312

children.text:
tasmāt tāpatrayāturair amṛtatvāya puruṣottamādipadavedanīyaṃ brahma jijñāsitavyam ity
          uktaṃ bhavati/ prakṛtipratyayau pratyayārthaprādhānyena saha brūta itaḥ sanonyatreti
          vacanabalād icchāyā iṣyamāṇapradhānatvād iṣyamāṇaṃ jñānam iha vidheyam/ tac ca
          dhyānopāsanādiśabdavācyaṃ vedanaṃ na tu vākyajanyam āpātajñānam/ padasaṃdarbhaśrāviṇo
          vyutpannasya vidhānam antareṇāpi prāptatvāt/ ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ śrotavyo mantavyo
          nididhāsitavyaḥ ātmety evopāsīta vijñāya prajñāṃ kurvīta anuvidya vijānāti
          ityādiśrutibhyaḥ/ atra śrotavya ity anuvādaḥ/ adhyayanavidhinā sāṅgasya svādhyāyasya
          grahaṇe ’dhītavedasya puruṣasya prayojanavadarthadarśanāt tannirṇayāya svarasata eva
          śravaṇe pravartamānatayā tasya prāptatvāt/ mantavya iti cānuvādaḥ/
          śravaṇapratiṣṭhārthatvena mananasyāpi prāptatvāt/ aprāpte śāstram arthavad iti nyāyāt/
          dhyānaṃ ca tailadhārāvad avicchinnasmṛtisaṃtānarūpā

dhruvā smṛtiḥ smṛtipratilambhe sarvagranthīnāṃ vipramokṣa iti dhruvāyāḥ smṛter eva
          mokṣopāyatvaśravaṇāt/ sā ca smṛtir darśanasamānākārā
children.translated_text: "a steady memory; upon the attainment of [such] memory, all knots are released" — since the means to liberation is heard to be that very steady memory. And that memory has the same form as direct vision:

Therefore, for those afflicted by the threefold suffering (<s>tāpatraya</s>), <s>Brahman</s> — knowable through the designation <s>Puruṣottama</s> and the like — should be inquired into for the sake of immortality; this is what is stated. From the force of the statement "From the root and the suffix, speak together with the predominance of the meaning of the suffix; hence from <s>san</s> [suffix, meaning desire] being other [than mere knowledge]" — since the desired [object] is predominant in desire, the desired knowledge is what is to be enjoined here. And that is the realization (<s>vedana</s>) expressible by the words meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>), worship (<s>upāsana</s>), and the like — not the immediate knowledge arising from [merely hearing] sentences. Because for one who is learned and has heard the composition of words, [such immediate knowledge] is already obtained even without an injunction. From the <s>śruti</s> passages: "The Self is indeed to be seen, to be heard, to be reflected upon, to be meditated upon"; "One should worship as the Self"; "Having known, one should cultivate wisdom"; "Having followed, one knows." Herein, "to be heard" is a restatement [of what is already known], since for a person who has studied the <s>Vedas</s> with their auxiliaries through the injunction of study, hearing is already accomplished through [seeing] a meaningful purpose in the content. "To be reflected upon" is also a restatement, since reflection too is already accomplished for the purpose of establishing what has been heard. [This accords with] the principle: "Scripture is meaningful regarding what is not [otherwise] accomplished." And meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) is in the form of an unbroken stream of memory, like a continuous flow of oil —
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder,

children.text: kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parāvare//
children.translated_text: and his <s>karmas</s> are exhausted — when that supreme and immanent [<s>Brahman</s>] is seen" —

children.text:
ity anenaikavākyatvāt/ tathā ca ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ ity anenāsyā darśanarūpatā
          vidhīyate/ bhavati ca bhāvanāprakarṣāt smṛter darśanarūpatvam/ vākyakāreṇaitat sarvaṃ
          prapañcitaṃ vedanam upāsanaṃ syād ityādinā/ tad eva dhyānaṃ viśinaṣṭi śrutiḥ:
children.translated_text: because of forming a single sentence with this [passage]. And thus, by the [statement] "The Self is indeed to be seen," its nature as vision is enjoined. And it is the case that through the intensification of meditation, memory attains the nature of vision. All this has been elaborated by the author of the <s>Vākyakāra</s> (Sentence-commentator) with [passages such as] "Realization, worship would be," and so forth. The <s>śruti</s> itself specifies that meditation:

children.text: nāyam ātmā pravacanena labhyo na medhayā na bahunā śrutena/
children.translated_text: "This Self is not obtained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much learning.

children.text: yam evaiṣa vṛṇute tena labhyas tasyaiṣa ātmā vivṛṇute tanūṃ svām// iti/
children.translated_text: He whom this [Self] chooses — by him it is obtained; to him this Self reveals its own form."

children.text:
priyatama eva hi varaṇīyo bhavati/ yathāyaṃ priyatama ātmānaṃ prāpnoti tathā svayam eva
          bhagavān prayatata iti bhagavataivābhihitam:
children.translated_text: For only the dearest one is to be chosen. Just as this [devotee] who is the dearest attains the Self, so the Blessed Lord himself makes the effort — as has been stated by the Blessed Lord himself:
"To those who are constantly devoted, who worship with love,

children.text: dadāmi buddhiyogaṃ taṃ yena mām upayānti te// iti/
children.translated_text: I give that <s>buddhiyoga</s> (yoga of understanding) by which they come to Me."

children.text: puruṣaḥ sa paraḥ pārtha bhaktyā labhyas tv ananyayā/ iti ca/
children.translated_text: And: "That Supreme Person, O <s>Pārtha</s>, is obtainable through devotion (<s>bhakti</s>) that is exclusive."
Section 4.344

children.text:
bhaktis tu niratiśayānandapriyānanyaprayojanasakaletaravaitṛṣṇyavajjñānaviśeṣa eva/
          tatsiddhiś ca vivekādibhyo bhavatīti vākyakāreṇoktaṃ tallabdhir
          vivekavimokābhyāsakriyākalyāṇānavasādānuddharṣebhyaḥ saṃbhavān nirvacanāc ceti/ tatra
          viveko nāmāduṣṭād annāt sattvaśuddhiḥ/ atra nirvacanam: āhāraśuddheḥ sattvaśuddhiḥ
          sattvaśuddhyā dhruvā smṛtir iti/ vimokaḥ kāmānabhiṣvaṅgaḥ/ śānta upāsīteti nirvacanam/
          punaḥ punaḥ saṃśīlanam abhyāsaḥ/ nirvacanaṃ ca smārtam udāhṛtaṃ bhāṣyakāreṇa "sadā
          tadbhāvabhāvitaḥ" iti/ śrautasmārtakarmānuṣṭhānaṃ śaktitaḥ kriyā/ kriyāvān eṣa
          brahmavidāṃ variṣṭha iti nirvacanam/ satyārjavadayādānādīni kalyāṇāni/ satyena labhyata
          ityādi nirvacanam/ dainyaviparyayo ’navasādaḥ/ nāyam ātmā balahīnena labhyaḥ iti
          nirvacanam/ tadviparyayajā tuṣṭir uddharṣaḥ/ tadviparyayo ’nuddharṣaḥ/ śānto dānta iti
          nirvacanam/
children.translated_text: <s>Bhakti</s> (devotion) is indeed a special kind of knowledge characterized by unsurpassed delight in the beloved [Lord], having no other purpose, and accompanied by the disregard for everything else. And its attainment comes from discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) and the like, as stated by the <s>Vākyakāra</s>: "Its attainment arises from discrimination, detachment, practice, ritual action, auspiciousness, non-despondency, and non-elation" — and from scriptural authority. Therein, discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) means the purity of the <s>sattva</s> [quality] through unpolluted food. The scriptural authority for this: "From the purity of food comes the purity of <s>sattva</s>; from the purity of <s>sattva</s> comes steady memory." Detachment (<s>vimoka</s>) means non-attachment to desires. The scriptural authority: "One should worship in tranquility." Repeated cultivation is practice (<s>abhyāsa</s>). The <s>smṛti</s> authority has been cited by the commentator (<s>bhāṣyakāra</s>): "Always absorbed in the thought of That." The performance of <s>Śrauta</s> and <s>Smārta</s> <s>karmas</s> according to one's ability is ritual action (<s>kriyā</s>). The scriptural authority: "He who is active in ritual is the best among the knowers of <s>Brahman</s>." Truthfulness, straightforwardness, compassion, generosity, and the like are auspicious qualities (<s>kalyāṇa</s>). The scriptural authority: "It is obtained through truth," and so forth. Non-despondency (<s>anavasāda</s>) is the opposite of dejection. The scriptural authority: "This Self is not obtained by one who is weak." Contentment born from the opposite of that is elation (<s>uddharṣa</s>); non-elation (<s>anuddharṣa</s>) is the opposite of that. The scriptural authority: "Tranquil, self-controlled."
Section 4.357

children.text:
tad evam
