children.translated_text: now describe the transmutation of the body, by which the power of moving through the sky (<s>khecarī gati</s>) is attained.

children.text: yathā lohe tathā dehe kartavyaḥ sūtakaḥ satā/
children.translated_text: Just as in metals, so in the body, mercury should be applied by the good practitioner;
it produces, O <s>Devī</s>, the same result in body and metal alike;

children.text: pūrvaṃ lohe parīkṣeta paścād dehe prayojayet// iti/
children.translated_text: first one should test it on metal, then apply it to the body. Thus.
reference marker

children.text:
nanu saccidānandātmakaparatattvasphuraṇād eva muktisiddhau kim anena
          divyadehasaṃpādanaprayāseneti cet — tad etad vārttam/ avārttaśarīrālābhe

children.translated_text: that accomplishment
is impossible. As stated in the <s>Rasahṛdaya</s> —

Now, if liberation is accomplished by the flashing forth of the supreme reality (<s>paratattva</s>) whose nature is being-consciousness-bliss (<s>saccidānanda</s>), what need is there for this effort of creating a divine body? This is ill-considered. Because without obtaining an accomplished body,
Even when consciousness-bliss (<s>cidānanda</s>), free from great conceptual construction, intended through all paths (<s>adhvans</s>),

children.text: sphurito ’py asphuritatanoḥ karoti kiṃ jantuvargasya// iti/
children.translated_text: has flashed forth, what does it do for the mass of beings whose body has not [correspondingly] flashed forth? Thus.
That [body] which is decayed by old age, afflicted by the sufferings of cough, asthma, and the like,

children.text: yogyaṃ yan na samādhau pratihatabuddhīndriyaprasaram// iti/
children.translated_text: which is unfit for <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption), with the activity of intellect and senses obstructed — thus.
A youth of sixteen years is infatuated with the taste of sensual pleasures; beyond that,

children.text: yātaviveko vṛddho martyaḥ katham āpnuyān muktim// iti/
children.translated_text: with faded discrimination, an old mortal — how shall he attain liberation? Thus.

children.text:
nanu jīvatvaṃ nāma saṃsāritvam/ tadviparītatvaṃ muktatvam/ tathā ca parasparaviruddhayoḥ
          katham ekāyatanatvam upapannaṃ syād iti cet — tad anupapannam/ vikalpānupapatteḥ/ muktis
          tāvat sarvatīrthakarasaṃmatā/ sā kiṃ jñeyapade niviśate na vā/ carame śaśaviṣāṇakalpā
          syāt/ prathame na jīvanaṃ varjanīyam/ ajīvato jñātṛtvānupapatteḥ/ tad uktaṃ
          raseśvarasiddhānte/
children.translated_text: Objection: 'Being a <s>jīva</s> (individual soul) means being in <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of rebirth). The opposite of that is being liberated (<s>mukta</s>). How then can one and the same locus possess both [these mutually] contradictory [properties]?' That is untenable — because [none of the] alternatives is tenable. Liberation is accepted by all <s>Tīrthaṅkaras</s> (founders of spiritual paths). Does it pertain to the domain of the knowable or not? In the latter case, it would be like a hare's horn [i.e., non-existent]. In the former case, life (<s>jīvana</s>) should not be abandoned — because without being alive, the status of knower is untenable. As stated in the <s>Raseśvara</s> doctrine:
'Liberation while alive (<s>jīvamokṣa</s>) is taught in the path marked by mercury (<s>rasa</s>), and not otherwise;
in doctrines that rely on other means of knowledge, which depend on varieties of reasoning —
know that in all <s>Tantras</s> this [pair of] the knower and the knowable is accepted;

children.text: nājīvañ jñāsyati jñeyaṃ yad ato ’sty eva jīvanam// iti/
children.translated_text: without being alive, one will not know the knowable — therefore life indeed exists [as a prerequisite].' Thus.

children.text:
na cedam adṛṣṭacaram iti mantavyam/ viṣṇusvāmimatānusāribhir nṛpañcāsyaśarīrasya
          nityatvopapādanāt/ tad uktaṃ sākārasiddhau —
children.translated_text: Nor should this be thought unprecedented — because those who follow the doctrine of <s>Viṣṇusvāmin</s> have established the eternality of the body of <s>Nṛpañcāsya</s> (the Man-Lion, i.e., <s>Narasiṃha</s>). As stated in the <s>Sākārasiddhi</s> (Proof of [God's] Embodied Form):

'I salute <s>Nṛpañcāsya</s> (the Man-Lion), who is of the nature of existence (<s>sat</s>), consciousness (<s>cit</s>), eternality, inconceivable self-nature, and complete bliss — a single embodiment —
as accepted by the illustrious <s>Viṣṇusvāmin</s>.' Thus.

children.text:
nanv etat sāvayavaṃ rūpavad avabhāsamānaṃ nṛkaṇṭhīravāṅgaṃ sad iti na saṃgacchata
          ityādinākṣepapuraḥsaraṃ sanakādipratyakṣa

children.translated_text: the <s>Śruti</s> (Vedic revelation) such as 'The <s>Puruṣa</s> of a thousand heads' and the like,

Objection: 'This [form], appearing as possessing parts, having form, and being the body of a man-lion — does not cohere [with being eternal].' Preceded by such objections, [the reply is:] through the threefold means of knowledge — the direct perception of <s>Sanaka</s> and others,

children.text: tam adbhutaṃ bālakam ambujekṣaṇaṃ caturbhujaṃ śaṅkhagadādyudāyudham/
children.translated_text: 'That wondrous child with lotus-eyes, four-armed, bearing the conch, mace, and other weapons' —

children.text:
ityādipurāṇalakṣaṇena pramāṇatrayeṇa siddhaṃ nṛpañcānanāṅgaṃ katham asat syād iti/
          sadādīni viśeṣaṇāni garbhaśrīkāntamiśrair viṣṇusvāmicaraṇapariṇatāntaḥkaraṇaiḥ
          pratipāditāni/ tasmād asmadiṣṭadehanityatvam atyantādṛṣṭaṃ na bhavatīti puruṣārthakāmukaiḥ
          puruṣair eṣṭavyam/ ata evoktam —
children.translated_text: and the <s>Purāṇa</s> (traditional scripture) of this kind — how can the body of the Man-Lion, established by these three means of knowledge, be non-existent? The qualifications such as existence (<s>sat</s>) and the rest have been explained by <s>Garbhaśrīkāntamiśra</s>, whose inner organ was refined through devotion to the feet of <s>Viṣṇusvāmin</s>. Therefore, the eternality of the body as maintained by us is not entirely unprecedented — and should be desired by those who seek the highest human goal. Hence it is stated:
'The abode of all sciences, the root of <s>dharma</s>, <s>artha</s>, <s>kāma</s>, and <s>mokṣa</s> —

children.text: śreyaḥ paraṃ kim anyac charīram ajarāmaraṃ vihāyaikam// iti/
children.translated_text: what higher good is there, apart from the one imperishable, ageless, and immortal body?' Thus.

children.text: ajarāmarīkaraṇasamarthaś ca rasendra eva/ tad āha —
children.translated_text: And the one capable of making [the body] ageless and immortal is <s>rasendra</s> (mercury, the king of essences) alone. As it states:

children.text: eko ’sau rasarājaḥ śarīram ajarāmaraṃ kurute/ iti/
children.translated_text: 'That king of essences (<s>rasarāja</s>) alone makes the body ageless and immortal.' Thus.

children.text:
kiṃ varṇyate rasasya māhātmyam/ darśanasparśanādināpi mahat phalaṃ bhavati/ tad uktaṃ
          rasārṇave —
children.translated_text: What can be said of the greatness of <s>rasa</s> (mercury)? Even by seeing, touching, and the like, great fruit arises. As stated in the <s>Rasārṇava</s> (Ocean of Mercury):

children.text: darśanāt sparśanāt tasya bhakṣaṇāt smaraṇād api//
children.translated_text: 'By seeing, touching, consuming, and even remembering it,

children.text: pūjanād rasadānāc ca dṛśyate ṣaḍvidhaṃ phalam//
children.translated_text: by worshipping it, and by giving mercury — sixfold fruit is observed.
Whatever <s>liṅgas</s> (sacred marks) exist on the earth — such as <s>Kedāra</s> and the like —

children.text: tāni dṛṣṭvā tu yat puṇyaṃ tat puṇyaṃ rasadarśanāt/ ityādinā/
children.translated_text: the merit [obtained] by seeing them — that [same] merit [comes] from seeing mercury.' And so on.
And elsewhere too:
'<s>Śiva</s> is attained through the worship of a mercury <s>liṅga</s>, more than through all the <s>liṅgas</s> of <s>Kāśī</s> and the rest;

children.text: prāpyate yena tal liṅgaṃ bhogārogyāmṛtapradam// iti/
children.translated_text: that <s>liṅga</s> bestows enjoyment, health, and immortality.' Thus.
The adverse consequence of disparaging mercury has also been shown:

children.text: pramādād rasanindāyāḥ śrutāv enaṃ smaret sudhīḥ/
children.translated_text: 'If one hears the disparagement of mercury through negligence, the wise person should remember this [warning];

children.text: drāk tyajen nindakaṃ nityaṃ nindayā pūritāśubham// iti/
children.translated_text: one should forever shun the disparager, who is filled with impurity through his disparagement.' Thus.

children.text:
tasmād asmaduktayā rītyā divyaṃ dehaṃ saṃpādya yogābhyāsavaśāt paratattve dṛṣṭe
          puruṣārthaprāptir bhavati/ tadā —
children.translated_text: Therefore, having obtained a divine body by the method we have described, when the supreme reality is perceived through the practice of <s>yoga</s>, the attainment of the highest human goal occurs. Then —
'That which is situated between the two brows, shining upon the world like a peacock's [plume], lightning, or the sun —
for some whose eyes are blessed with merit, the light of pure consciousness opens forth.
Of the single essence of supreme bliss, supreme, of the nature of light, beyond conceptualization,
free from all afflictions, [it is] to be known as peaceful, self-experienced.

children.text: tasminn ādhāya manaḥ sphurad akhilaṃ cinmayaṃ jagat paśyan/
children.translated_text: Fixing the mind upon that, seeing the entire universe flashing forth as pure consciousness,
with the bonds of <s>karma</s> destroyed, one attains <s>Brahman</s>-hood here in this very life.'

children.text:
śrutiś ca — raso vai saḥ/ rasaṃ hy evāyaṃ labdhvānandī bhavati iti/ tad itthaṃ
          bhavadainyaduḥkhabharataraṇopāyo rasa eveti siddham/ tathā ca rasasya parabrahmaṇā sāmyam
          iti pratipādakaḥ ślokaḥ —
children.translated_text: And the <s>Śruti</s> (Vedic revelation) [states]: '<s>Rasa</s> (essence) indeed is He.' 'Having obtained <s>rasa</s>, one becomes blissful.' Thus, the means of crossing the overwhelming flood of worldly misery and sorrow is <s>rasa</s> (mercury/essence) alone — this is established. And thus the verse that demonstrates the identity of <s>rasa</s> (mercury) with <s>Parabrahman</s> (the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>):

children.text: yaḥ syāt prāvaraṇāvimocanadhiyāṃ sādhyaḥ prakṛtyā punaḥ
children.translated_text: 'He who is to be achieved by those whose minds are set on removing the covering [of ignorance], yet who by nature

children.text: saṃpannaḥ sahate na dīvyati paraṃ vaiśvānare jāgrati/
children.translated_text: is self-sufficient, who endures, who does not gamble, who awakens in [the fire of] <s>Vaiśvānara</s> (universal fire),

children.text: jñāto yady aparaṃ na vedayati ca svasmāt svayaṃ dyotate
children.translated_text: who, when known, does not perceive anything other [than himself], who shines forth from himself by himself —

children.text: sa dainyasaṃsṛtibhayāt pāyād asau pāradaḥ// iti//
children.translated_text: may that <s>pārada</s> (mercury) protect [us] from the fear of the cycle of worldly misery!' Thus.
he who is <s>Brahman</s> itself —
Thus concludes the <s>Raseśvara</s> (Lord of Mercury) philosophy in the <s>Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha</s>.
Now the <s>Aulūkya</s> (Vaiśeṣika) Philosophy //10//

children.text:
iha khalu nikhilaprekṣāvān nisargapratikūlavedanīyatayā nikhilātmasaṃvedanasiddhaṃ
          duḥkhaṃ jihāsus taddhānopāyaṃ jijnāsuḥ parameśvarasākṣātkāram upāyam ākalayati/
children.translated_text: Here indeed, every discerning person, wishing to abandon suffering — which is established through the self-experience of all beings as being by nature contrary to [their] innate [desire for happiness] — and wishing to know the means of abandoning it, considers the direct realization of the Supreme Lord to be the means,
'When human beings will roll up the sky like a hide,
then, without knowing <s>Śiva</s>, there will be an end to suffering' —

children.text:
ityādivacananicayaprāmāṇyāt/ parameśvarasākṣātkāraś ca śravaṇamananabhāvanābhir
          bhāvanīyaḥ/ yad āha —
children.translated_text: on the authority of such collections of statements. And the direct realization of the Supreme Lord is to be cultivated through hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and meditation (<s>bhāvanā</s>). As stated:
'By scripture (<s>āgama</s>), by inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and by the force of the practice of meditation (<s>dhyāna</s>) —

children.text: tridhā prakalpayan prajñāṃ labhate yogam uttamam// iti/
children.translated_text: cultivating wisdom in three ways, one attains the supreme <s>yoga</s>.' Thus.

children.text:
tatra mananam anumānādhīnam/ anumānaṃ ca vyāptijñānādhīnam/ vyāptijñānaṃ ca
          padārthavivekasāpekṣam/ ataḥ padārthaṣaṭkam athāto dharmaṃ vyākhyāsyāmaḥ ityādikāyāṃ
          daśalakṣaṇyāṃ kaṇabhakṣeṇa bhagavatā vyavasthāpitam/
children.translated_text: Therein, reflection (<s>manana</s>) depends on inference (<s>anumāna</s>). And inference depends on the knowledge of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>). And the knowledge of pervasion requires the discrimination of categories (<s>padārthas</s>). Therefore, the sixfold system of categories has been established by the blessed <s>Kaṇabhakṣa</s> (<s>Kaṇāda</s>) in the [work beginning with] 'Now, therefore, we shall explain <s>dharma</s>' — the <s>Daśalakṣaṇī</s> (the work of ten chapters).

children.text:
tatrāhnikadvayātmake prathame ’dhyāye samavetāśeṣapadārthakathanam akāri/ tatrāpi
          prathamāhnike jātimannirūpaṇam/ dvitīyāhnike jātiviśeṣayor nirūpaṇam/ āhnikadvayayukte
          dvitīye ’dhyāye dravyanirūpaṇam/ tatrāpi prathamāhnike bhūtaviśeṣalakṣaṇam/ dvitīye
          dikkālapratipādanam/ āhnikadvayayukte tṛtīya ātmāntaḥkaraṇalakṣaṇam/ tatrāpy ātmalakṣaṇaṃ
          prathame/ dvitīye ’ntaḥkaraṇalakṣaṇam/ āhnikadvayayukte caturthe
          śarīratadupayogivivecanam/ atrāpi prathame tadupayogivivecanam/ dvitīye śarīravivecanam/
          āhnikadvayavati pañcame karmapratipādanam/ tatrāpi prathame śarīrasaṃbandhikarmacintanam/
          dvitīye mānasakarmacintanam/ āhnikadvayaśālini ṣaṣṭhe śrautadharmanirūpaṇam/ tatrāpi
          prathame dānapratigrahadharmavivekaḥ/ dvitīye cāturāśramyocitadharmanirūpaṇam/ tathāvidhe
          saptame guṇasamavāyapratipādanam/ tatrāpi prathame buddhinirapekṣaguṇapratipādanam/
          dvitīye tatsāpekṣaguṇapratipādanaṃ samavāyapratipādanaṃ ca/ aṣṭame
          nirvikalpakasavikalpakapratyakṣapramāṇacintanam/ navame buddhiviśeṣapratipādanam/ daśame
          ’numānabhedapratipādanam/
children.translated_text: Therein, in the first chapter (<s>adhyāya</s>), consisting of two lessons (<s>āhnikas</s>), the enumeration of all the categories collectively was made. And therein, in the first lesson, the determination of the universal (<s>jāti</s>) and particularity (<s>man</s>, i.e., <s>viśeṣa</s>). In the second lesson, the determination of the universal and <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity). In the second chapter, consisting of two lessons, the determination of substance (<s>dravya</s>). And therein, in the first lesson, the definitions of the particular elements (<s>bhūtaviśeṣa</s>). In the second, the exposition of space (<s>dik</s>) and time (<s>kāla</s>). In the third [chapter], consisting of two lessons, the definition of the self (<s>ātman</s>) and the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). Therein, the definition of the self in the first [lesson]; of the inner organ in the second. In the fourth [chapter], consisting of two lessons, the examination of the body and what is useful for it. Therein, in the first, the examination of what is useful for it; in the second, the examination of the body. In the fifth [chapter], having two lessons, the exposition of action (<s>karma</s>). Therein, in the first, the consideration of action relating to the body; in the second, the consideration of mental action. In the sixth [chapter], adorned with two lessons, the determination of Vedic <s>dharma</s>. Therein, in the first, the discrimination of the <s>dharma</s> of giving and receiving; in the second, the determination of <s>dharma</s> appropriate to the four <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life). In the seventh [chapter], of the same kind, the exposition of quality (<s>guṇa</s>) and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). Therein, in the first, the exposition of qualities independent of cognition; in the second, the exposition of qualities dependent on cognition, and the exposition of inherence. In the eighth, the consideration of non-conceptual (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>) and conceptual (<s>savikalpaka</s>) perceptual means of knowledge. In the ninth, the exposition of particular cognitions. In the tenth, the exposition of the varieties of inference.

children.text:
tatroddeśo lakṣaṇaṃ parīkṣā ceti trividhāsya śāstrasya pravṛttiḥ/ nanu vibhāgāpekṣayā
          cāturvidhye vaktavye kathaṃ traividhyam uktam iti cet — maivaṃ maṃsthāḥ/ vibhāgasya
          viśeṣoddeśarūpatvād uddeśa evāntarbhāvāt/ tatra dravyaguṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyā iti
          ṣaḍ eva te padārthā ity uddeśaḥ/ kim atra kramaniyame kāraṇam/ ucyate/
          samastapadārthāyatanatvena pradhānasya dravyasya prathamam uddeśaḥ/ anantaraṃ
          guṇatvopādhinā sakaladravyavṛtter guṇasya/ tadanu sāmānyavattvasāmyāt karmaṇaḥ/ paścāt
          tattritayāśritasya sāmānyasya/ tadanantaraṃ samavāyādhikaraṇasya viśeṣasya/ ante
          ’vaśiṣṭasya samavāyasyeti/
children.translated_text: Therein, enumeration (<s>uddeśa</s>), definition (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), and examination (<s>parīkṣā</s>) — this is the threefold procedure of this science. Objection: 'Since, with reference to division (<s>vibhāga</s>), a fourfold [procedure] should be stated, how is threefoldness stated?' Do not think so — because division, being of the nature of a particular enumeration, is included within enumeration itself. Therein, 'substance, quality, action, universal, particularity, and inherence — these alone are the six categories' — this is the enumeration. What is the reason for the fixed order herein? It is stated: because substance, being the substratum of all categories, is primary, its enumeration comes first. Next, quality (<s>guṇa</s>), which by the qualifier of quality-hood inheres in all substances. Then action (<s>karma</s>), because of its similarity [with quality] in possessing universals. After that, the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), which resides in that triad [of substance, quality, and action]. Then <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity), which is the substratum of inherence. At the end, the remaining [category], inherence (<s>samavāya</s>).

children.text:
nanu ṣaḍ eva padārthā iti kathaṃ kathyate/ abhāvasyāpi sadbhāvād iti cet — maivaṃ vocaḥ/
          nañarthānullikhitadhīviṣayatayā bhāvarūpatayā ṣaḍ eveti vivakṣitatvāt/ tathāpi kathaṃ ṣaḍ
          eveti niyama upapadyate/ vikalpānupapatteḥ/ tathā hi/ niyamavyavacchedyaṃ pramitaṃ na vā/
          pramitatve kathaṃ niṣedhaḥ/ apramitatve kathaṃtarām/ na hi kaścit prekṣāvān mūṣikaviṣāṇaṃ
          pratiṣeddhuṃ yatate/ tataś cānupapatter na niyama iti cet — maivaṃ bhāṣiṣṭhāḥ/ saptamatayā
          pramite ’ndhakārādau bhāvatvasya bhāvatayā pramite śaktisādṛśyādau saptamatvasya ca
          niṣedhād iti kṛtaṃ vistareṇa/
children.translated_text: Objection: 'How can it be said that there are only six categories — since absence (<s>abhāva</s>) also exists?' Do not say so — because the intent of 'only six' is stated with reference to entities of a positive nature (<s>bhāvarūpa</s>), whose domain is cognition that does not involve the meaning of the negative particle (<s>nañ</s>). 'Even so, how is the restriction to exactly six justified?' Because [none of the] alternatives is tenable. For consider: is that which is to be excluded by the restriction known or not? If known, how can it be negated? If not known, all the more so [how can it be negated]? For no discerning person strives to negate the horns of a mouse. Therefore, the restriction is untenable due to impossibility — if [one objects] thus, do not speak so! Because, when darkness and the like are known as a seventh [category], their being positive entities is negated; and when power (<s>śakti</s>), similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>), and the like are known as positive entities, their being a seventh [category] is negated. Enough with elaboration.

children.text:
tatra dravyāditritayasya dravyatvādijātir lakṣaṇam/ dravyatvaṃ nāma
          gaganāravindasamavetatve sati nityatve sati gandhāsamavetatvam/ guṇatvaṃ nāma
          samavāyikāraṇāsamavetāsamavāyikāraṇabhinnasamavetasatttāsākṣād- vyāpyajātiḥ/ karmatvaṃ
          nāma nityāsamavetatvasahitasattāsākṣādvyāpyajātiḥ/ sāmānyaṃ tu
          pradhvaṃsapratiyogitvarahitam anekasamavetam/ viśeṣo nāmānyonyābhāvavirodhisāmānyarahitaḥ
          samavetaḥ/ samavāyas tu samavāyarahitaḥ saṃbandha iti ṣaṇṇāṃ lakṣaṇāni vyavasthitāni/
children.translated_text: Therein, the universal (<s>jāti</s>) such as substance-hood and the like is the definition of the triad of substance and the rest. Substance-hood (<s>dravyatva</s>) is: that which, while not being co-inherent in a sky-lotus, while being eternal, is not co-inherent with smell. Quality-hood (<s>guṇatva</s>) is: the universal that is directly pervaded by existence (<s>sattā</s>), which is co-inherent in what is different from the inherent cause and from what is co-inherent in the non-inherent cause. Action-hood (<s>karmatva</s>) is: the universal that is directly pervaded by existence, conjoined with non-co-inherence in eternal [entities]. <s>Sāmānya</s> (universal) is that which is devoid of being the counter-correlate of destruction and is co-inherent in many [entities]. <s>Viśeṣa</s> (particularity) is that which is co-inherent [in eternal substances], devoid of the universal that is opposed to mutual absence. <s>Samavāya</s> (inherence) is a relation that is itself devoid of [another] inherence — thus the definitions of the six [categories] are established.

children.text:
dravyaṃ navavidhaṃ pṛthivyaptejovāyvākāśakāladigātmamanāṃsīti/ tatra
          pṛthivyādicatuṣṭayasya pṛthivītvādijātir lakṣaṇam/ pṛthivītvaṃ nāma
          pākajarūpasamānādhikaraṇadravyatvasākṣādvyāpyajātiḥ/ aptvaṃ nāma saritsāgarasamavetatve
          sati jvalanāsamavetaṃ sāmānyam/ tejastvaṃ nāma candracāmīkarasamavetatve sati
          salilāsamavetaṃ sāmānyam/ vāyutvaṃ nāma tvagindriyasamavetadravyatvasākṣādvyāpyajātiḥ/
          ākāśakāladiśām ekaikatvād aparajātyabhāve pāribhāṣikyas tisraḥ saṃjñā bhavanti ākāśaḥ kālo
          dig iti/ saṃyogājanyajanyaviśeṣaguṇasamānādhikaraṇaviśeṣādhikaraṇam ākāśam/ vibhutve sati
          digasamavetaparatvāsamavāyikāraṇādhikaraṇaḥ kālaḥ/ akālatve saty aviśeṣaguṇā mahatī dik/
          ātmamanasor ātmatvamanastve/ ātmatvaṃ nāmāmūrtasamavetadravyatvāparajātiḥ/ manastvaṃ nāma
          dravyasamavāyikāraṇatvarahitāṇusamavetadravyatvāparajātiḥ/
children.translated_text: Substance (<s>dravya</s>) is ninefold: earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>), water (<s>ap</s>), fire (<s>tejas</s>), air (<s>vāyu</s>), ether (<s>ākāśa</s>), time (<s>kāla</s>), direction (<s>dik</s>), self (<s>ātman</s>), and mind (<s>manas</s>). Therein, the universal such as earth-hood and the like is the definition of the tetrad of earth and the rest. Earth-hood (<s>pṛthivītva</s>) is: the universal that is directly pervaded by substance-hood, which shares the same locus as color produced by heat (<s>pākajarūpa</s>). Water-hood (<s>aptva</s>) is: the universal that is co-inherent in rivers and oceans and not co-inherent in flame. Fire-hood (<s>tejastva</s>) is: the universal that is co-inherent in the moon and gold and not co-inherent in water. Air-hood (<s>vāyutva</s>) is: the universal that is directly pervaded by substance-hood, which is co-inherent in the sense-organ of touch (<s>tvagindriya</s>). Since ether, time, and direction are each singular, in the absence of another universal, three conventional designations are [given]: 'ether,' 'time,' and 'direction.' Ether (<s>ākāśa</s>) is the substratum of a <s>viśeṣa</s> (particularity) that shares the same locus as a particular quality (<s>viśeṣaguṇa</s>) that is not produced by contact (<s>saṃyoga</s>). Time (<s>kāla</s>) is: that which, while being all-pervading, is the substratum of the non-inherent cause of the [quality of] remoteness (<s>paratva</s>) that is not co-inherent in direction. Direction (<s>dik</s>) is the great [substance] that, while not being time, is devoid of particular qualities. Self-hood (<s>ātmatva</s>) and mind-hood (<s>manastva</s>) [are the definitions] of self and mind [respectively]. Self-hood is: the non-ultimate universal (<s>aparajāti</s>) of substance-hood co-inherent in what is formless (<s>amūrta</s>). Mind-hood is: the non-ultimate universal of substance-hood co-inherent in atoms (<s>aṇu</s>) that are devoid of being the inherent cause of [another] substance.

children.text:
rūparasagandhasparśasaṃkhyāparimāṇapṛthaktvasaṃyogavibhāga-paratvāparatvabuddhisukhaduḥkhecchādveṣaprayatnāś
          ca kaṇṭhoktāḥ saptadaśa caśabdasamuccitā gurutvadravatvasnehasaṃskārādṛṣṭaśabdāḥ
          saptaivety evaṃ caturviṃśatir guṇāḥ/ tatra rūpādiśabdāntānāṃ rūpatvādijātir lakṣaṇam/
          rūpatvaṃ nāma nīlasamavetaguṇatvāparajātiḥ/ anayā diśā śiṣṭānāṃ lakṣaṇāni draṣṭavyāni/
children.translated_text: Form (<s>rūpa</s>), taste (<s>rasa</s>), smell (<s>gandha</s>), touch (<s>sparśa</s>), number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), dimension (<s>parimāṇa</s>), separateness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>), remoteness (<s>paratva</s>), proximity (<s>aparatva</s>), cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), and effort (<s>prayatna</s>) -- these seventeen are explicitly stated [in the sūtra]; and aggregated by the word 'and' are heaviness (<s>gurutva</s>), fluidity (<s>dravatva</s>), viscidity (<s>sneha</s>), latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>), unseen merit (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>), and sound (<s>śabda</s>) -- just seven more. Thus there are twenty-four <s>guṇas</s> (qualities). Among these, the definition of form and the rest up to sound is the universal (<s>jāti</s>) of form-ness and the like. Form-ness (<s>rūpatva</s>) is the lower universal that is 'quality-ness inhering in blue.' By this method, the definitions of the remaining [qualities] should be understood.
reference marker

children.text:
karma pañcavidham/ utkṣepaṇāpakṣepaṇākuñcanaprasāraṇagamanabhedāt/ bhramaṇarecanādīnāṃ
          gamana evāntarbhāvaḥ/ utkṣepaṇādīnām utkṣepaṇatvādijātir lakṣaṇam/ tatrotkṣepaṇatvaṃ
          nāmordhvadeśasaṃyogāsamavāyikāraṇasamavetakarmatvāparajātiḥ/ evam apakṣepaṇādīnāṃ

children.translated_text: should be formulated.

<s>Karma</s> (action) is fivefold, by the distinction of upward throwing (<s>utkṣepaṇa</s>), downward throwing (<s>apakṣepaṇa</s>), contraction (<s>ākuñcana</s>), expansion (<s>prasāraṇa</s>), and locomotion (<s>gamana</s>). Rotation (<s>bhramaṇa</s>), evacuation (<s>recana</s>), and the like are included within locomotion alone. The definition of upward throwing and the rest is the universal of upward-throwing-ness and the like. Therein, upward-throwing-ness is the lower universal that is 'action-ness that inheres in what is the non-inherent cause of conjunction with an upper location.' Similarly, the definitions of downward throwing and the rest
reference marker

children.text:
sāmānyaṃ dvividhaṃ param aparaṃ ca/ paraṃ sattā dravyaguṇasamavetā/ aparaṃ dravyatvādi/
          tallakṣaṇaṃ prāg evoktam/
children.translated_text: Universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is twofold: higher (<s>para</s>) and lower (<s>apara</s>). The higher is existence (<s>sattā</s>), which inheres in substance, quality, [and action]. The lower is substance-ness (<s>dravyatva</s>) and the like. Its definition has been stated previously.
reference marker

children.text:
viśeṣāṇām anantatvāt samavāyasya caikatvād vibhāgo na saṃbhavati/ tallakṣaṇaṃ ca prāg
          evāvādi/
children.translated_text: Since ultimate differentiators (<s>viśeṣas</s>) are infinite and since inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) is one, no division [of these categories] is possible. Their definitions too have been stated previously.
reference marker

children.text: dvitve ca pākajotpattau vibhāge ca vibhāgaje/
children.translated_text: In [the topic of] twoness, in production from heat-transformation (<s>pākaja</s>), and in disjunction produced by disjunction --

children.text: yasya na skhalitā buddhis taṃ vai vaiśeṣikaṃ viduḥ//
children.translated_text: he whose understanding does not stumble is truly known as a <s>Vaiśeṣika</s>.

children.text:
ity ābhāṇakasya sadbhāvād dvitvādyutpattiprakāraḥ pradarśyate/ tatra prathamam
          indriyārthasaṃnikarṣaḥ (1)/ tasmād ekatvasāmānyajñānam (2)/ tato ’pekṣābuddhiḥ (3)/ tato
          dvitvotpattiḥ (4)/ tato dvitvatvasāmānyajñānam (5)/ tasmād dvitvaguṇajñānam (6)/ tato dve
          dravye iti dhīḥ (7)/ tataḥ saṃskāraḥ/ tad āha —
children.translated_text: Since such a popular saying exists, the mode of production of twoness and the like is demonstrated. Therein, first: contact of the sense-organ with the object (1); therefrom, cognition of the universal of oneness (2); therefrom, the cognition of expectation (<s>apekṣābuddhi</s>) (3); therefrom, the production of twoness (4); therefrom, cognition of the universal of twoness-ness (5); therefrom, cognition of the quality of twoness (6); therefrom, the cognition 'two substances' (7); therefrom, the latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>). Thus it is stated:
At first, from the occurrence of sense-organ contact, [arises] the cognition of the universal of oneness;

children.text: ekatvobhayagocarā matir ato dvitvaṃ tato jāyate/
children.translated_text: the cognition having both [items'] oneness as its object -- from that, twoness arises.
Then the cognition of twoness-ness; then after that, immediately after the cognition of twoness,

children.text: dve dravye iti dhīr iyaṃ nigaditā dvitvodayaprakriyā// iti/
children.translated_text: the cognition 'two substances' -- this is declared to be the process of the arising of twoness.

children.text:
dvitvāder apekṣābuddhijanyatve kiṃ pramāṇam/ atrāhur ācāryāḥ — apekṣābuddhir dvitvāder
          utpādikā bhavitum arhati/ vyañjakatvānupapattau tenānuvidhīyamānatvāt/ śabdaṃ prati
          saṃyogavad iti/ vayaṃ tu brūmaḥ — dvitvādikam ekatvadvayaviṣayānityabuddhivyaṅgyaṃ na
          bhavati anekāśritaguṇatvāt pṛthaktvādivad iti/
children.translated_text: What is the proof that twoness and the like are produced from the cognition of expectation (<s>apekṣābuddhi</s>)? Here the teachers say: the cognition of expectation is fit to be the producer of twoness and the like, because [twoness] conforms to it when the possibility of being merely a manifester is untenable -- like conjunction with respect to sound. We, however, say: twoness and the like are not manifested by a non-eternal cognition having two onenesses as its object, because [twoness] is a quality residing in more than one [substance], like separateness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>) and the like.
reference marker

children.text:
nivṛttikramo nirūpyate — apekṣābuddhita ekatvasāmānyajñānasya dvitvotpattisamakālaṃ
          nivṛttiḥ/ apekṣābuddher dvitvatvasāmānyajñānād dvitvaguṇabuddhisamasamayam/
          dvitvasyāpekṣābuddhinivṛtter dravyabuddhisamakālam/ guṇabuddher dravyabuddhitaḥ
          saṃskārotpattisamakālam/ dravyabuddhes tadanantaraṃ saṃskārād iti/
children.translated_text: The sequence of cessation is determined: the cessation of the cognition of the universal of oneness from the cognition of expectation is simultaneous with the production of twoness. [The cessation] of the cognition of expectation from the cognition of the universal of twoness-ness is simultaneous with the cognition of the quality of twoness. [The cessation] of twoness from the cessation of the cognition of expectation is simultaneous with the cognition of substance. [The cessation] of the cognition of quality from the cognition of substance is simultaneous with the production of the latent impression. [The cessation] of the cognition of substance is thereafter from the latent impression.
And thus the summary verses:
First, by the cognition of expectation, the cognition of the universal of oneness is destroyed;
simultaneously with the arising of twoness; afterwards, that [cognition of expectation is destroyed] by the cognition of the universal [of twoness-ness].
At the time of the cognition of the quality called twoness, then twoness ceases;
by the destruction of the cognition of expectation, from the time of the birth of the cognition of substance.
The cognition of quality [ceases] by the cognition of substance, from the time of the production of the latent impression;

children.text: dravyabuddhiś ca saṃskārād iti nāśakramo mataḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: and the cognition of substance [ceases] from the latent impression -- this is considered the sequence of destruction.
reference marker

children.text:
buddher buddhyantaravināśyatve saṃskāravināśyatve ca pramāṇam — vivādādhyāsitāni jñānāny
          uttarottarakāryavināśyāni kṣaṇikavibhuviśeṣaguṇatvāc chabdavat/ kvacid
          dravyārambhakasaṃyogapratidvandvivibhāgajanakakarmasamakālam
          ekatvasāmānyacintayāśrayanivṛtter eva dvitvanivṛttiḥ/ karmasamakālam apekṣābuddhicintanād
          ubhābhyām iti/ saṃkṣepaḥ/
children.translated_text: The proof that a cognition is destroyed by another cognition and [also] destroyed by a latent impression: the cognitions under dispute are destroyed by their successive effects, because they are qualities of a momentary, all-pervading <s>viśeṣa</s> (individual differentiator) -- like sound. In some cases, the cessation of twoness is from the cessation of the substratum alone through the contemplation of the universal of oneness, simultaneously with the action that generates a disjunction opposed to the conjunction that originates substances. Simultaneously with the action, from the contemplation of the cognition of expectation, by both [means]. This is the summary.

children.text: apekṣābuddhir nāma vināśakavināśapratiyoginī buddhir iti boddhavyam/
children.translated_text: The cognition of expectation should be understood as a cognition whose counter-correlate is the destroyer of the destroyer.
reference marker

children.text:
atha dvyaṇukanāśam ārabhya katibhiḥ kṣaṇaiḥ punar anyad dvyaṇukam utpadya rūpādimad
          bhavatīti jijñāsāyām utpattiprakāraḥ kathyate — nodanādikrameṇa dvyaṇukanāśaḥ/ naṣṭe
          dvyaṇuke paramāṇāv agnisaṃyogāc chyāmādīnāṃ nivṛttiḥ/ nivṛtteṣu śyāmādiṣu punar anyasmād
          agnisaṃyogād raktādīnām utpattiḥ/ utpanneṣu raktādiṣv adṛṣṭavadātmasaṃyogāt paramāṇau
          dravyārambhaṇāya kriyā/ tayā pūrvadeśād vibhāgaḥ/ vibhāgena pūrvadeśasaṃyoganivṛttiḥ/
          tasmin nivṛtte paramāṇvantareṇa saṃyogotpattiḥ/ saṃyuktābhyāṃ paramāṇubhyāṃ
          dvyaṇukārambhaḥ/ ārabdhe dvyaṇuke kāraṇaguṇādibhyaḥ kāryaguṇādīnāṃ rūpādīnām utpattir iti
          yathākramaṃ nava kṣaṇāḥ/ daśakṣaṇādiprakārāntaraṃ vistarabhayān neha pratanyate/ itthaṃ
          pīlupākaprakriyā/ piṭharapākaprakriyā naiyāyikadhīsaṃmatā/
children.translated_text: Now, beginning from the destruction of a dyad (<s>dvyaṇuka</s>), the mode of production is stated in response to the inquiry: by how many moments does another dyad arise and come to possess form and the like? The destruction of the dyad [occurs] through the sequence of impulse and the like. When the dyad is destroyed, from the conjunction of the atom (<s>paramāṇu</s>) with fire, the cessation of dark colors and the like [occurs]. When the dark colors and the like have ceased, from another conjunction with fire, the production of red colors and the like [occurs]. When the red colors and the like have been produced, from the conjunction of <s>adṛṣṭa</s> (unseen merit) with the self, action for the origination of substance [arises] in the atom. By that [action], disjunction from the previous location [occurs]. By the disjunction, the cessation of conjunction with the previous location [occurs]. When that has ceased, the production of conjunction with another atom [occurs]. From the two conjoined atoms, the origination of a dyad [occurs]. When the dyad has been originated, the production of the effect-qualities such as form and the like from the cause-qualities and the like -- these are nine moments in sequence. The alternative of ten moments and the like is not elaborated here for fear of prolixity. Thus is the process of <s>pīlupāka</s> (atomic heat-transformation). The process of <s>piṭharapāka</s> (pot-baking) is approved by the understanding of the <s>Naiyāyikas</s>.
reference marker

children.text:
vibhāgajavibhāgo dvividhaḥ — kāraṇamātravibhāgajaḥ kāraṇākāraṇavibhāgajaś ca/ tatra
          prathamaḥ kathyate — kāryavyāpte kāraṇe karmotpannaṃ yadāvayavāntarād vibhāgaṃ vidhatte na
          tadākāśādideśād vibhāgaḥ/ yadā tv ākāśādideśād vibhāgo na tadāvayavāntarād iti
          sthitiniyamaḥ/ karmaṇo gaganavibhāgākartṛtvasya
          dravyārambhakasaṃyogavirodhivibhāgārambhakatvena dhūmasya dhūmadhvajavargeṇeva
          vyabhicārānupalambhāt/ tataś cāvayavakarmāvayavāntarād eva vibhāgaṃ karoti nākāśādideśāt/
          tasmād vibhāgād dravyārambhakasaṃyoganivṛttiḥ/ tataḥ kāraṇābhāvāt kāryābhāva iti nyāyād
          avayavinivṛttiḥ/ nivṛtte ’vayavini tatkāraṇayor avayavayor vartamāno vibhāgaḥ
          kāryavināśaviśiṣṭaṃ kālaṃ svatantraṃ vāvayavam apekṣya sakriyasyaivāvayavasya
          kāryasaṃyuktād ākāśadeśād vibhāgam ārabhate na niṣkriyasya/ kāraṇābhāvāt/
children.translated_text: Disjunction born of disjunction is twofold: born of cause-only disjunction and born of cause-and-non-cause disjunction. Therein, the first is stated: when action arises in a cause pervaded by the effect, it produces disjunction from one part but not disjunction from the spatial location of ether (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like. But when there is disjunction from the spatial location of ether and the like, there is not [disjunction] from another part -- this is the rule of fixity. Because of the non-observation of deviation -- since the action's not being the producer of disjunction from space [is explained by] its being the originator of a disjunction that opposes the conjunction originating substances, like smoke with the class of fire. Therefore, the action of the part produces disjunction only from another part, not from the spatial location of ether and the like. From that disjunction, the cessation of the conjunction originating substances [occurs]. Therefrom, by the principle 'from the absence of the cause, the absence of the effect,' the cessation of the composite [occurs]. When the composite has ceased, the disjunction present in the two parts that are the causes of that [composite] -- with reference to the time distinguished by the destruction of the effect, or with reference to the independent part -- originates disjunction from the spatial location of ether conjoined with the effect only for the part that possesses action, not for the actionless one, because of the absence of a cause.

children.text: dvitīyas tu haste karmotpannam avayavāntarād vibhāgaṃ akurvad

ākāśādideśebhyo vibhāgān ārabhate/ te kāraṇākāraṇavibhāgāḥ karma yāṃ diśaṃ prati
          kāryārambhābhimukhaṃ tām apekṣya kāryākāryavibhāgam ārabhante/ yathā hastākāśavibhāgāc
          charīrākāśavibhāgaḥ/ na cāsau śarīrakriyākāryaḥ/ tadā tasya niṣkriyatvāt/ nāpi
          hastakriyākāryaḥ vyadhikaraṇasya karmaṇo vibhāgakartṛtvānupapatteḥ/ ataḥ pāriśeṣyāt
          kāraṇākāraṇavibhāgas tasya kāraṇam aṅgīkaraṇīyam/
children.translated_text: it originates disjunctions from spatial locations of ether and the like. These cause-and-non-cause disjunctions, with reference to the direction toward which the action is oriented for originating its effect, originate effect-and-non-effect disjunction. For example, from the disjunction of the hand from ether, the disjunction of the body from ether [follows]. And this [latter] is not the effect of the body's action, because at that time it is actionless. Nor is it the effect of the hand's action, because of the impossibility of action in a different locus being the producer of disjunction. Therefore, by the method of elimination, a cause-and-non-cause disjunction must be accepted as its cause.
The second [type], however: not producing disjunction from another part when action arises in the hand,
reference marker

children.text:
yad avādy andhakārādau bhāvatvaṃ niṣidhyata iti tad asaṃgatam/ tatra caturdhā
          vivādasaṃbhavāt/ tathā hi/ dravyaṃ tama iti bhāṭṭā vedāntinaś ca bhaṇanti/ āropitaṃ
          nīlarūpam iti śridharācāryāḥ/ ālokajñānābhāvaḥ iti prābhāraikadeśinaḥ/ ālokābhāva iti
          naiyāyikādaya iti cet
children.translated_text: What was stated -- that positive existence is denied with respect to darkness and the like -- that is inconsistent. Because a fourfold dispute is possible there. For thus: the <s>Bhāṭṭas</s> and the <s>Vedāntins</s> declare that darkness is a substance. The teacher <s>Śrīdhara</s> [says it is] a superimposed blue form. Some followers of <s>Prabhākara</s> [say it is] the absence of the cognition of light. The <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others [say it is] the absence of light.

children.text:
tatra dravyatvapakṣo na ghaṭate/ vikalpānupapatteḥ/ dravyaṃ bhavadandhakārākhyaṃ
          pṛthivyādyanyatamam anyad vā/ nādyaḥ/ yatrāntarbhāvo 'sya tasya yāvanto guṇās
          tāvadguṇakatvaprasaṅgāt/ na dvitīyaḥ/ nirguṇasya tasya dravyatvāsaṃbhavena
          dravyāntaratvasya sutarām asaṃbhavāt/
children.translated_text: Therein, the position that [darkness is] a substance does not work, because of the impossibility of the alternatives. Is this so-called darkness-substance one of the [established substances] such as earth and the like, or something else? Not the first -- because of the absurd consequence that it would possess as many qualities as the [substance] within which it is subsumed. Not the second -- because, since the substance without qualities cannot be a substance, its being a different substance is all the more impossible.

children.text: nanu tamālaśyāmalatvenopalabhyamānaṃ tamaḥ kathaṃ nirguṇaṃ syād iti cet
children.translated_text: Objection: 'How can darkness, which is perceived as dark like the <s>tamāla</s> tree, be without qualities?'
That is without substance.
reference marker
Because the blue form, which pervades smell and the like, ceases when those [smell etc.] cease.

children.text: atha nīlaṃ tama iti gateḥ kā gatir iti cet
children.translated_text: Objection: 'Since we understand that darkness is blue, what is the explanation?'

children.text:
nīlaṃ nabha itivad bhrāntir evety alaṃ vṛddhavīvadhayā/ ata eva nāropitarūpaṃ tamaḥ/
          adhiṣṭhānapratyayam antareṇāropāyogāt/ bāhyālokasahakārirahitasya cakṣuṣo rūpārope
          sāmarthyānupalambhāc ca/ na cāyam acākṣuṣaḥ pratyayaḥ/ tadanuvidhānasyānanyathāsiddhatvāt/
          ata eva nālokajñānābhāvaḥ/ abhāvasya pratiyogigrāhakendriyagrāhyatvaniyamena
          mānasatvaprasaṅgāt/ tasmād ālokābhāva eva tamaḥ/
children.translated_text: It is merely an error, like [the perception] 'the sky is blue' -- enough with the slaughter of the aged! Therefore, darkness is not a superimposed form either -- because superimposition is impossible without the cognition of a substratum, and because no capacity is observed in the eye, deprived of the cooperation of external light, for the superimposition of form. Nor is this an extrasensory cognition, because its conformity to that [sense-organ] is not otherwise explicable. Therefore, [darkness] is not the absence of the cognition of light either -- because, by the rule that absence is apprehensible by the sense-organ that apprehends the counter-correlate, the absurd consequence would arise that it is mental. Therefore, darkness is the absence of light alone.

children.text:
na ca vidhipratyayavedyatvenābhāvatvāyoga iti sāmpratam/ pralayavināśāvasānādiṣu
          vyabhicārāt/ na cābhāve bhāvadharmādhyāropo durupapādaḥ/ duḥkhābhāve sukhatvāropasya
          saṃyogābhāve vibhāgatvābhimānasya ca dṛṣṭatvāt/
children.translated_text: Nor is it currently tenable [to object] that, because [darkness] is cognized by a positive cognition, it cannot be an absence. Because there is deviation in [cases such as] the cessation of dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>), destruction, and the like. Nor is the superimposition of the properties of a positive entity upon an absence difficult to explain -- because the superimposition of pleasure upon the absence of pain, and the attribution of disjunction-ness upon the absence of conjunction, are observed.

children.text:
na cālokābhāvasya ghaṭādyabhāvavad
          rūpavadabhāvatvenālokasāpekṣacakṣurjanyajñānaviṣayatvaṃ syād ity eṣitavyam/ yadgrahe
          yadapekṣaṃ cakṣus tadabhāvagrahe 'pi tad apekṣata iti nyāyenālokagraha ālokāpekṣāyā
          abhāvena tadabhāvagrahe 'pi tadapekṣāyā abhāvāt/
children.translated_text: Nor should it be urged that the absence of light, like the absence of a pot and the like, being an absence possessing form, would be the object of cognition produced by the eye dependent on light. Because, by the principle 'whatever the eye depends upon for apprehending something, it depends upon the same for apprehending its absence,' since there is absence of the dependence on light for the apprehension of light, there is also absence of that dependence for the apprehension of the absence of light.

children.text:
na cādhikaraṇagrahaṇāvaśyaṃbhāvaḥ/ abhāvapratītāv adhikaraṇagrahaṇāvaśyaṃbhāvānaṅgīkārāt/
          aparathā nivṛttaḥ kolāhala iti śabdapradhvaṃsaḥ pratyakṣo na syād iti aprāmāṇikaṃ
          paravacanam/ tat sarvam abhisaṃdhāya bhagavān kaṇādaḥ praṇināya sūtraṃ
          dravyaguṇakarmaniṣpattivaidharmyād abhāvas tamaḥ iti
children.translated_text: Nor is the apprehension of the substratum necessarily required. Because we do not accept the necessary requirement of substratum-apprehension in the cognition of absence. Otherwise, 'the commotion has ceased' -- the destruction of sound would not be perceptible -- and the words of others [who claim it must be perceived through a substratum] are without authority. Keeping all this in mind, the blessed <s>Kaṇāda</s> composed the <s>sūtra</s>: 'Due to its dissimilarity from the production of substance, quality, and action, darkness is an absence.'
reference marker

children.text:
abhāvas tu niṣedhamukhapramāṇagamyaḥ saptamo nirūpyate — sa cāsamavāyatve saty
          asamavāyaḥ/ saṃkṣepato dvividhaḥ/ saṃsargābhāvānyonyābhāvabhedāt/ saṃsargābhāvo 'pi
          trividhaḥ/ prākpradhvaṃsātyantābhāvabhedāt/ tatrānityo 'nāditamaḥ prāgabhāvaḥ/ utpattimān
          avināśī pradhvaṃsaḥ/ pratiyogyāśrayo 'bhāvo 'tyantābhāvaḥ/ atyantābhāvavyatiriktatve saty
          anavadhir abhāvo anyonyābhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: Absence (<s>abhāva</s>), however, which is cognizable through the means of knowledge in the form of negation, is discussed as the seventh [category]. It is: that which is a non-inherence while being a non-inherence [i.e., not connected by inherence with anything]. In summary, it is twofold: by the distinction of relational absence (<s>saṃsargābhāva</s>) and mutual absence (<s>anyonyābhāva</s>). Relational absence too is threefold: by the distinction of prior absence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>), posterior absence (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>), and absolute absence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>). Therein, beginningless, non-eternal darkness is prior absence. That which has an origin but is indestructible is posterior absence (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>). Absence that has the counter-correlate as its substratum is absolute absence. That absence which, while being different from absolute absence, is without a limit -- is mutual absence (<s>anyonyābhāva</s>).
Objection: 'Is not mutual absence simply absolute absence?'

children.text:
aho rājamārga eva bhramaḥ/ anyonyābhāvo hi tādātmyapratiyogikaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ yathā ghataḥ
          paṭātmā na bhavatīti/ saṃsargapratiyogikaḥ pratiṣedho 'tyantābhāvaḥ/ yathā vāyau
          rūpasaṃbandho nāstīti/ na cāsya puruṣārthaupayikatvaṃ nāstīty āśaṅkanīyam/
          duḥkhātyantocchedāparaparyāyaniḥśreyasarūpatvena paramapuruṣārthatvāt//
children.translated_text: Alas, this is an error on the royal road! For mutual absence (<s>anyonyābhāva</s>) is a negation whose counter-positive is identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) — as in 'A pot is not of the nature of a cloth.' A negation whose counter-positive is conjunction (<s>saṃsarga</s>) is absolute absence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>) — as in 'There is no connection of color in wind.' Nor should it be doubted that this has no utility for the goals of human life — because, being synonymous with the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) in the form of the absolute cessation of suffering, it is the supreme goal of human existence.
Thus [ends] the <s>Aulūkya</s> (Vaiśeṣika) system in the <s>Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha</s>.
Now, the <s>Ākṣapāda</s> (Nyāya) system. //11//

children.text:
tattvajñānād duḥkhātyantocchedalakṣaṇaṃ niḥśreyasaṃ bhavatīti samānatantre 'pi
          pratipāditam/ tad āha sūtrakāraḥ — pramāṇaprameyetyāditattvajñānān niḥśreyasādhigama iti/
          idaṃ nyāyaśāstrasyādimaṃ sūtram/ nyāyaśāstraṃ ca pañcādhyāyātmakam/ tatra pratyadhyāyam
          āhnikadvayam/ tatra prathamādhyāyasya prathamāhnike bhagavatā gautamena
          pramāṇādipadārthanavakalakṣaṇanirūpaṇaṃ vidhāya dvitīye
          vādādisaptapadārthalakṣaṇanirūpaṇaṃ kṛtam/ dvitīyasya prathame saṃśayaparīkṣaṇaṃ
          pramāṇacatuṣṭayāprāmāṇyaśaṅkānirākaraṇam/ dvitīye 'rthāpattyāder antarbhāvanirūpaṇam/
          tṛtīyasya prathama ātmaśarīrendriyārthaparīkṣaṇam/ dvitīye buddhimanaḥparīkṣaṇam/
          caturthasya prathame pravṛttidoṣapretyabhāvaphaladuḥkhāpavargaparīkṣaṇam/ dvitīye
          doṣanimittakatvanirūpaṇam avayavyādinirūpaṇaṃ ca/ pañcamasya prathame jātibhedanirūpaṇam/
          dvitīye nigrahasthānabhedanirūpaṇam/
children.translated_text: That the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), characterized by the absolute cessation of suffering, comes from the knowledge of reality — this has been established in the allied system as well. Thus the author of the <s>sūtras</s> states: 'From the knowledge of the realities — the means of knowledge, the knowable, and so forth — the attainment of the highest good [results].' This is the first <s>sūtra</s> of the <s>Nyāya</s> scripture. And the <s>Nyāya</s> scripture consists of five chapters. Therein, each chapter has two sections (<s>āhnika</s>). In the first section of the first chapter, the blessed <s>Gautama</s>, having determined the definitions of the nine categories beginning with the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), in the second [section] determined the definitions of the seven categories beginning with debate (<s>vāda</s>). In the first [section] of the second [chapter], there is the examination of doubt and the refutation of objections against the four means of knowledge. In the second, the determination of the subsumption of presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) and the like [within the four]. In the first [section] of the third [chapter], the examination of the self, body, sense-faculties, and objects. In the second, the examination of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) and mind (<s>manas</s>). In the first [section] of the fourth [chapter], the examination of activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), faults (<s>doṣa</s>), transmigration (<s>pretyabhāva</s>), fruit (<s>phala</s>), suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). In the second, the determination of the causal nature of faults, and the determination of the composite whole (<s>avayavin</s>) and the like. In the first [section] of the fifth [chapter], the determination of the divisions of futile rejoinders (<s>jāti</s>). In the second, the determination of the divisions of the grounds for defeat (<s>nigrahasthāna</s>).

children.text:
mānādhīnā meyasiddhir iti nyāyena pramāṇasya prathamam uddeśe tadanusāreṇa lakṣaṇasya
          kathanīyatayā prathamoddiṣṭasya pramāṇasya prathamaṃ lakṣaṇaṃ kathyate —
          sādhanāśrayāvyatiriktatve sati pramāvyāptaṃ pramāṇam/ evaṃ ca pratitantrasiddhāntasiddhaṃ
          parameśvaraprāmāṇyaṃ saṃgṛhītaṃ bhavati/ yad acakathat sūtrakāraḥ —
          mantrāyurvedaprāmāṇyavac ca tatprāmāṇyam āptaprāmāṇyāt iti/ tathā ca
          nyāyanayapārāvārapāradṛśvā viśvavikhyātakīrtir udayanācāryo 'pi nyāyakusumāñjalau caturthe
          stabake —
children.translated_text: By the principle that the establishment of the knowable depends on the means of knowledge, and since the definition of what is first enumerated must be stated in accordance with [the order of] enumeration, the definition of the means of knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), which was first enumerated, is stated first: 'The means of knowledge is that which pervades valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>) while being non-different from its basis and its instrument (<s>sādhana</s>).' And thus, the validity of the supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>), established as a <s>siddhānta</s> (accepted conclusion) within the system, is subsumed. As the author of the <s>sūtras</s> stated: 'The validity of that [the Veda] is like the validity of <s>mantras</s> and <s>Āyurveda</s>, [and arises] from the validity of the trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>).' And thus, <s>Udayanācārya</s>, of world-renowned fame, who saw across the ocean of the <s>Nyāya</s> method, [stated] in the fourth cluster of the <s>Nyāyakusumāñjali</s>:
'Correct ascertainment is valid cognition (<s>miti</s>); its possession is the status of being a valid knower;
the exclusion of its absence is validity (<s>prāmāṇya</s>) — in <s>Gautama</s>'s view.' Thus.
'For the one who is a direct perceiver, eternally conjoined, established in a state independent of any other gateway,
in whom the order of all things presented in the experience of actual reality is entered,
in whom the husk of doubt has fallen away through the departure of faulty vision caused by even a trace [of ignorance],

children.text: śaṅkonmeṣakalaṅkibhiḥ kim aparais tan me pramāṇaṃ śivaḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: what [use is there] of other [means], which are tainted by the stain of the sprouting of doubt? That <s>Śiva</s> is my means of knowledge.' Thus.
That [means of knowledge] is fourfold, through the division into direct perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), analogy (<s>upamāna</s>), and verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>).

children.text:
pramāyāṃ yad dhi pratibhāsate tat prameyam/ tac ca dvādaśaprakāram —
          ātmaśarīrendriyārthabuddhimanaḥpravṛttidoṣapretyabhāvaphala-duḥkhāpavargabhedāt/
children.translated_text: That which appears in valid cognition (<s>pramā</s>) is the knowable (<s>prameya</s>). And it is of twelve kinds — through the division into self (<s>ātman</s>), body (<s>śarīra</s>), sense-faculties (<s>indriya</s>), objects (<s>artha</s>), intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), mind (<s>manas</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), faults (<s>doṣa</s>), transmigration (<s>pretyabhāva</s>), fruit (<s>phala</s>), suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), and liberation (<s>apavarga</s>).
Cognition whose nature is non-determination is doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>). It is threefold, through the division based on common properties, uncommon properties, and conflicting opinions.

children.text: yam adhikṛtya pravartante puruṣās tat prayojanam/ tad dvividham/ dṛṣṭādṛṣṭabhedāt/
children.translated_text: That for the sake of which persons engage [in action] is the purpose (<s>prayojana</s>). It is twofold, through the division into the seen (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>) and the unseen (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>).

The ground for the ascertainment of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) is the example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>). It is twofold, through the division into positive similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) and negative dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>).

A thesis accepted as established by valid means is a <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion). It is fourfold, through the division into universally accepted (<s>sarvatantra</s>), system-specific (<s>pratitantra</s>), topic-specific (<s>adhikaraṇa</s>), and hypothetically accepted (<s>abhyupagama</s>).

A component of the sentence of inference-for-others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) is a member (<s>avayava</s>). It is fivefold, through the division into thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>), reason (<s>hetu</s>), example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>), application (<s>upanaya</s>), and conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>).

The superimposition of the pervaded leading to the superimposition of the pervader is hypothetical reasoning (<s>tarka</s>). It is of eleven kinds, through the division into self-contradiction (<s>vyāghāta</s>), self-dependence (<s>ātmāśraya</s>), mutual dependence (<s>itaretarāśraya</s>), circular dependence (<s>cakraka</s>), infinite regress (<s>anavasthā</s>), counter-establishment (<s>pratibandhi</s>), cumbersome assumption (<s>kalpanāgaurava</s>), parsimony of assumption (<s>kalpanālāghava</s>), exception to a rule (<s>utsargāpavāda</s>), and heterogeneity (<s>vaijātya</s>).

children.text:
yathārthānubhavaparyāyā pramitir nirṇayaḥ/ sa caturvidhaḥ/
          sākṣātkṛtyanumityupamitiśābdabhedāt/
children.translated_text: Ascertainment, synonymous with veridical experience, is determination (<s>nirṇaya</s>). It is fourfold, through the division into direct perception (<s>sākṣātkṛti</s>), inference (<s>anumiti</s>), analogical cognition (<s>upamiti</s>), and verbal cognition (<s>śābda</s>).

children.text:
tattvanirṇayaphalaḥ kathāviśeṣo vādaḥ/ ubhayasādhanavatī vijigīṣukathā jalpaḥ/
          svapakṣasthāpanahīnaḥ kathāviśeṣo vitaṇḍā/ kathā nāma vādiprativādinoḥ
          pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahaḥ/
children.translated_text: A special kind of discourse whose fruit is the determination of reality is debate (<s>vāda</s>). A discourse for victory possessing arguments on both sides is disputation (<s>jalpa</s>). A special kind of discourse devoid of the establishment of one's own position is cavil (<s>vitaṇḍā</s>). 'Discourse' means the adoption of a position and counter-position by the proponent and the opponent.

A non-establishing [reason] that is presented as if it were a reason is a fallacious reason (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>). It is fivefold, through the division into the erratic (<s>savyabhicāra</s>), the contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), the counterbalanced (<s>prakaraṇasama</s>), the equally unproved (<s>sādhyasama</s>), and the untimely (<s>atītakāla</s>).

A ground for objection through the perversion of the function of words is quibble (<s>chala</s>). It is threefold, through the division based on the perversion of denotation (<s>abhidhāna</s>), purport (<s>tātparya</s>), and figurative usage (<s>upacāravṛtti</s>).

presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>), non-difference (<s>aviśeṣa</s>), tenability (<s>upapatti</s>), perception (<s>upalabdhi</s>), non-perception (<s>anupalabdhi</s>), permanence (<s>nitya</s>), impermanence (<s>anitya</s>), effect (<s>kārya</s>), and equality (<s>sama</s>).

A reply that is self-contradictory is a futile rejoinder (<s>jāti</s>). It is of twenty-four kinds, through the division into [those based on] similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>), dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>), superiority (<s>utkarṣa</s>), inferiority (<s>apakarṣa</s>), the statable (<s>varṇya</s>), the unstatable (<s>avarṇya</s>), alternative (<s>vikalpa</s>), attainment of the provable (<s>sādhyaprāpti</s>), non-attainment (<s>aprāpti</s>), extensibility (<s>prasaṅga</s>), counter-example (<s>pratidṛṣṭānta</s>), non-origination (<s>anutpatti</s>), doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>), topic-circularity (<s>prakaraṇa</s>), absence of reason (<s>ahetu</s>),

The ground for defeat is called <s>nigrahasthāna</s>. It is of twenty-two kinds, through the division into abandonment of the thesis (<s>pratijñāhāni</s>), shifting the thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>), contradicting the thesis (<s>pratijñāvirodha</s>), renouncing the thesis (<s>pratijñāsaṃnyāsa</s>), shifting the reason (<s>hetvantara</s>), shifting the topic (<s>arthāntara</s>), the meaningless (<s>nirarthaka</s>), the unintelligible (<s>avijñātārtha</s>), the incoherent (<s>apārthaka</s>), the untimely (<s>aprāptakāla</s>), the deficient (<s>nyūna</s>), the redundant (<s>adhika</s>), repetition (<s>punarukta</s>), failure to respond (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>), ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), lack of ready wit (<s>apratibhā</s>), evasion (<s>vikṣepa</s>), admission of the opponent's position (<s>matānujñā</s>), overlooking what ought to be challenged (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>), challenging what ought not to be challenged (<s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s>), departure from one's own doctrine (<s>apasiddhānta</s>), and fallacious reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>).

children.text:
atra sarvāntargaṇikas tu viśeṣas tatra śāstre vispaṣṭo 'pi vistarabhiyā na
          prastūyate/
children.translated_text: Herein, the internal reckoning of all [these categories] — though clearly [set forth] in that scripture — is not discussed here for fear of prolixity.

children.text:
nanu pramāṇādipadārthaṣoḍaśake pratipādyamāne katham idaṃ nyāyaśāstram iti vyapadiśyate/
          satyam/ tathāpy asādhāraṇyena vyapadeśā bhavantīti nyāyena nyāyasya
          parārthānumānāparaparyāyasya sakalavidyānugrāhakatayā sarvakarmānuṣṭhānasādhanatayā
          pradhānatvena tathā vyapadeśo yujyate/ tathābhāṇi sarvajñena so 'yaṃ paramo nyāyo
          vipratipannapuruṣaṃ prati pratipādakatvāt/ tathā pravṛttihetutvāc ca iti/ pakṣilasvāminā
          ca seyam ānvīkṣikī vidyā pramāṇādibhiḥ padārthaiḥ pravibhajyamānā —
children.translated_text: Now, when the sixteen categories beginning with the means of knowledge are being taught, how is this [treatise] designated as the '<s>Nyāya</s> scripture'? True. Nevertheless, by the principle that designations are made on the basis of what is distinctive, it is fitting that [the treatise] is so designated, because <s>nyāya</s> — which is synonymous with inference-for-others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>) — is preeminent, by virtue of being beneficial to all branches of knowledge and being the means for the performance of all actions. Thus it was stated by the Omniscient One [i.e., <s>Gautama</s>]: 'This is the supreme <s>nyāya</s>, because of its power to instruct a person of conflicting views; and because it is the cause of engagement [in right action].' And by <s>Pakṣilasvāmin</s> (<s>Vātsyāyana</s>): 'This science of inquiry (<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>), analyzed through the categories beginning with the means of knowledge, [is]:
a lamp for all sciences, a means for all actions,
and a foundation for all <s>dharmas</s> — [thus] it has been examined in the exposition of sciences.' Thus.

children.text:
nanu tattvajñānān niḥśresayaṃ bhavatīty uktam/ tatra kiṃ tattvajñānād anantaram eva
          niḥśresayaṃ saṃpadyate/ nety ucyate/ kiṃ tu tattvajñānād
          duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣamithyājñānānām uttarottarāpāye tadanantarāpāyād apavarga iti/ tatra
          mithyājñānaṃ nāmānātmani dehādāv ātmabuddhiḥ/ tadanukūleṣu rāgaḥ/ tatpratikūleṣu dveṣaḥ/
          vastutas tv ātmanaḥ pratikūlam anukūlaṃ vā na kiṃcid vastv asti/ parasparānubandhitvāc ca
          rāgādīnāṃ mūḍho rajyati rakto muhyati mūḍhaḥ kupyati kupito muhyatīti/ tatas tair doṣaiḥ
          preritaḥ prāṇī pratiṣiddhāni śarīreṇa hiṃsāsteyādīny ācarati/ vācā anṛtādīni/ manasā
          paradrohādīni/ seyaṃ pāparūpā pravṛttir adharmaḥ/ śarīreṇa praśastāni
          dānaparaparitrāṇādīni/ vācā hitasatyādīni/ manasā ajighāṃsādīni/ seyaṃ puṇyarūpā pravṛttir
          dharmaḥ/ seyam ubhayī pravṛttiḥ/ tataḥ svānurūpaṃ praśastaṃ ninditaṃ vā janma punaḥ
          śarīrādeḥ prādurbhāvaḥ/ tasmin sati pratikūlavedanīyatayā bādhanātmakaṃ duḥkhaṃ bhavati/
          [na hy apravṛttasya duḥkhaṃ pratyāpadyata iti kaścit prapadyate/]
This sentence is missing in IV p. 115.

ta ime mithyājñānādayo duḥkhāntā avicchedena pravartamānāḥ saṃsāraśabdārtho
          ghaṭīcakravan niravadhir anuvartate/ yadā kaścit puruṣadhaureyaḥ
          purākṛtasukṛtaparipākavaśād ācāryopadeśena sarvam idaṃ duḥkhāyatanaṃ duḥkhānuṣaktaṃ ca
          paśyati tadā tat sarvaṃ heyatvena budhyate/ tatas tannirvartakam avidyādi nivartayitum
          icchati/ tannivṛttyupāyaś ca tattvajñānam iti/ kasyacic catasṛbhir vibhaktaṃ prameyaṃ
          bhāvayataḥ samyagdarśanapadavedanīyatayā tattvajñānaṃ jāyate/ tattvajñānān mithyājñānam
          apaiti/ mithyājñānāpāye doṣā apayānti/ doṣāpāye pravṛttir apaiti/ pravṛttyapāye
          janmāpaiti/ janmāpāye duḥkham atyantaṃ nivartate/ sātyantikī duḥkhanivṛttir apavargaḥ/
          nivṛtter ātyantikatvaṃ nāma nivartyasajātīyasya punas tatrānutpāda iti/ tathā ca
          pāramarṣaṃ sūtram — duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣamithyājñānānām uttarottarāpāye tadanantarāpāyād
          apavargaḥ iti/
children.translated_text: These [factors] beginning with false knowledge and ending with suffering, continuing without interruption, constitute what is meant by the word '<s>saṃsāra</s>' (the cycle of existence) — revolving endlessly like a waterwheel. When a certain foremost among men, by the force of the ripening of merit previously accumulated, through the instruction of a teacher, sees all this as a receptacle of suffering and as connected with suffering, then he understands all of that as what is to be abandoned. Then he wishes to remove ignorance and the like, which produce it. And the means for their removal is the knowledge of reality. For one who contemplates the knowable as divided fourfold [into self, body, etc.], the knowledge of reality arises as that which is cognizable under the designation 'right vision' (<s>samyagdarśana</s>). From the knowledge of reality, false knowledge departs; from the departure of false knowledge, faults depart; from the departure of faults, activity departs; from the departure of activity, birth departs; from the departure of birth, suffering is absolutely removed. The absolute removal of suffering is liberation (<s>apavarga</s>). 'Absoluteness' of the removal means the non-arising again therein of something of the same kind as what was removed. And thus the <s>sūtra</s> of the Sage [<s>Gautama</s>]: 'From the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, faults, and false knowledge, liberation [results] from the removal of that which immediately follows [the preceding].'

Now, it has been said that the highest good arises from the knowledge of reality. Therein, does the highest good come about immediately after the knowledge of reality? No, it is said. Rather, from the knowledge of reality, through the successive removal of false knowledge (<s>mithyājñāna</s>), faults (<s>doṣa</s>), activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), birth (<s>janma</s>), and suffering (<s>duḥkha</s>), liberation (<s>apavarga</s>) [comes about] from the removal of that which immediately follows [the preceding removal]. Therein, false knowledge means the cognition of the self in what is not the self, such as the body and the like. Attachment (<s>rāga</s>) toward what is favorable to that [falsely conceived self]; aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>) toward what is unfavorable to it. But in reality, nothing whatsoever is favorable or unfavorable to the self. And because attachment and the like are mutually connected: the deluded person becomes attached; the attached becomes deluded; the deluded becomes angry; the angry becomes deluded. Then, impelled by those faults, the living being performs with the body prohibited acts such as violence, theft, and the like; with speech, falsehood and the like; with mind, malice toward others and the like. This sinful activity is <s>adharma</s> (demerit). With the body, praiseworthy acts such as giving, protecting others, and the like; with speech, beneficial and truthful [words] and the like; with mind, non-injury and the like. This meritorious activity is <s>dharma</s> (merit). This is the twofold activity. From that, in accordance [with one's karma], either praiseworthy or blameworthy birth — the arising again of a body and the like. When that [birth] exists, suffering arises — affliction in the form of that which is experienced as unfavorable. [For no one concedes that suffering befalls one who has not acted.]

children.text:
nanu duḥkhātyantocchedo 'pavarga ity etad adyāpi kaphoṇiguḍāyitaṃ vartate/ tat kathaṃ
          siddhavatkṛtya vyavahriyate iti cet —
children.translated_text: Now, [the thesis that] the absolute cessation of suffering is liberation — this still remains a matter of dispute [literally: 'an elbow-lump']. How then is it treated as if established? If [one objects] thus —

children.text:
maivam/ sarveṣāṃ mokṣavādinām apavargadaśāyām ātyantikī duḥkhanivṛttir astīty asyārthasya
          sarvatantrasiddhāntasiddhatayā ghaṇṭāpathatvāt/
children.translated_text: Do not say so! Because for all proponents of liberation, the thesis that in the state of liberation there is the absolute cessation of suffering — this proposition, being an established conclusion accepted by all systems (<s>sarvatantrasiddhānta</s>), is like a well-trodden highway.

children.text:
tathā hi — ātmocchedo mokṣa iti mādhyamikamate duḥkhocchedo 'stīty etāvat tāvad avivādam/
          atha manyethāḥ — śarīrādivad ātmāpi duḥkhahetutvād ucchedya iti tan na saṃgacchate/
          vikalpānupapatteḥ/ kim ātmā jñānasaṃtāno vivakṣitas tadatirikto vā/ prathame na
          vipratipattiḥ/ kaḥ khalv anukūlam ācarati pratikūlam ācaret/ dvitīye tasya nityatve
          nivṛttir aśakyavidhānaiva/ anityatve pravṛttyanupapattiḥ/ vyavahārānupapattiś cādhikaṃ
          dūṣaṇam/ na khalu kaścit prekṣāvān ātmanas tu kāmāya sarvaṃ priyaṃ bhavatīti sarvataḥ
          priyatamasyātmanaḥ samucchedāya prayatate/ sarvo hi prāṇī sati dharmiṇi mukta iti
          vyavaharati nanu/
children.translated_text: For thus — "The annihilation of the Self is liberation" according to the <s>Mādhyamika</s> view: the cessation of suffering exists — this much at least is undisputed. Now, if you think: "Like the body and the like, the Self too, being a cause of suffering, should be annihilated" — that does not hold, because the alternatives are untenable. Is the Self intended as the stream of cognitions, or as something distinct from that? In the first case, there is no disagreement, for who indeed, while doing what is favorable, would do what is unfavorable? In the second case, if it is permanent, cessation is impossible to accomplish; if impermanent, activity is untenable. And the impossibility of conventional usage is a further defect. For surely no discerning person strives for the complete annihilation of the Self, which is dearest of all, as [scripture says]: "For the sake of the Self indeed is everything dear." For every living being, when the substrate (<s>dharmin</s>) exists, uses the expression "liberated."

children.text:
dharminivṛttau nirmalajñānodayo mahodaya iti vijñānavādivāde sāmagryabhāvaḥ
          sāmānādhikaraṇyānupapattiś ca/ bhāvanācatuṣṭayaṃ hi tasya kāraṇam abhīṣṭam/ tac ca
          kṣaṇabhaṅgapakṣe sthiraikādhārāsaṃbhavāl laṅghanābhyāsādivad anāsāditaprakarṣaṃ na sphuṭam
          abhijñānam abhijanayituṃ prabhavati/ sopaplavasya jñānasaṃtānasya baddhatve nirupaplavasya
          ca muktatve yo baddhaḥ sa eva mukta iti sāmānādhikaraṇyaṃ na saṃgacchate/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Vijñānavāda</s> (Consciousness-only) position, [according to which] upon the cessation of the substrate, the arising of stainless knowledge is the great attainment — there is the absence of the aggregate of causes and the impossibility of co-referentiality (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>). For the fourfold meditation is the desired cause of that [liberation]. And in the position of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>), since a stable single substrate is impossible, like the practice of leaping [where progress is not visible without a stable practitioner], it is not capable of producing clear, developed cognition. When the stream of cognition with disturbances is bound, and when the one without disturbances is liberated — the co-referentiality "the very one who was bound is liberated" does not hold.

children.text:
āvaraṇamuktir muktir iti jainajanābhimato 'pi mārgo na nisargato nirargalaḥ/ aṅga bhavān
          pṛṣṭo vyācaṣṭām kim āvaraṇam/ dharmādharmabhrāntaya iti cet — iṣṭam eva/ atha deham
          evāvaraṇam/ tathā ca tannivṛttau pañjarān muktasya śukasyevātmanaḥ satatordhvagamanaṃ
          muktir iti cet — tadā vaktavyam/ kim ayam ātmā mūrto 'mūrto vā/ prathame niravayavaḥ
          sāvayavo vā/ niravayavatve niravayavo mūrtaḥ paramāṇur iti paramāṇulakṣaṇāpattyā
          paramāṇudharmavad ātmadharmāṇām atīndriyatvaṃ prasajyeta/ sāvayavatve yat sāvayavaṃ tad
          anityam iti pratibandhabalenānityatvāpattau kṛtapraṇāśākṛtābhyāgamau niṣpratibandhau
          prasaretām/ amūrtatve gamanam anupapannam eva/ calanātmikāyāḥ kriyāyā
          mūrtatvapratibandhāt/
children.translated_text: The path favored by the <s>Jaina</s> people — that liberation is the removal of obscuration (<s>āvaraṇa</s>) — is also not naturally unobstructed. Please, sir, when asked, explain: what is the obscuration? If [one says] "<s>dharma</s>, <s>adharma</s>, and delusion" — that is acceptable. But if [one says] the body itself is the obscuration, and thus, upon its cessation, liberation is the Self's constant upward movement, like a parrot released from its cage — then it must be said: Is this Self corporeal or incorporeal? In the first case, is it partless or does it have parts? If partless, then by falling into the definition of an atom — "a partless corporeal entity is an atom" — the properties of the Self would, like the properties of atoms, have the absurd consequence of being beyond the senses. If it has parts, then by the force of the invariable connection "whatever has parts is impermanent," upon the consequence of impermanence, the [doctrines of] the destruction of what has been done and the accrual of what has not been done would proceed unrestrained. If incorporeal, movement is simply untenable, because activity, which is of the nature of motion, is restricted to the corporeal.

children.text:
pāratantryaṃ bandhaḥ svātantryaṃ mokṣa iti cārvākapakṣe 'pi svātantryaṃ duḥkhanivṛttiś
          cet — avivādaḥ/ aiśvaryaṃ cet — sātiśayatayā sadṛkṣatayā ca prekṣāvatāṃ nābhimatam/
children.translated_text: In the <s>Cārvāka</s> position that "dependence is bondage, independence is liberation" too — if independence means the cessation of suffering, there is no dispute; if [it means] sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya</s>), it is not accepted by discerning people, because of its being surpassable and because of its having equals.

children.text:
prakṛtipuruṣānyatvakhyātau prakṛtyuparame puruṣasya svarūpeṇāvasthānaṃ muktir iti
          sāṃkhyākhyāte 'pi pakṣe duḥkhocchedo 'sty eva/ vivekajñānaṃ puruṣāśrayaṃ prakṛtyāśrayaṃ
          vety etāvad avaśiṣyate/ tatra puruṣāśrayam iti na śliṣyate/ puruṣasya
          kauṭasthyāvasthānanirodhāpātāt/ nāpi prakṛtir āśrayaḥ
ASS, IV, A. The masculine compound

(in all editions) makes no sense. The
              preceding context favors neuter

.
              However, since there is a back reference to feminine
in the immediately following sentence, I have accepted the reading

/ acetanatvāt tasyāḥ/ kiṃ ca prakṛtiḥ pravṛttisvabhāvā nivṛttisvabhāvā vā/ ādye
          'nirmokṣaḥ/ svabhāvasyānapāyāt/ dvitīye saṃprati saṃsāro 'stam iyāt/
children.translated_text: — because of its being insentient. Moreover, is <s>Prakṛti</s> of the nature of activity or of the nature of cessation? In the first case, there would be no liberation, since its own nature does not depart. In the second case, <s>saṃsāra</s> would come to an end right now.

In the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>-proclaimed position too — that liberation is the Self's abiding in its own nature upon the cessation of <s>Prakṛti</s>, through the knowledge of the difference between <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> — the cessation of suffering certainly exists. Only this much remains [as a question]: Is the discriminative knowledge (<s>vivekajñāna</s>) seated in <s>Puruṣa</s> or in <s>Prakṛti</s>? Therein, "seated in <s>Puruṣa</s>" does not cohere, because of the absurd consequence of destroying the immutable abiding of <s>Puruṣa</s>. Nor is <s>Prakṛti</s> the substrate

children.text:
nityaniratiśayasukhābhivyaktir muktir iti bhaṭṭasarvajñādyabhimate 'pi duḥkhanivṛttir
          abhimataiva/ paraṃ tu nityasukhaṃ na pramāṇapaddhatim adhyāste/ śrutis tatra pramāṇam iti
          cet — na/ yogyānupalabdhibādhite tadanavakāśāt/ avakāśe vā grāvaplave 'pi
          tathābhāvaprasaṅgāt/
children.translated_text: In the position favored by <s>Bhaṭṭa Sarvajña</s> and others — that liberation is the manifestation of eternal, unsurpassable bliss — the cessation of suffering is indeed accepted. But the eternal bliss does not tread the path of valid evidence. If [one says] <s>śruti</s> is the evidence there — no, because it is contradicted by qualified non-apprehension (<s>yogyānupalabdhi</s>), which leaves no room for it. And if there were room, then even the floating of a stone would have the absurd consequence of being so [i.e., of being evidenced].
Section 11.144

children.text:
nanu sukhābhivyaktir muktir iti pakṣaṃ parityajya duḥkhanivṛttir eva muktir iti svīkāraḥ
          kṣīraṃ vihāyārocakagrastasya sauvīrarucim anubhāvayatīti cet — tad etan nāṭakapakṣapatitaṃ
          tvadvaca ity upekṣyate/ sukhasya sātiśayatayā sadṛkṣatayā bahupratyanīkākrāntatayā
          sādhanaprārthanaparikliṣṭatayā ca duḥkhāvinābhūtatvena viṣānuṣaktamadhuvad
          duḥkhapakṣanikṣepāt/ nanv ekam anusaṃdhitsato 'paraṃ pracyavata iti nyāyena duḥkhavat
          sukham apy ucchidyata ity akāmyo 'yam pakṣa iti cet — maivaṃ maṃsthāḥ/ sukhasaṃpādane
          duḥkhasādhanabāhulyānuṣaṅganiyamena taptāyaḥpiṇḍe tapanīyabuddhyā pravartamānena
          sāmyāpātāt/ tathā hi nyāyopārjiteṣu viṣayeṣu kiyantaḥ sukhakhadyotāḥ kiyanti
          duḥkhadurdināni/ anyāyopārjiteṣu tu yad bhaviṣyati tan manasāpi cintayituṃ na śakyam iti/
          etat svānubhavam apracchādayantaḥ santo vidāṃkurvantu vidāṃ varā bhavantaḥ/ tasmāt
          pariśeṣāt parameśvarānugrahavaśāc chravaṇādikrameṇātmatattvasākṣātkāravataḥ
          puruṣadhaureyasya duḥkhanivṛttir ātyantikī niḥśreyasam iti niravadyam/
children.translated_text: Now, if [one says]: "Abandoning the position that liberation is the manifestation of bliss and accepting that liberation is merely the cessation of suffering is like one afflicted with anorexia who, abandoning milk, experiences a taste for <s>sauvīra</s> (sour gruel)" — this speech of yours is a mere theatrical pose and is disregarded. Because bliss, being surpassable, having equals, overwhelmed by many adversaries, and tormented by the desire for means [of obtaining it], is inseparable from suffering — like honey mixed with poison — it is placed in the category of suffering. Now, if [one says]: "By the principle that when one desires to synthesize one thing, the other drops away — like suffering, bliss too would be annihilated, and this position is undesirable" — do not think so! Because, in the acquisition of bliss, there is an invariable concomitance with an abundance of means that are [themselves] suffering — like one who, approaching a heated iron ball thinking it is gold, encounters equality [of suffering and pleasure]. For thus: in wealth acquired by just means, how few are the fireflies of happiness, how many the dark clouds of suffering! And in wealth acquired by unjust means, what will happen cannot even be thought of in the mind. Let the virtuous, not concealing this [truth] of their own experience, make it known — may you be the best of the wise!
