Therefore, even for present-day [students], activity therein would not be established [without stating the purpose]. Lest that [activity] perish, the purpose conveying its <s>Vedāṅga</s> status must be explained. If, even after the purpose has been explained, they would not engage [in study], then, being devoid of the knowledge of the refinement of worldly words, they would become partakers of sin (<s>pratyavāya</s>) in sacrificial rites. They would fall from <s>dharma</s>. For this very reason, the ritualists recite: "One who has established the sacred fires, having used an incorrect word, should perform the expiatory <s>Sārasvatī iṣṭi</s> (offering to <s>Sarasvatī</s>)." Therefore, for the purpose of the explanatory statement conveying its <s>Vedāṅga</s> status, it is called "instruction of words" (<s>śabdānuśāsana</s>), not "grammar" (<s>vyākaraṇa</s>). And the refinement of words (<s>śabdasaṃskāra</s>) is the purpose of the science of grammar, because it operates with that aim. Just as heaven is the purpose of a sacrifice performed with the aim of heaven. Therefore, the instruction of words — knowable through the designation "refinement" — is the purpose of <s>śabdānuśāsana</s>.
Section 13.63

children.text:
nanv evam apy abhimataṃ prayojanaṃ na labhyate/ tadupāyābhāvāt/ atha pratipadapāṭha
          evabhyupāya iti manyethās tarhi sa hy anabhyupāyaḥ śabdānāṃ pratipattau pratipadapāṭho
          bhavet/ śabdāpaśabdabhedenānantyāc chabdānām/ evaṃ hi samāmnāyate bṛhaspatir indrāya
          divyaṃ varṣasahasraṃ pratipadapāṭhavihitānāṃ śabdānāṃ śabdapārāyaṇaṃ provāca nāntaṃ
          jagāma/ bṛhaspatiś ca pravaktā indro ’dhyetā divyaṃ varṣasahasram adhyayanakālaḥ/ na ca
          pārāvāptir abhūt/ kim utādya yaś ciraṃ jīvati sa varṣaśataṃ jīvati/
          adhītibodhācaraṇapracāraiś caturbhir hy upāyair vidyopayuktā bhavati/
          tatrādhyayanakālenaiva sarvam āyur upayuktaṃ syāt/ tasmād anabhyupāyaḥ śabdānāṃ
          pratipattau pratipadapāṭha iti prayojanaṃ na sidhyed iti cet
children.translated_text: Now, even so, the desired purpose is not obtained, because of the absence of a means [to achieve it]. If you think that word-by-word recitation is the means — that is indeed no means for the comprehension of words, because of the infinity of words through the division into correct words and incorrect words. For thus it is traditionally reported: <s>Bṛhaspati</s> taught <s>Indra</s> the word-by-word recitation of prescribed words for a divine thousand years, and did not reach the end. And <s>Bṛhaspati</s> was the teacher, <s>Indra</s> the student, and a divine thousand years the period of study — and yet there was no completion. How much less [could it be completed] nowadays, when one who lives long lives a hundred years. Knowledge is put to use through the four means of study (<s>adhīti</s>), understanding (<s>bodha</s>), practice (<s>ācaraṇa</s>), and propagation (<s>pracāra</s>). Of these, the entire lifespan would be consumed by the time of study alone. Therefore, word-by-word recitation is no means for the comprehension of words, and the purpose would not be established — if [one argues] thus,

children.text:
maivam/ śabdapratipatteḥ pratipadapāṭhasādhyatvānaṅgīkārāt/ prakṛtyādivibhāgakalpanāvatsu
          lakṣyeṣu sāmānyaviśeṣarūpāṇāṃ lakṣaṇānāṃ parjanyavat sakṛd eva pravṛttau bahūnāṃ śabdānām
          anuśāsanopalambhāc ca/ tathā hi/ karmaṇy aṇ (Pā° sū° 3.2.1) ity ekena sāmānyarūpeṇa
          lakṣaṇena karmopapadād dhātumātrād aṇpratyaye kṛte kumbhakāraḥ kāṇḍalāva ityādīnāṃ bahūnāṃ
          śabdānām anuśāsanam upalabhyate/ evam āto ’nupasarge kaḥ (Pā° sū° 3.2.18) ity ekena
          viśeṣalakṣaṇenākārāntād dhātoḥ kapratyaye kṛte dhānyado dhanada ityādīnāṃ bahūnāṃ śabdānām
          anuśāsanam upalabhyate/ bṛhaspatir indrāyeti pratipadapāṭhasyāśakyatvapratipādanaparo
          ’rthavādaḥ/
children.translated_text: Do not say so! Because we do not accept that the comprehension of words is to be accomplished by word-by-word recitation. And because, when general and specific rules are applied to the usages (<s>lakṣya</s>) which involve the analysis of roots (<s>prakṛti</s>) and the like, the instruction of many words is observed [to be accomplished] through a single application, like rain [falling once and nourishing many]. For thus: by the single general rule "<s>aṇ</s> [is affixed] when the object [is intended]" (<s>Pāṇini</s> 3.2.1), when the <s>aṇ</s> suffix is applied to any verbal root followed by an object-denoting word, the instruction of many words such as <s>kumbhakāra</s> (potter), <s>kāṇḍalāva</s> (reed-cutter), and the like is observed. Likewise, by the single specific rule "<s>ka</s> [is affixed] after [a root ending in] <s>ā</s>, without a prefix" (<s>Pāṇini</s> 3.2.18), when the <s>ka</s> suffix is applied to a root ending in <s>ā</s>, the instruction of many words such as <s>dhānyada</s> (grain-giver), <s>dhanada</s> (wealth-giver), and the like is observed. The [story that] "<s>Bṛhaspati</s> [taught] <s>Indra</s>" is an <s>arthavāda</s> (explanatory passage) aimed at conveying the impossibility of word-by-word recitation.
Section 13.83

children.text:
nanv anyeṣv apy aṅgeṣu satsu kim ity etad evādriyate/ ucyate: pradhānaṃ ca ṣaṭsv aṅgeṣu
          vyākaraṇam/ pradhāne ca kṛto yatnaḥ phalavān bhavati/ tad uktam:
children.translated_text: Now, when other <s>aṅgas</s> (auxiliary disciplines) also exist, why is this one alone valued? It is said: Grammar is the chief among the six <s>aṅgas</s>. And effort applied to the chief bears fruit. As stated:

children.text: āsannaṃ brahmaṇas tasya tapasām uttamaṃ tapaḥ/
children.translated_text: "Close to <s>Brahman</s>, the supreme <s>tapas</s> (austerity) among austerities,

children.text: prathamaṃ chandasām aṅgam āhur vyākaraṇaṃ budhāḥ//
children.translated_text: the wise call grammar the foremost auxiliary of the <s>Vedas</s>."

children.text:
iti/ tasmād vyākaraṇaśāstrasya śabdānuśāsanaṃ bhavati sākṣāt prayojanam/ pāraṃparyeṇa tu
          vedarakṣādīni/ ata evoktaṃ bhagavatā bhāṣyakāreṇa: rakṣohāgamalaghvasaṃdehāḥ prayojanam
          iti/
children.translated_text: Therefore, the direct purpose of the science of grammar is the instruction of words. And indirectly, the preservation of the <s>Vedas</s> and the like. For this very reason, the blessed commentator (<s>bhāṣyakāra</s>) has stated: "Preservation, observance, tradition, conciseness, and removal of doubt are the purpose."
Section 13.91

children.text:
sādhuśabdaprayogavaśād abhyudayo ’pi bhavati/ tathā ca kathitaṃ kātyāyanena:
          śāstrapūrvake prayoge ’bhyudayas tat tulyaṃ vedaśabdeneti / anyair apy uktam: ekaḥ śabdaḥ
          samyag jñātaḥ suṣṭhu prayuktaḥ svarge loke kāmadhuk bhavatīti/ tathā
children.translated_text: Through the use of correct words, worldly prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>) also results. And thus <s>Kātyāyana</s> has stated: "In usage preceded by grammar, prosperity [arises]; that is equal to a Vedic word." Others too have said: "A single word, correctly known and properly used, becomes a wish-fulfilling cow in the heavenly world." And likewise:
"Those who go to heaven, the desired happiness, with well-formed and bound verbal compositions —
but those who speak incorrectly go downward."
Section 13.97

children.text: nanv acetanasya śabdasya katham īdṛśaṃ sāmarthyam upapadyata iti cet:
children.translated_text: Now, if [one asks]: How is such power tenable for an insentient word?

children.text: maivaṃ manyethāḥ/ mahatā devena sāmyaśravaṇāt/ tad āha śrutiḥ:
children.translated_text: Do not think so! Because [speech] is heard to be equal to the great deity. Thus the <s>śruti</s> states:

children.text: catvāri śṛṅgā trayo asya pādā dve śīrṣe sapta hastāso asya/
children.translated_text: "Four are his horns, three his feet, two his heads, seven his hands;

children.text: tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti maho devo martyāṃ āviveśa/
children.translated_text: bound threefold, the bull roars loudly — the great deity has entered mortals."

children.text:
vyācakāra ca bhāṣyakāraḥ: catvāri śṛṅgāṇi catvāri padajātāni nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ/
          trayo asya pādā laḍādiviṣayās trayo bhūtabhaviṣyadvartamānakālāḥ/ dve śīrṣe dvau
          śabdātmānau nityaḥ kāryaś ca/ vyaṅgyavyañjakabhedāt/ sapta hastāso asya tiṅā saha sapta
          subvibhaktayaḥ/ tridhā baddhas triṣu sthāneṣu urasi kaṇṭhe śirasi ca baddhaḥ/ vṛṣabha iti
          prasiddhavṛṣabhatvena rūpaṇaṃ kriyate/ varṣaṇāt/ varṣaṇaṃ ca jñānapūrvakānuṣṭhānena
          phalapradatvam/ roravīti śabdaṃ karoti/ rautiḥ śabdakarmā/ iha śabdaśabdena prapañco
          vivakṣitaḥ/ maho devo martyāṃ āviveśa/ mahān devaḥ śabdo martyā maraṇadharmāṇo manuṣyās
          tān āviveśeti/ mahatā devena pareṇa brahmaṇā sāmyam uktaṃ syāt iti/
children.translated_text: And the commentator (<s>bhāṣyakāra</s>) has explained: The four horns are the four classes of words: nouns (<s>nāma</s>), verbs (<s>ākhyāta</s>), prefixes (<s>upasarga</s>), and particles (<s>nipāta</s>). His three feet are the three domains of <s>laṭ</s> and the like — the three tenses: past, future, and present. His two heads are the two natures of the word-essence: the eternal and the produced — through the distinction of the signified and the signifier. His seven hands are the seven case-endings (<s>sup vibhaktis</s>) together with the verbal endings (<s>tiṅ</s>). Bound threefold: bound in three places — the chest, the throat, and the head. "Bull" — the description is made through its well-known bull-nature, from "raining" (<s>varṣaṇa</s>). And raining means bestowing fruit through practice preceded by knowledge. "Roars" — makes sound. The root <s>rau</s> has the meaning of sound-making. Here, by the word "sound," the manifest world (<s>prapañca</s>) is intended. "The great deity has entered mortals" — the great deity, speech, has entered mortals, i.e., mortal human beings. The equality [of speech] with the great deity, the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>, has thus been stated.
Section 13.113

children.text: jagannidānaṃ sphoṭākhyo niravayavo nityaḥ śabdo brahmaiveti hariṇābhāṇi brahmakāṇḍe:
children.translated_text: That the cause of the world is the partless, eternal word called <s>sphoṭa</s>, which is <s>Brahman</s> itself — was stated by <s>Hari</s> (<s>Bhartṛhari</s>) in the <s>Brahmakāṇḍa</s>:
"Without beginning or end, <s>Brahman</s>, whose essence is the word-reality, the imperishable —
from which the world's creative process proceeds as a transformation into the form of meaning."
Section 13.117

children.text: nanu nāmākhyātabhedena padadvaividhyapratīteḥ kathaṃ cāturvidhyam uktam iti cet:
children.translated_text: Now, since a twofold division of words into nouns and verbs is known, how has the fourfold [classification] been stated? —

children.text: maivam/ prakārāntarasya prasiddhatvāt/ tad uktam prakīrṇake:
children.translated_text: Do not say so! Because another mode [of classification] is well known. As stated in the <s>Prakīrṇaka</s>:

children.text: dvidhā kaiścit padaṃ bhinnaṃ caturdhā pañcadhāpi vā/
children.translated_text: "The word (<s>pada</s>) is divided into two by some, into four, and even into five,
having been extracted from sentences, like roots and suffixes."

children.text:
karmapravacanīyena vai pañcamena saha padasya pañcavidhatvam iti helārājo vyākhyātavān/
          karmapravacanīyās tu kriyāviśeṣopajanitasaṃbandhāvacchedahetava iti
          saṃbandhaviśeṣadyotanadvāreṇa kriyāviśeṣadyotanād upasargeṣv evāntarbhavantīty
          abhisaṃdhāya padacāturvidhyaṃ bhāṣyakāreṇoktam yuktam iti vivektavyam/
children.translated_text: <s>Helārāja</s> has explained that, with the <s>karmapravacanīya</s> (a fifth category), the fivefold classification of words [obtains]. But the <s>karmapravacanīyas</s>, being causes of delimiting the relation produced by a specific action, are included within prefixes (<s>upasargas</s>) themselves, since they indicate a specific action through indicating a specific relation — with this understanding, the fourfold classification of words stated by the commentator (<s>bhāṣyakāra</s>) should be regarded as appropriate.
Section 13.126

children.text:
nanu bhavatā sphoṭātmā nityaḥ śabda iti nijāgadyate/ tan na mṛṣyāmahe/ tatra
          pramāṇābhāvād iti kecit/
children.translated_text: Now, you assert that the word whose essence is <s>sphoṭa</s> is eternal — we do not tolerate that. Because of the absence of a means of valid knowledge therein — so say some.

children.text:
atrocyate: pratyakṣam evātra pramāṇam/ gaur ity ekaṃ padam iti
          nānāvarṇātiriktaikapadāvagateḥ sarvajanīnatvāt/ na hy asati bādhake padānubhavaḥ śakyo
          mithyeti vaktum/ padārthapratītyanyathānupapattyāpi sphoṭo ’bhyupagantavyaḥ/ na ca
          varṇebhya eva tatpratyayaḥ prādurbhavatīti parīkṣākṣamam/ vikalpāsahatvāt/ kiṃ varṇāḥ
          samastā vyastā vārthapratyayaṃ janayanti/ nādyaḥ/ varṇānāṃ kṣaṇikānāṃ samūhāsaṃbhavāt/
          nāntyaḥ/ vyastavarṇebhyo ’rthapratyayāsaṃbhavāt/ na ca vyāsasamāsābhyām anyaḥ prakāraḥ
          samastīti/ tasmād varṇānāṃ vācakatvānupapattau yadbalād arthapratipattiḥ sa sphoṭaḥ/
          varṇātirikto varṇābhivyaṅgyo ’rthapratyāyako nityaḥ śabdaḥ sphoṭa iti tadvido vadanti/ ata
          eva sphuṭyate vyajyate varṇair iti sphoṭo varṇābhivyaṅgyaḥ sphuṭati sphuṭībhavaty asmād
          artha iti sphoṭo ’rthapratyāyaka iti sphoṭaśabdārtham ubhayathā nirāhuḥ/ tathā coktaṃ
          bhagavatā patañjalinā mahābhāṣye: atha gaur ity atra kaḥ śabdo yenoccāritena
          sāsnālāṅgūlakakudakhuraviṣāṇināṃ saṃpratyayo bhavati sa śabdaḥ iti/ vivṛtaṃ ca kaiyaṭena:
          vaiyākaraṇā varṇavyatiriktasya padasya vācakatvam icchanti/ varṇānāṃ vācakatve
          dvitīyādivarṇoccāraṇānarthakyaprasaṅgād ityādinā tadvyatiriktaḥ sphoṭo nādābhivyaṅgyo
          vācako vistareṇa vākyapadīye vyavasthāpita ityantena prabandhena/
children.translated_text: Here it is replied: Direct perception itself is the valid evidence here. Because the cognition of a single word, distinct from the various phonemes, [when hearing] "cow" (<s>gaur</s>) as one word, is universal [i.e., experienced by everyone]. For, in the absence of a contradicting [cognition], the experience of the word cannot be called false. And <s>sphoṭa</s> must be accepted also because the cognition of word-meaning cannot be otherwise explained. And it does not withstand examination [to say] that the cognition arises from the phonemes themselves, because the alternatives are untenable. Do the phonemes, collectively or individually, produce the cognition of meaning? Not the first, because the aggregation of phonemes, which are momentary, is impossible. Not the second, because the cognition of meaning from individual phonemes is impossible. And there is no mode other than collective and individual. Therefore, since the phonemes are incapable of being denotative, that by the power of which the comprehension of meaning [occurs] is the <s>sphoṭa</s>. The knowers of that say: "<s>Sphoṭa</s> is an eternal word, distinct from phonemes, manifested by phonemes, and conveying meaning." For this very reason, they have explained the meaning of the word <s>sphoṭa</s> in two ways: "It is manifested (<s>sphuṭyate</s>), i.e., revealed by phonemes" — hence <s>sphoṭa</s> is what is manifested by phonemes; and "meaning bursts forth (<s>sphuṭati</s>) from it" — hence <s>sphoṭa</s> conveys meaning. And thus it is stated by the blessed <s>Patañjali</s> in the <s>Mahābhāṣya</s>: "Now, in "cow" (<s>gaur</s>), what is the word by the utterance of which the cognition of [a being with] a dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns arises? That is the word." And <s>Kaiyaṭa</s> has explained: "The grammarians hold that the word, distinct from the phonemes, is the denotative [entity]. Because, if the phonemes were the denotative [entities], the utterance of the second and subsequent phonemes would become purposeless" — and so on, up to: "That <s>sphoṭa</s>, distinct from phonemes, manifested by <s>nāda</s> (sound), and denotative, has been established at length in the <s>Vākyapadīya</s>" — with this continuous [exposition].
Section 13.147

children.text:
nanu sphoṭasyāpy arthapratyāyakatvaṃ na ghaṭate/ vikalpāsahatvāt/ kim abhivyaktaḥ sphoṭo
          ’rthaṃ pratyāyayaty anabhivyakto vā/ na caramaḥ/
          sarvapadārthapratyayalakṣaṇakāryotpādaprasaṅgāt/ sphoṭasya nityatvābhyupagamena
          nirapekṣasya hetoḥ sadā sattvena kāryasya vilambāyogāt/
          athaitaddoṣaparijihīrṣayābhivyaktaḥ sphoṭo ’rthaṃ pratyāyayatīti kakṣīkriyate tathāpy
          abhivyañjayanto varṇāḥ kiṃ pratyekam abhivyañjayanti saṃbhūya vā/ pakṣadvaye ’pi varṇānāṃ
          vācakatvapakṣe bhavatā ye doṣā bhāṣitās ta eva sphoṭābhivyañjakatvapakṣe vyāvartanīyāḥ/
          tad uktaṃ bhaṭṭācāryair mīmāṃsāślokavārtike:
children.translated_text: Now, the capacity of <s>sphoṭa</s> too to convey meaning does not hold, because the alternatives are untenable. Does the manifested <s>sphoṭa</s> convey meaning, or the unmanifested? Not the latter, because of the absurd consequence of the production of the effect — namely, the cognition of all word-meanings — [at all times]. Since, by the acceptance of the eternality of <s>sphoṭa</s>, a cause that is without dependence [on other factors], being always present, would not allow any delay in the effect. If, wishing to avoid this fault, it is maintained that the manifested <s>sphoṭa</s> conveys meaning — even so, do the manifesting phonemes manifest [it] individually or collectively? In both alternatives, the very faults stated by you against the position that the phonemes are the denotative [entities] must be addressed [equally] against the position that the phonemes are the manifestors of <s>sphoṭa</s>. As stated by the <s>Bhaṭṭācāryas</s> (i.e., <s>Kumārila</s>) in the <s>Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika</s>:
"That partless <s>sphoṭa</s> which is manifested by cognitions of the phonemes —
even it is not freed from a single objection upon cross-examination."

children.text:
vibhaktyanteṣv eva varṇeṣu suptiṅantaṃ padam iti pāṇininā te vibhaktyantāḥ padam iti
          gautamena ca padasaṃjñāyā vihitatvāt saṃketagraheṇānugrahavaśād varṇeṣv eva padabuddhir
          bhaviṣyati/ tarhi sara ity etasmin pade yāvanto varṇās tāvanta eva rasa ity atrāpi/ evaṃ
          vanaṃ navaṃ nadī dīnā rāmo māro rājā jāretyādiṣv arthabhedapratītir na syād iti cen
children.translated_text: Since the designation 'word' (<s>pada</s>) has been prescribed by <s>Pāṇini</s> — 'that which ends in a case-ending or a verbal ending is a word' — for phonemes ending in inflectional suffixes alone, and by <s>Gautama</s> — 'those ending in inflectional suffixes are a word' — the cognition of a word will arise in the phonemes alone by the force of the apprehension of the convention. Then, in the word 'sara,' there are as many phonemes as in 'rasa' as well. Thus, in [pairs such as] 'vanaṃ' and 'navaṃ,' 'nadī' and 'dīnā,' 'rāmo' and 'māro,' 'rājā' and 'jāre' — the cognition of different meanings would not arise. If [one argues thus] —

children.text: na/ kramabhedena bhedasaṃbhavāt/ tad uktam tautātitaiḥ:
children.translated_text: No. Because difference is possible through difference in sequence. As stated by the followers of <s>Kumārila</s>:
'However many, of whatever kind, and whichever phonemes, in the conveyance of whatever meaning —
those phonemes, whose capacity is known [by convention], convey [meaning] in just that way.' Thus.

children.text:
tasmād yaś cobhayoḥ samo doṣo na tenaikaś codyo bhavatīti nyāyād varṇānām eva
          vācakatvopapattau nātiriktasphoṭakalpanāvakalpata iti cet
children.translated_text: Therefore, by the principle that 'a fault common to both [positions] cannot be used to challenge one alone,' since the denotative capacity of phonemes alone is tenable, the hypothesis of a superfluous <s>sphoṭa</s> is inadmissible — if [one argues] thus,

children.text:
tad etat kāśakuśāvalambanakalpam/ vikalpānupapatteḥ/ kiṃ varṇamātraṃ
          padapratyayāvalambanaṃ varṇasamūho vā/ nādyaḥ/ parasparavilakṣaṇavarṇamālāyām abhinnaṃ
          nimittaṃ puṣpeṣu vinā sūtraṃ mālāpratyayavad ity ekaṃ padam iti pratipatter anupapatteḥ/
          nāpi dvitīyaḥ/ uccaritapradhvastānāṃ varṇānāṃ samūhabhāvāsaṃbhavāt/ tatra hi
          samūhavyapadeśo ye padārthā ekasmin pradeśe sahāvasthitatayā bahavo ’nubhūyante/
          yathaikasmin pradeśe sahāvasthitatayānubhūyamāneṣu dhavakhadirapalāśādiṣu samūhavyapadeśo
          yathā vā gajanaraturagādiṣu/ na ca te varṇās tathānubhūyante/ utpannapradhvastatvāt/
          abhivyaktipakṣe ’pi krameṇaivābhivyaktiḥ/ samūhāsaṃbhavāt/ nāpi varṇeṣu kālpanikaḥ samūhaḥ
          kalpanīyaḥ/ parasparāśrayaprasaṅgāt/ ekārthapratyāyakatvasiddhau tadupādhinā varṇeṣu
          padatvapratītis tatsiddhāv ekārthapratyāyakatvasiddhir iti/ tasmād varṇānāṃ
          vācakatvāsaṃbhavāt sphoṭo ’bhyupagantavyaḥ/
children.translated_text: that is like grasping at <s>kāśa</s>-grass and <s>kuśa</s>-grass [for support], because the alternatives do not hold. Is the word-cognition based on mere individual phonemes, or on an aggregate of phonemes? Not the first — because, in a garland of mutually distinct phonemes, without a single [unitary] cause, the cognition 'This is one word' — like the cognition of a garland without a thread in [separate] flowers — is untenable. Nor the second — because phonemes, which are destroyed as soon as uttered, cannot form an aggregate. For therein, the designation 'aggregate' [applies to] those entities that are experienced as many, co-existing in a single location — just as the designation 'aggregate' [applies to] <s>dhava</s>, <s>khadira</s>, <s>palāśa</s> trees and the like co-existing in a single location; or to elephants, men, horses, and the like. But those phonemes are not experienced in that way — because they arise and perish [successively]. Even on the theory of manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>), the manifestation is only sequential; an aggregate is impossible. Nor should a fictional aggregate be posited in the phonemes — because of the undesirable consequence of mutual dependence: the cognition of word-hood in the phonemes [depends on] their being qualified by the capacity to convey a single meaning; the establishment of [that capacity] depends on [establishing] the capacity to convey a single meaning — [which is circular]. Therefore, since the denotative capacity of phonemes is impossible, <s>sphoṭa</s> must be accepted.

children.text:
nanu sphoṭavyañjakatāpakṣe ’pi prāguktavikalpaprasareṇa ghaṭṭakuṭīprabhātāyitam iti
          cet,
children.translated_text: Now, even on the theory that [phonemes are] manifestors of <s>sphoṭa</s>, by the proliferation of the previously stated alternatives, things have dawned as a logician's hut [i.e., ended up in confusion] — if [one argues] thus,

children.text:
tad etan manorājyavijṛmbhaṇam/ vaiṣamyasaṃbhavāt/ tathā hi/ abhivyañjako ’pi prathamo
          dhvaniḥ sphoṭam asphuṭam abhivyanakti/ uttarottarābhivyañjakakrameṇa sphuṭaṃ sphuṭataraṃ
          sphuṭatamam/ yathā svādhyāyaḥ sakṛt paṭhyamāno nāvadhāryate/ abhyāsena tu sphuṭāvasāyaḥ/
          yathā vā ratnatattvaṃ prathamapratītau sphuṭaṃ na cakāsti/ carame cetasi yathāvad
          abhivyajyate/
children.translated_text: that is mere indulgence in fantasy, because dissimilarity [between the two cases] is possible. For thus: even the first sound, as manifestor, manifests the <s>sphoṭa</s> — though indistinctly. Through the sequence of successive manifestors, [it becomes] distinct, more distinct, and most distinct. Just as a lesson (<s>svādhyāya</s>), when recited once, is not grasped, but through repetition, clear comprehension [arises]. Or just as the true nature of a gem does not clearly shine at the first cognition, but in the final cognition it is manifested as it really is.
'In the intellect in which the seed has been planted by the [preceding] sounds, together with the final sound,
in [that intellect] ripened by repetition, the word (<s>śabda</s>) is apprehended' —

children.text:
iti prāmāṇikokteḥ/ tasmād asmāc chabdād arthaṃ pratipadyāmaha iti vyavahāravaśād varṇānām
          arthavācakatvānupapatteḥ prathame kāṇḍe tatrabhavadbhir bhartṛharibhir abhihitatvān
          niravayavam arthapratyāyakaṃ śabdatattvaṃ sphoṭākhyam abhyupagantavyam iti/ etat sarvaṃ
          paramārthasaṃvillakṣaṇasattājātir eva sarveṣāṃ śabdānām artha iti pratipādanapare
          jātisamuddeśe pratipāditam/
children.translated_text: thus is the statement of the authoritative [teacher, <s>Bhartṛhari</s>]. Therefore, from the conventional usage 'We understand the meaning from this word,' since the denotative capacity of phonemes for meaning is untenable, and since it has been stated by the venerable <s>Bhartṛhari</s> in the first <s>kāṇḍa</s> [of the <s>Vākyapadīya</s>], the word-reality (<s>śabdatattva</s>) called <s>sphoṭa</s>, which is partless and conveys meaning, must be accepted. All this has been demonstrated in the section on the exposition of <s>jāti</s> (universal), which is devoted to establishing that the <s>jāti</s> (universal) of existence (<s>sattā</s>), whose nature is supreme consciousness (<s>paramārthasaṃvit</s>), is indeed the meaning of all words.

children.text:
yadi sattaiva sarveṣāṃ śabdānām arthas tarhi sarveṣāṃ śabdānāṃ paryāyatā syāt/ tathā ca
          kvacid api yugapat tricaturapadaprayogāyoga iti mahac cāturyam āyuṣmataḥ/ tad uktam:
children.translated_text: If existence (<s>sattā</s>) alone is the meaning of all words, then all words would be synonyms. And thus, the simultaneous use of three or four words anywhere would be impossible — what great cleverness of yours! As stated:
'The use of synonyms simultaneously is not desired;

children.text: paryāyeṇaiva te yasmād vadanty arthaṃ na saṃhatāḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: because they express the meaning only in alternation, not conjoined.' Thus.

children.text: tasmād ayaṃ pakṣo na kṣodakṣama iti cet
children.translated_text: Therefore, this position cannot withstand the slightest scrutiny — if [one argues] thus,

children.text:
tad etad gaganaromanthakalpam/ nīlalohitapītādyuparañjakadravyabhedena sphaṭikamaṇer iva
          saṃbandhibhedāt sattāyās tadātmanābhedena pratipattisiddhau
          gosattādirūpagotvādibhedanibandhanavyavahāravailakṣaṇyopapatteḥ/ tathā cāptavākyam:
children.translated_text: that is like chewing the cud in the sky [i.e., purely imaginary]. Just as a crystal gem, through the difference of juxtaposed substances such as blue, red, yellow, and the like, [appears differently] — so too, since existence (<s>sattā</s>), through the difference of its relata, is cognized non-differently as having their nature, the tenability of the distinctness of conventional usage — grounded in the differentiations such as 'cow-existence' and the like, or 'cow-ness' and the like — is [established]. And thus the authoritative statement:

children.text: sphaṭikaṃ vimalaṃ dravyaṃ yathā yuktaṃ pṛthak pṛthak/
children.translated_text: 'Just as a pure crystal substance, conjoined separately
with blue, red, yellow, and the like, is perceived as having their color.' Thus.
And thus <s>Hari</s> (<s>Bhartṛhari</s>) too has stated:
'Existence (<s>sattā</s>) itself, being differentiated through the difference of relata, in cows and the like,

children.text: jātir ity ucyate tasyāṃ sarve śabdā vyavasthitāḥ//
children.translated_text: is called <s>jāti</s> (universal); in that, all words are established.',

children.text: tāṃ prātipadikārthaṃ ca dhātvarthaṃ ca pracakṣate/
children.translated_text: 'They call it the meaning of the nominal base (<s>prātipadikārtha</s>) and the meaning of the verbal root (<s>dhātvārtha</s>);

children.text: sā nityā sā mahān ātmā tām āhus tvatalādayaḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: it is eternal, it is the great Self — the suffixes <s>-tva</s>, <s>-tal</s>, and the like express it.' Thus.

children.text:
āśrayabhūtaiḥ saṃbandhibhir bhidyamānā kalpitabhedā gavāśvādiṣu sattaiva mahāsāmānyam eva
          jātiḥ/ gotvādikam aparaṃ sāmānyaṃ paramārthatas tato bhinnaṃ na bhavati/ gosattaiva gotvaṃ
          nāparam anvayi pratibhāsate/ evam aśvasattāśvatvam ityādi vācyam/ evaṃ ca tasyām eva
          gavādibhedabhinnāyāṃ sattāyāṃ jātau sarve gośabdādayo vācakatvena vyavasthitāḥ/
          prātipadikārthaś ca satteti prasiddham/ bhāvavacano dhātur iti pakṣe bhāvaḥ sattaiveti
          dhātvarthaḥ sattā bhavaty eva/ kriyāvacano dhātur iti pakṣe ’pi
children.translated_text: Existence (<s>sattā</s>), the great universal itself, differentiated with imposed distinctions through its relata that are its substrates, in cows, horses, and the like, is <s>jāti</s>. Cow-ness and other subordinate universals are not, in ultimate reality, different from it. Cow-existence itself is cow-ness; no other continuous [entity] appears. Likewise, horse-existence is horse-ness — and so on. And thus, in that very <s>jāti</s> of existence, differentiated into the distinctions of cow and the like, all words such as 'cow' and the like are established as denotators. And that the meaning of the nominal base (<s>prātipadikārtha</s>) is existence — this is well known. In the view that verbal roots denote being (<s>bhāva</s>), since being is existence itself, the meaning of the verbal root is indeed existence. Even in the view that verbal roots denote action (<s>kriyā</s>),
'Others call the universal (<s>jāti</s>) residing in many individuals action (<s>kriyā</s>)' —

children.text:
iti kriyāsamuddeśe kriyāyā jātirūpatvapratipādanād dhātvarthaḥ sattā bhavaty eva/ tasya
          bhāvas tvatalau (P. 5.1.119) iti bhāvārthe tvatalādīnāṃ vidhānāt sattāvācitvaṃ yuktam/ sā
          ca sattodayavyayavaidhuryān nityā/ sarvasya prapañcasya tadvivartatayā deśataḥ kālato
          vastutaś ca paricchedarāhityāt sā sattā mahān ātmeti vyapadiśyata iti
          kārikādvayārthaḥ/
children.translated_text: since the universal nature of action has been established in the section on the exposition of action, the meaning of the verbal root is indeed existence. Since the suffixes <s>-tva</s> and <s>-tal</s> are prescribed [by <s>Pāṇini</s> 5.1.119] in the sense of 'being' (<s>bhāva</s>), their denotation of existence is fitting. And that existence is eternal — because of the absence of origination and destruction. Because the entire manifold world is a transformation of it, and because of the absence of limitation in respect of space, time, and substance, that existence is designated 'the great Self' — this is the meaning of the two verses.

children.text:
dravyapadārthavādino ’pi naye saṃvillakṣaṇaṃ tattvam eva sarvaśabdārtha iti
          saṃbandhasamuddeśe samarthitam:
children.translated_text: Even in the system of those who hold that the substance-category [is the primary meaning], the reality characterized by consciousness (<s>saṃvit</s>) alone is the meaning of all words — this has been argued in the section on the exposition of relation (<s>saṃbandhasamuddeśa</s>):
'The real entity is apprehended through its unreal forms;
through unreal limiting adjuncts, it is the real alone that is denoted by words.',
'Just as the house of <s>Devadatta</s>, through an impermanent indicator,
is grasped, [so] by the word 'house,' it is the pure [entity] alone that is denoted.' Thus.

children.text:
bhāṣyakāreṇāpi siddhe śabdārthasaṃbandha ity etad vārtikavyākhyāvasare dravyaṃ hi nityam
          ity anena granthenāsatyopādhyavacchinnaṃ brahmatattvaṃ dravyaśabdavācyaṃ sarvaśabdārtha
          iti nirūpitam/
children.translated_text: By the commentator (<s>Bhāṣyakāra</s>, i.e., <s>Patañjali</s>) too, on the occasion of explaining the <s>Vārttika</s> 'the relation of word and meaning is established,' by the passage 'for substance is eternal,' the <s>Brahman</s>-reality, delimited by unreal limiting adjuncts, denoted by the word 'substance,' is determined to be the meaning of all words.

children.text:
jātiśabdārthavācino vājapyāyanasya mate gavādayaḥ śabdā bhinnadravyasamavetajātim
          abhidadhati/ tasyām avagāhyamānāyāṃ tatsaṃbandhāt dravyam avagamyate/ śuklādayaḥ śabdā
          guṇasamavetāṃ jātim ācakṣate/ guṇe tatsaṃbandhāt pratyayaḥ/ dravye saṃbandhisaṃbandhāt/
          saṃjñāśabdānām utpattiprabhṛty ā vināśāc chaiśavakaumārayauvanādyavasthādibhede ’pi sa
          evāyam ity abhinnapratyayabalāt siddhā devadattatvādijātir abhyupagantavyā/ kriyāsv api
          jātir ālakṣyate/ saiva dhātuvācyā/ pacatītyādāv anuvṛttapratyayasya prādurbhāvāt/
          dravyapadārthavādivyāḍinaye śabdasya vyaktir evābhidheyatayā pratibhāsate/ jātis
          tūpalakṣaṇatayeti nānantyādidoṣāvakāśaḥ/ pāṇinyācāryasyobhayaṃ saṃmatam/ yato
          jātipadārtham abhyupagamya jātyākhyāyām ekasmin bahuvacanam anyatarasyām ityādivyavahāraḥ/
          dravyapadārtham aṅgīkṛtya sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣa ekavibhaktau ityādiḥ/ vyākaraṇasya
          sarvapārṣadatvān matadvayābhyupagame na kaścid virodhaḥ/ tasmād advayaṃ satyaṃ paraṃ
          brahmatattvaṃ sarvaśabdārtha iti sthitam/ tad uktam:
children.translated_text: In the view of <s>Vājapyāyana</s>, who holds that the meaning of words is the universal (<s>jāti</s>): words like 'cow' and the like denote the universal inherent in distinct substances. When that [universal] is apprehended, the substance is apprehended through its connection. Words like 'white' and the like denote the universal inherent in qualities. The cognition is of the quality through its connection; of the substance through the connection of the connected. For proper names (<s>saṃjñā</s>-words), the universal such as <s>Devadatta</s>-ness and the like must be accepted as established by the force of the unitary cognition 'This is the same one' — despite the difference of states such as infancy, youth, adolescence, and the like, from birth to death. In actions too, a universal is discerned; that very [universal] is denoted by the verbal root — because of the occurrence of a persistent cognition in [expressions like] 'he cooks.' In the system of <s>Vyāḍi</s>, who holds that the individual (<s>vyakti</s>) is the meaning of words: it is the individual alone that appears to the word as the thing to be denoted; the universal serves as a distinguishing marker — hence there is no scope for the fault of infinity and the like. Both [views] are accepted by the teacher <s>Pāṇini</s>. Because, accepting the universal as the meaning of words, the usage such as 'the plural when there are many [individuals] is used in the name of the universal' and 'in the case of one or the other' [follows]; and accepting the individual as the meaning, [the rule] 'of those having the same form, one remains in a single inflection' and the like [follows]. Since grammar is universal [i.e., acceptable to all schools], there is no contradiction in accepting both views. Therefore, it is established that the non-dual, real, supreme <s>Brahman</s>-reality is the meaning of all words. As stated:
'Therefore, through the division of power, all [meaning], whose nature is existence, is real;
the one meaning, when denoted by words, manifests as having many forms.' Thus.
The nature of reality has also been stated by <s>Hari</s> (<s>Bhartṛhari</s>) in the section on the exposition of relation:

children.text: yatra draṣṭā ca dṛśyaṃ ca darśanaṃ cāvikalpitam/
children.translated_text: 'Where the seer, the seen, and the seeing are undifferentiated —
the knowers of the end of the three [Vedas] declare the reality of that very object.' Thus.
And in the section on the exposition of substance:
'When modification ceases, what is real is gold, as in [the case of gold] earrings;

children.text: vikārāpagamo yatra tām āhuḥ prakṛtiṃ parām// iti/
children.translated_text: where modification ceases — that they call the supreme <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature).' Thus.
To sustain the accepted non-duality, the non-difference of the signified and the signifier has been shown:

children.text: vācyā sā sarvaśabdānāṃ śabdāc ca na pṛthak tataḥ/
children.translated_text: 'She [existence] is the signified of all words, and is not separate from the word; therefore,

children.text: apṛthaktve ’pi saṃbandhas tayor jīvātmanor iva// iti/
children.translated_text: even though non-separate, there is a relation between those two, like that of the individual soul and the Self.' Thus.

children.text:
tattadupādhiparikalpitabhedabahulatayā vyavahārasyāvidyāmātrakalpitatvena
          pratiniyatākāropadhīyamānarūpabhedaṃ brahmatattvaṃ sarvaśabdaviṣayaḥ/ abhede ca
          pāramārthike saṃvṛtivaśād vyavahāradaśāyāṃ svapnāvasthāvad uccāvacaḥ prapañco vivartata
          iti kārikārthaḥ/ tad āhur vedāntavādanipuṇāḥ:
children.translated_text: The <s>Brahman</s>-reality, whose form-differentiation is imposed through specific limiting adjuncts, being rich with distinctions constructed by various limiting adjuncts, [yet] with all conventional usage being merely constructed by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) — is the object of all words. And when there is ultimate non-difference, through the force of conventional [appearance], in the state of empirical activity, the manifold world of high and low evolves as in the dream-state — this is the meaning of the verse. Thus say those skilled in the <s>Vedānta</s> doctrine:
'Just as this dream-manifestation is an expansion of <s>Māyā</s> in me,
so too the waking-manifestation is an expansion of <s>Māyā</s> in me.' Thus.

children.text:
tad itthaṃ kūṭasthe parasmin brahmaṇi saccidānandarūpe pratyag abhinne ’vagate
          ’nādyavidyānivṛttau tādṛgbrahmātmanāvasthānalakṣaṇaṃ

children.translated_text: will be accomplished.

Thus, when the immutable supreme <s>Brahman</s>, of the nature of being-consciousness-bliss (<s>saccidānanda</s>), non-different from the inner Self, is known, upon the cessation of beginningless <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), characterized by abiding as <s>Brahman</s> of such a nature,

children.text:
śabdabrahmaṇi niṣṇātaḥ paraṃ brahmādhigacchati ity abhiyuktokteḥ/ tathā ca
          śabdānuśāsanaśāstrasya niḥśreyasasādhanatvaṃ siddham/ tad uktam:
children.translated_text: 'One who is well-versed in the word-<s>Brahman</s> (<s>śabdabrahman</s>) attains the supreme <s>Brahman</s>' — by the statement of the learned. And thus, the character of the science of grammar (<s>śabdānuśāsana</s>) as a means to the highest good is established. As stated:
'That [grammar] is the gateway to liberation, the cure for the impurities of speech,
the purifier of all sciences — they declare it the super-science (<s>adhividyā</s>).' Thus.
And also:
'This is the primary station of words, a step on the stairway of accomplishments;

children.text: iyaṃ sā mokṣamāṇānām ajihmā rājapaddhatiḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: this is the straight royal highway for those who are being liberated.' Thus.
Therefore, it is established that the science of grammar should be studied as a means to the supreme goal of human existence.
Thus [ends] the <s>Pāṇini</s> (Grammarian) system in the <s>Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha</s>.
Now, the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> system. //14//

children.text:
atha sāṃkhyair ākhyāte pariṇāmavāde paripanthini jāgarūke kathaṃkāraṃ vivartavāda
          ādaraṇīyo bhavet/ eṣa hi teṣām āghoṣaḥ/
children.translated_text: Now, when the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>' doctrine of real transformation (<s>pariṇāmavāda</s>) stands alert as an obstacle [to the <s>Vedānta</s> position], how could the doctrine of apparent transformation (<s>vivartavāda</s>) be worthy of acceptance? For this is their proclamation:

children.text:
saṃkṣepeṇa hi sāṃkhyaśāstre catasro vidhāḥ saṃbhāvyante/ kaścid arthaḥ prakṛtir eva
          kaścid vikṛtiḥ prakṛtiś ca kaścid vikṛtir eva kaścid anubhaya iti/
children.translated_text: In brief, four types are conceivable in the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> teaching: something is <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) alone; something is both a modification (<s>vikṛti</s>) and a <s>prakṛti</s>; something is a modification alone; and something is neither.
reference marker

children.text:
tatra kevalā prakṛtiḥ pradhānapadena vedanīyā mūlaprakṛtiḥ/ nāsāv anyasya kasyacid
          vikṛtiḥ/ prakarotīti prakṛtir iti vyutpattyā sattvarajastamoguṇānāṃ sāmyāvasthāyā
          abhidhānāt/ tad uktaṃ mūlaprakṛtir avikṛtiḥ iti/ mūlaṃ cāsau prakṛtiś ca mūlaprakṛtiḥ/
          mahadādeḥ kāryakalāpasyāsau mūlaṃ na tv asya pradhānasya mūlāntaram asti/ anavasthāpātāt/
          na ca bījāṅkuravad anavasthādoṣo na bhavatīti vācyam/ pramāṇābhāvād iti bhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: Among these, the sole <s>prakṛti</s>, to be known by the term <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter), is the root <s>prakṛti</s> (<s>mūlaprakṛti</s>). It is not a modification of anything else. By the etymology 'it produces, therefore it is <s>prakṛti</s>,' it denotes the state of equilibrium of the <s>guṇas</s> — <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>. As stated: 'the root <s>prakṛti</s> is unmodified.' It is both root (<s>mūla</s>) and <s>prakṛti</s>, hence <s>mūlaprakṛti</s>. It is the root of the aggregate of effects beginning with <s>mahat</s> (the great principle), but there is no further root of this <s>pradhāna</s> — because of the fallacy of infinite regress. Nor should one say 'there is no fault of infinite regress, as in the case of seed and sprout' — because there is no [such] evidence. This is the intention.
reference marker

children.text:
vikṛtayaś ca prakṛtayaś ca mahadahaṃkāratanmātrāṇi/ tad apy uktaṃ mahadādyāḥ
          prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ sapta iti/ asyārthaḥ/ prakṛtayaś ca tā vikṛtayaś ceti prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ
          sapta mahadādīni tattvāni/ tatrāntaḥkaraṇādipadavedanīyaṃ mahattattvam ahaṃkārasya
          prakṛtiḥ/ mūlaprakṛtes tu vikṛtiḥ/ evam ahaṃkāratattvam abhimānāparanāmadheyaṃ mahato
          vikṛtiḥ/ prakṛtiś ca tad evāhaṃkāratattvaṃ tāmasaṃ sat pañcatanmātrāṇāṃ sūkṣmābhidhānam/
          tad eva sāttvikaṃ sat prakṛtir ekādaśendriyāṇāṃ buddhīndriyāṇāṃ
          cakṣuḥśrotraghrāṇarasanātvagākhyānāṃ karmendriyāṇāṃ vākpāṇipādapāyūpasthākhyānām
          ubhayātmakasya manasaś ca/ rajasas tūbhayatra kriyotpādanadvāreṇa kāraṇatvam astīti na
          vaiyarthyam/ tad uktam īśvarakṛṣṇena —
children.translated_text: Those that are both modifications and <s>prakṛtis</s> are <s>mahat</s> (the great principle), <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego), and the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements). As stated: 'the seven beginning with <s>mahat</s> are both <s>prakṛtis</s> and modifications.' The meaning is: they are <s>prakṛtis</s> and they are modifications — hence <s>prakṛtivikṛtis</s>; the seven <s>tattvas</s> (principles) beginning with <s>mahat</s>. Among these, the <s>mahat</s> principle, to be known by the term <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (inner instrument) and the like, is the <s>prakṛti</s> of <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, but a modification of <s>mūlaprakṛti</s>. Similarly, the <s>ahaṃkāra</s> principle, also called <s>abhimāna</s> (self-assertion), is a modification of <s>mahat</s>. And that very <s>ahaṃkāra</s> principle, when <s>tāmasic</s>, is the <s>prakṛti</s> of the five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements), called the subtle [elements]. That same [<s>ahaṃkāra</s>], when <s>sāttvic</s>, is the <s>prakṛti</s> of the eleven <s>indriyas</s> (sense organs): the five <s>buddhīndriyas</s> (cognitive organs) called sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch; the five <s>karmendriyas</s> (organs of action) called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and the mind (<s>manas</s>), which partakes of both natures. <s>Rajas</s>, however, has a causal role in both [categories] through producing activity — hence it is not purposeless. As stated by <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s> —
Self-assertion is <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego); from it proceeds a twofold creation:
the group of eleven organs and the set of five <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements).
The <s>sāttvic</s> group of eleven proceeds from the modified (<s>vaikṛta</s>) <s>ahaṃkāra</s>;

children.text: bhūtādes tanmātraḥ sa tāmasas taijasād ubhayam//
children.translated_text: from the elemental (<s>bhūtādi</s>) [<s>ahaṃkāra</s>] proceed the <s>tanmātras</s> — that is <s>tāmasic</s>; from the <s>taijasa</s> (rajasic) proceed both.
The cognitive organs (<s>buddhīndriyas</s>) are called sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch;
speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals — these they call the organs of action (<s>karmendriyas</s>).

children.text: ubhayātmakam atra manaḥ saṃkalpakam indriyaṃ ca sādharmyāt/ iti/
children.translated_text: The mind (<s>manas</s>) here partakes of both natures; it is deliberative and is also a sense organ, because of its similarity [to both]. Thus.
And this was explained in the <s>Tattvakaumudī</s> by the teacher <s>Vācaspati</s>.
reference marker

children.text:
kevalā vikṛtis tu viyadādīni pañca mahābhūtāni ekādaśendriyāṇi ca/ tad uktaṃ ṣoḍaśakas tu
          vikāraḥ iti/ ṣoḍaśasaṃkhyāvacchinno gaṇaḥ ṣoḍaśako vikāra eva na prakṛtir ity arthaḥ/ yady
          api pṛthivyādayo goghaṭādīnāṃ prakṛtis tathāpi na te pṛthivyādibhyas tattvāntaram iti na
          prakṛtiḥ/ tattvāntaropādānatvaṃ ceha prakṛtitvam abhimatam/ goghatādīnāṃ
          sthūlatvendriyagrāhyatvayoḥ samānatvena tattvāntaratvābhāvaḥ/ tatra
          śabdasparśarūparasagandhatanmātrebhyaḥ pūrvapūrvasūkṣmabhūtasahitebhyaḥ pañca mahābhūtāni
          viyadādīni krameṇaikadvitricatuṣpañcaguṇāni jāyante/ indriyasṛṣṭis tu prāg evoktā/ tad
          uktam —
children.translated_text: The mere modifications are the five great elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>) beginning with space (<s>vyoman</s>) and the eleven sense organs. As stated: 'the group of sixteen is modification.' A group delimited by the number sixteen is modification only, not <s>prakṛti</s> — this is the meaning. Although earth and the like are the <s>prakṛti</s> of cows, pots, and the like, still, since they are not a principle (<s>tattva</s>) different from earth and the like, they are not [counted as] <s>prakṛti</s>. For what is intended here as <s>prakṛti</s>-hood is being the material cause of a different principle. Because cows, pots, and the like, being identical in grossness and perceptibility by the senses, are not different principles. Among these, from the <s>tanmātras</s> of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell — together with the preceding subtle elements — the five great elements beginning with space arise in succession, having one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively. The creation of the sense organs was already stated earlier. As stated —

children.text: prakṛter mahāṃs tato 'haṃkāras tasmād gaṇaś ca ṣoḍaśakaḥ/
children.translated_text: From <s>prakṛti</s> [comes] <s>mahat</s> (the great principle); from that, <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego); from that, the group of sixteen;

children.text: tasmād api ṣoḍaśakāt pañcabhyaḥ pañca bhūtāni// iti/
children.translated_text: and from five of those sixteen, the five great elements (<s>bhūtas</s>). Thus.
reference marker

children.text:
anubhayātmakaḥ puruṣaḥ/ tad uktaṃ na prakṛtir na vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ iti/ puruṣas tu
          kūṭasthanityo 'pariṇāmī na kasyacit prakṛtir nāpi vikṛtiḥ kasyacid ity arthaḥ/
children.translated_text: That which is neither [<s>prakṛti</s> nor <s>vikṛti</s>] is <s>puruṣa</s> (consciousness/spirit). As stated: '<s>puruṣa</s> is neither <s>prakṛti</s> nor modification.' <s>Puruṣa</s> is eternally unchanging (<s>kūṭasthanitya</s>), untransformed — it is not the <s>prakṛti</s> of anything, nor is it a modification of anything. This is the meaning.
reference marker

children.text: etatpañcaviṃśatitattvasādhakatvena pramāṇatrayam abhimatam/ tad apy uktam —
children.translated_text: Three means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇas</s>) are accepted as establishing these twenty-five principles. As stated —
Perception (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and the testimony of an authoritative person (<s>āptavacana</s>) — since all means of valid knowledge are established [within these],

children.text: trividhaṃ pramāṇam iṣṭaṃ prameyasiddhiḥ pramāṇād dhi// iti/
children.translated_text: the threefold <s>pramāṇa</s> is accepted; for the establishment of objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) is from <s>pramāṇa</s> indeed. Thus.
reference marker

children.text:
iha kāryakāraṇabhāve caturdhā vipratipattiḥ prasarati/ asataḥ saj jāyata iti saugatāḥ
          saṃgirante/ naiyāyikādayaḥ sato 'saj jāyata iti/ vedāntinaḥ sato vivartaḥ kāryajātaṃ na
          vastusad iti/ sāṃkhyāḥ punaḥ sataḥ saj jāyata iti/
children.translated_text: Here, regarding the cause-effect relation, fourfold disagreement prevails. The Buddhists (<s>Saugatas</s>) maintain that 'from non-being, being arises.' The <s>Naiyāyikas</s> and others [hold that] 'from being, non-being arises.' The <s>Vedāntins</s> [hold that] 'from being there is apparent transformation (<s>vivarta</s>) — the aggregate of effects is not ultimately real.' But the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> [hold that] 'from being, being arises.'
reference marker

children.text:
tatrāsataḥ saj jāyata iti na prāmāṇikaḥ pakṣaḥ/ asato nirupākhyasya śaśaviṣāṇavat
          kāraṇatvānupapatteḥ/ tucchātucchayos tādātmyānupapatteś ca/
children.translated_text: Among these, 'from non-being, being arises' is not a valid position — because non-being, being without any nature like a hare's horn, cannot serve as a cause. And because identity between the utterly void and the non-void is impossible.
reference marker

children.text:
nāpi sato 'saj jāyate/ kārakavyāpārāt prāg asataḥ śaśaviṣāṇavat
          sattāsaṃbandhalakṣaṇotpattyanupapatteḥ/ na hi nīlaṃ nipuṇatamenāpi pītaṃ kartuṃ pāryate/
          nanu sattvāsattve ghaṭasya dharmāv iti cet — tad acāru/ asati dharmiṇi taddharma iti
          vyapadeśānupapattyā dharmiṇaḥ sattvāpatteḥ/
children.translated_text: Nor does 'non-being arise from being.' Because for what is non-existent prior to the operation of causal agents, like a hare's horn, origination — defined as the connection with existence — is impossible. For blue cannot be made yellow even by the most skillful person. Now, if [one argues that] existence and non-existence are properties of the pot — that is not well-taken. Because, since in the absence of the property-bearer the statement 'that is its property' is impossible, the existence of the property-bearer follows.
reference marker

children.text:
tasmāt kārakavyāpārāt prāg api kāryaṃ sad eva/ sataś cābhivyaktir upapadyate/ yathā
          pīḍanena tileṣu tailasya dohanena saurabheyīṣu payasaḥ/ asataḥ kāraṇe kim api nidarśanaṃ
          na dṛśyate/ kiṃ ca kāryeṇa kāraṇaṃ saṃbaddhaṃ tajjanakam asaṃbaddhaṃ vā/ prathame kāryasya
          sattvam āyātam/ sator eva saṃbandha iti niyamāt/ carame sarvaṃ kāryajātaṃ sarvasmāj
          jāyeta/ asaṃbaddhatvāviśeṣāt/ tad ākhyāyi sāṃkhyācāryaiḥ —
children.translated_text: Therefore, even prior to the operation of causal agents, the effect exists. And the manifestation of what exists is consistent — just as oil [already exists] in sesame seeds and is manifested by pressing, and milk in cows by milking. Of non-being [existing] in a cause, no illustration whatsoever is seen. Moreover, is the cause connected with the effect when it generates it, or unconnected? In the first case, the existence of the effect is obtained — because the rule is that connection is only between existing things. In the second case, every aggregate of effects would arise from everything — because there would be no distinction in non-connection. As the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> teachers have declared —
Because of non-being, there is no connection with causes that are associated with existence;

children.text: asaṃbaddhasya cotpattim icchato na vyavasthitiḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: and for one who desires the origination of what is unconnected, there is no fixed order. Thus.
reference marker

children.text:
athaivam ucyetāsaṃbaddham api tat tad eva janayati yatra yacchaktam/ śaktiś ca
          kāryadarśanonneyeti/ tan na saṃgacchate/ tileṣu tailajananaśaktir ity atra tailasyāsattve
          saṃbaddhatvāsaṃbaddhatvavikalpena tacchaktir iti nirūpaṇāyogāt/ kāryakāraṇayor abhedāc ca
          kāraṇāt pṛthak kāryasya sattvaṃ na bhavati/ paṭas tantubhyo na bhidyate/ taddharmatvāt/ na
          yad evaṃ na tad evaṃ yathā gor aśvaḥ/ taddharmaś ca paṭaḥ/ tasmān nārthāntaram/
children.translated_text: If one were to say: 'even what is unconnected generates only that for which it has the power, and power is to be inferred from the observation of effects' — that does not hold. In 'sesame has the power to generate oil,' if oil is non-existent, the power for it cannot be determined by the alternative of being connected or unconnected [with it]. And because of the non-difference of cause and effect, the existence of the effect as separate from the cause does not obtain. A cloth is not different from threads — because it has the same properties. What is not so is not that, just as a horse is [not] a cow. And the cloth has the same properties [as threads]; therefore it is not a different thing.

children.text: tarhi pratyekaṃ ta eva prāvaraṇakāryaṃ kuryur iti cen na/
children.translated_text: Then, if each individual [thread] would perform the function of covering — no,

children.text:
saṃsthānabhedenāvirbhūtapaṭabhāvānāṃ prāvaraṇārthakriyākāritvopapatteḥ/ yathā hi
          kūrmasyāṅgāni kūrmaśarīre niviśamānāni tirobhavanti niḥsaranti cāvirbhavanti evaṃ
          kāraṇasya tantvādeḥ paṭādayo viśeṣā niḥsaranta āvirbhavanta utpadyanta ity ucyante/
          niviśamānās tirobhavanto vinaśyantīty ucyante/ na punar asatām utpattiḥ satāṃ vā vināśaḥ/
          yathoktaṃ bhagavadgītāyām —
children.translated_text: because it is consistent that threads in which the cloth-state has become manifest through a difference of configuration have the efficacy for the function of covering. Just as the limbs of a tortoise, when entering the tortoise's body, disappear, and when extending, appear — so too the particularizations such as cloth that emerge from the causal [threads] and the like are said to 'arise' when they appear, and are said to 'perish' when they enter and disappear. But there is no origination of non-existents or destruction of existents. As stated in the <s>Bhagavadgītā</s> —

children.text: nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ/ iti/
children.translated_text: The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being. Thus.
reference marker

children.text: tataś ca kāryānumānāt tatpradhānasiddhiḥ/ tad uktam —
children.translated_text: And from inference based on the effect, the establishment of that <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter) [follows]. As stated —
Because the non-existent cannot be produced, because there is apprehension of a material cause, because of the impossibility of all things arising from all,

children.text: śaktasya śakyakaraṇāt kāraṇabhāvāc ca sat kāryam/ iti/
children.translated_text: because what is capable produces what it is capable of, and because of the nature of the cause — the effect pre-exists (<s>sat kāryam</s>). Thus.
reference marker

children.text:
nāpi sato brahmatattvasya vivartaḥ prapañcaḥ/ bādhānupalambhāt/ adhiṣṭhānāropyayoś
          cijjaḍayoḥ kaladhautaśuktyādivat sārūpyābhāvenāropāsaṃbhavāc ca/
children.translated_text: Nor is the phenomenal world a mere apparent transformation (<s>vivarta</s>) of the existent <s>Brahman</s> principle. Because no sublation (<s>bādha</s>) is apprehended. And because superimposition (<s>āropa</s>) is impossible between the substrate and the superimposed — consciousness and insentient matter — since, unlike gold-silver and nacre, there is no similarity of form.
reference marker

children.text:
tataś ca sukhaduḥkhamohātmakasya prapañcasya tathāvidhakāraṇam avadhāraṇīyam/ tathā ca
          prayogaḥ: vimataṃ bhāvajātaṃ sukhaduḥkhamohātmakakāraṇakaṃ tadanvitatvāt/ yad yenānvīyate
          tat tatkāraṇakaṃ yathā rucakādikaṃ suvarṇānvitaṃ suvarṇakāraṇakam/ tathā cedaṃ tasmāt
          tatheti/ tatra jagatkāraṇe yeyaṃ sukhātmakatā tat sattvaṃ yā duḥkhātmakatā tad rajo yā ca
          mohātmakatā tat tama iti triguṇātmakakāraṇasiddhiḥ/ tathā hi/ pratyekaṃ bhāvās
          traiguṇyavanto ’nubhūyante/ yathā maitradāreṣu satyavatyāṃ maitrasya sukham āvirasti/ taṃ
          prati sattvaguṇaprādurbhāvāt/ tatsapatnīnāṃ duḥkham/ tāḥ prati rajoguṇaprādurbhāvāt/ tām
          alabhamānasya caitrasya moho bhavati/ taṃ prati tamoguṇasamudbhavāt/ evam anyad api
          ghaṭādikaṃ labhyamānaṃ sukhaṃ karoti/ parair apahriyamāṇaṃ duḥkhākaroti/
          udāsīnasyopekṣāviṣayatvenopatiṣṭhate/ upekṣāviṣayatvaṃ nāma mohaḥ/ muha vaicittye ity
          asmād dhātor mohaśabdaniṣpatteḥ/ upekṣaṇīyeṣu cittavṛttyanudayāt/ tasmāt sarvaṃ bhāvajātaṃ
          sukhaduḥkhamohātmakaṃ triguṇapradhānakāraṇakam avagamyate/ tathā śvetāśvataropaniṣadi
          śrūyate :
children.translated_text: Therefore, for the phenomenal world whose nature is pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), and delusion (<s>moha</s>), a cause of the same nature must be ascertained. And the inference is: the disputed aggregate of existents has a cause whose nature is pleasure, pain, and delusion — because it is pervaded by those. Whatever is pervaded by something has that as its cause, just as bracelets and the like, pervaded by gold, have gold as their cause. And so this is like that; therefore [it is] thus. Among these, the pleasure-nature in the cause of the world is <s>sattva</s>; the pain-nature is <s>rajas</s>; and the delusion-nature is <s>tamas</s> — thus the cause consisting of the three <s>guṇas</s> is established. For thus: individual things are experienced as having the three <s>guṇas</s>. For example, when among <s>Maitra's</s> wives, <s>Satyavatī</s> is present, <s>Maitra</s> has pleasure — because of the manifestation of the <s>sattva</s> quality toward him. Her co-wives have pain — because of the manifestation of the <s>rajas</s> quality toward them. And <s>Caitra</s>, who does not obtain her, has delusion — because of the arising of the <s>tamas</s> quality toward him. Similarly, other things too, such as a pot, when obtained produce pleasure; when taken away by others produce pain; and for one who is indifferent, present themselves as objects of indifference. Being an object of indifference is called delusion — because the word <s>moha</s> is derived from the root 'muh' meaning 'bewilderment of mind,' since mental activity does not arise regarding things worthy of indifference. Therefore, the entire aggregate of existents, being of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is understood to have as its cause the <s>pradhāna</s> consisting of three <s>guṇas</s>. And in the <s>Śvetāśvataropaniṣad</s> it is heard:
The one unborn (<s>ajā</s>), red, white, and black,
producing many offspring of similar form —
one unborn male (<s>aja</s>) lies with her, enjoying;
another unborn male abandons her after her pleasures are exhausted. Thus.

Here the words 'red,' 'white,' and 'black' are intended to denote the three <s>guṇas</s> — <s>rajas</s>, <s>sattva</s>, and <s>tamas</s> — because of the similarity [of these colors] to their properties of coloring (agitating), illuminating, and concealing respectively.
reference marker

children.text:
nanv acetanaṃ pradhānaṃ cetanānadhiṣṭhitaṃ mahadādikārye na vyāpriyate/ ataḥ kenacic
          cetanenādhiṣṭhātrā bhavitavyam/ tathā ca sarvārthadarśī parameśvaraḥ svīkartavyaḥ syād iti
          cet — tad asaṃgatam/ acetanasyāpi pradhānasya prayojanavaśena pravṛttyupapatteḥ/ dṛṣṭaṃ
          cācetanaṃ cetanānādhiṣṭhitaṃ puruṣārthāya pravartamānaṃ yathā vatsavivṛddhyartham acetanaṃ
          kṣīraṃ pravartate yathā ca jalam acetanaṃ lokopakārāya pravartate tathā prakṛtir acetanāpi
          puruṣavimokṣāya pravartsyati/ tad uktam —
children.translated_text: Now, the insentient <s>pradhāna</s>, not governed by a conscious being, does not engage in the production of effects beginning with <s>mahat</s>. Therefore, there must be some conscious governor; and thus the all-seeing Supreme Lord must be accepted — if so, that is inconsistent. Because even the insentient <s>pradhāna</s> can engage in activity on account of a purpose. And an insentient thing not governed by a conscious being, acting for the sake of a person (<s>puruṣa</s>), is indeed observed — just as insentient milk flows for the growth of the calf, and just as insentient water flows for the benefit of the world, so too <s>prakṛti</s>, though insentient, will act for the liberation of <s>puruṣa</s>. As stated —
Just as the activity of insentient milk is for the purpose of the calf's nourishment,
so too is the activity of <s>pradhāna</s> for the purpose of the liberation of <s>puruṣa</s>. Thus.
reference marker

children.text:
yas tu parameśvaraḥ karuṇayā pravartaka iti parameśvarāstitvavādināṃ ḍiṇḍimaḥ sa
          garbhasrāveṇa gataḥ/ vikalpānupapatteḥ/ sa kiṃ sṛṣṭeḥ prāk pravartate sṛṣṭyuttarakālaṃ vā/
          ādye śarīrādyabhāvena duḥkhānutpattau jīvānāṃ duḥkhaprahāṇecchānupapattiḥ/ dvitīye
          parasparāśrayaprasaṅgaḥ/ karuṇayā sṛṣṭiḥ sṛṣṭyā ca kāruṇyam iti/ tasmād acetanasyāpi
          cetanānadhiṣṭhitasya pradhānasya mahadādirūpeṇa pariṇāmaḥ puruṣārthaprayuktaḥ
          pradhānapuruṣasaṃyoganimittaḥ/ yathā nirvyāpārasyāpy ayaskāntasya saṃnidhānena lohasya
          vyāpāras tathā nirvyāpārasya puruṣasya saṃnidhānena pradhānavyāpāro yujyate/
          prakṛtipuruṣasaṃbandhaś ca paṅgvandhavat parasparāpekṣānibandhanaḥ/ prakṛtir hi bhogyatayā
          bhoktāraṃ puruṣam apekṣate/ puruṣo 'pi bhedāgrahād buddhicchāyāpattyā tadgataṃ
          duḥkhatrayaṃ vārayamāṇaḥ kaivalyam apekṣate/ tat prakṛtipuruṣavivekanibandhanaṃ na ca
          tadantareṇa yuktam iti kaivalyārthaṃ puruṣaḥ pradhānam apekṣate/ yathā khalu kaucit
          paṅgvandhau pathi sārthena gacchantau daivakṛtād upaplavāt parityaktasārthau mandamandam
          itaḥ tataḥ paribhramantau bhayākulau daivavaśāt saṃyogam upagacchetām/ tatra cāndhena
          paṅguḥ skandham āropitaḥ/ tataḥ paṅgudarśitena mārgeṇāndhaḥ samīhitaṃ sthānaṃ prāpnoti
          paṅgur api skandhādhirūḍhaḥ/ tathā parasparāpekṣapradhānapuruṣanibandhanaḥ sargaḥ/
          yathoktam —
children.translated_text: As for the drumbeat of those who assert the existence of the Supreme Lord — [claiming] that the Supreme Lord, out of compassion, is the instigator — that has been expelled by a miscarriage. Because [none of the] alternatives is tenable. Does He instigate before creation or after creation? In the first case, since in the absence of bodies and the like, suffering would not arise, the desire of <s>jīvas</s> (individual souls) to abandon suffering would be untenable. In the second case, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence: creation [would depend] on compassion, and compassion on creation. Therefore, even though <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) is non-conscious and not superintended by a conscious [being], its transformation into the form of <s>Mahat</s> (the Great Principle) and the like is motivated by the purpose of the <s>Puruṣa</s> (soul), and is occasioned by the conjunction of <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>. Just as a loadstone, though itself without activity, causes activity in iron by its mere proximity — so too the activity of <s>Pradhāna</s> through the mere proximity of the inactive <s>Puruṣa</s> is justified. And the connection between <s>Prakṛti</s> (nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> is grounded in mutual dependence — like a lame man and a blind man. For <s>Prakṛti</s>, as the enjoyed, depends on the <s>Puruṣa</s> as the enjoyer. <s>Puruṣa</s> too, not grasping the distinction [between himself and <s>Prakṛti</s>], and through the reflection of the image of the intellect (<s>buddhicchāyāpatti</s>) wishing to ward off the threefold suffering that belongs to it [the intellect], desires <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute isolation). And that [<s>kaivalya</s>] is grounded in the discrimination of <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>, and is not possible without it — therefore, for the sake of <s>kaivalya</s>, <s>Puruṣa</s> depends on <s>Pradhāna</s>. Just as, indeed, a certain lame man and blind man traveling on a road with a caravan, abandoned by the caravan due to a calamity caused by fate, wandering slowly here and there, distressed with fear, by the force of fate come into conjunction — and therein, the lame man is raised onto the blind man's shoulders; and then, by the path shown by the lame man, the blind man reaches the desired destination, and the lame man too, mounted on the shoulders [reaches it] — so too, creation is grounded in the mutual dependence of <s>Pradhāna</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s>. As stated:
'For the sake of the seeing of the <s>Puruṣa</s>, and for the sake of the isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) of <s>Pradhāna</s>,

children.text: paṅgvandhavad ubhayor api saṃbandhas tatkṛtaḥ sargaḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: the conjunction of the two — like the lame and the blind — from that, creation is produced.' Thus.

children.text:
nanu puruṣārthanibandhanā bhavatu prakṛteḥ pravṛttiḥ/ nivṛttis tu katham upapadyata iti
          cet — ucyate/ yathā bhartrā dṛṣṭadoṣā svairiṇī bhartāraṃ punar nopaiti yathā vā
          kṛtaprayojanā nartakī nivartate tathā prakṛtir api/ yathoktam:
children.translated_text: Objection: 'Let the activity of <s>Prakṛti</s> be grounded in the purpose of <s>Puruṣa</s>. But how is [its] cessation justified?' Reply: Just as a loose woman, whose faults have been seen by her husband, does not approach the husband again; or just as a dancer, having fulfilled her purpose, withdraws — so too <s>Prakṛti</s>. As stated:

children.text: raṅgasya darśayitvā nivartate nartakī yathā nṛtyāt/
children.translated_text: 'Just as a dancer withdraws from dancing after having displayed herself on stage,

children.text: puruṣasya tathātmānaṃ prakāśya vinivartate prakṛtiḥ// iti/
children.translated_text: so too <s>Prakṛti</s>, having manifested herself to <s>Puruṣa</s>, withdraws.' Thus.
This is the doctrine presented following the views of <s>Kapila</s> and others, the founders of the <s>Nirīśvara Sāṃkhya</s> (Sāṃkhya without God) system.
Thus concludes the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> philosophy in the <s>Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha</s>.
Now the <s>Pātañjala</s> (Yoga) Philosophy //15//
Now the doctrine of those who follow the views of <s>Patañjali</s> and other sages, the founders of <s>Seśvara Sāṃkhya</s> (Sāṃkhya with God), is presented.

children.text:
tatra sāṃkhyapravacanāparanāmadheyaṃ yogaśāstraṃ patañjalipraṇītaṃ pādacatuṣṭayātmakam/
          tatra prathame pāde — atha yogānuśāsanam iti yogaśāstrārambhapratijñāṃ vidhāya yogaś
          cittavṛttinirodhaḥ ityādinā yogalakṣaṇam abhidhāya samādhiṃ saprapañcaṃ niradikṣad
          bhagavān patañjaliḥ/ dvitīye tapaḥsvādhyāyeśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ ityādinā
          vyutthitacittasya kriyāyogaṃ yamādīni ca pañca bahirāṅgāṇi sādhanāni/ tṛtīye deśabandhaś
          cittasya dhāraṇā ityādinā dhāraṇādhyānasamādhitrayam antaraṅgaṃ saṃyamapadavācyaṃ
          tadavāntaraphalaṃ vibhūtijātam/ caturthe janmauṣadhimantratapaḥsamādhijāḥ siddhayaḥ
          ityādinā siddhipañcakaprapañcanapuraḥsaraṃ paramaṃ prayojanaṃ kaivalyam/ pradhānādīni
          pañcaviṃśatitattvāni prācīnāny eva saṃmatāni/ ṣaḍviṃśas tu parameśvaraḥ
          kleśakarmavipākāśayair aparāmṛṣṭaḥ puruṣaḥ svecchayā nirmāṇakāyam adhiṣṭhāya
          laukikavaidikasaṃpradāyapravartakaḥ saṃsārāṅgāre tapyamānānāṃ prāṇabhṛtām anugrāhakaś
          ca/
children.translated_text: Therein, the <s>Yoga</s> scripture, also known as <s>Sāṃkhyapravacana</s>, composed by <s>Patañjali</s>, consists of four sections (<s>pādas</s>). In the first section — having set forth the introductory declaration of the <s>Yoga</s> scripture with '<s>atha yogānuśāsanam</s>' (Now, the instruction of <s>Yoga</s>), and having stated the definition of <s>Yoga</s> with '<s>yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ</s>' (Yoga is the cessation of the modifications of the mind) and the like — the blessed <s>Patañjali</s> taught <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption) in detail. In the second section, with '<s>tapaḥsvādhyāyeśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ</s>' (Austerity, self-study, and surrender to God constitute the <s>yoga</s> of action) and the like, [he taught] <s>kriyāyoga</s> (the yoga of action) for the mind in its extroverted state, and the five external means (<s>bahiraṅga</s>) beginning with <s>yama</s> (restraints). In the third section, with '<s>deśabandhaś cittasya dhāraṇā</s>' (Fixing the mind on a location is <s>dhāraṇā</s>) and the like, [he taught] the triad of <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>samādhi</s> — the internal means, designated by the term <s>saṃyama</s> (constraint) — and their subsidiary results, the class of <s>vibhūtis</s> (supernatural powers). In the fourth section, with '<s>janmauṣadhimantratapaḥsamādhijāḥ siddhayaḥ</s>' (Attainments arise from birth, herbs, <s>mantras</s>, austerity, and <s>samādhi</s>) and the like, preceded by the elaboration of the fivefold <s>siddhis</s> (attainments), [he taught] the supreme purpose — <s>kaivalya</s> (absolute isolation). The twenty-five <s>tattvas</s> (principles) beginning with <s>Pradhāna</s> are accepted as before [i.e., as in Sāṃkhya]. But the twenty-sixth is the Supreme Lord — a <s>Puruṣa</s> untouched by <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>vipāka</s> (fruition), and <s>āśaya</s> (latent impressions), who, by His own will, presiding over a projected body (<s>nirmāṇakāya</s>), is the initiator of both worldly and Vedic traditions, and the bestower of grace upon living beings who are tormented in the embers of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence).

children.text:
nanu puṣkarapalāśavan nirlepasya tasya tapyabhāvaḥ katham upapadyate yena parameśvaro
          'nugrāhakatayā kakṣīkriyata iti cet — ucyate/ tāpakasya rajasaḥ sattvam eva tapyaṃ
          buddhyātmanā pariṇatam iti sattve paritapyamāne tadāropavaśena tadabhedāvagāhipuruṣo 'pi
          tapyata ity ucyate/ tad uktam ācāryaiḥ —
children.translated_text: Objection: 'How is it tenable that He, who is untouched [by <s>karma</s>] like a lotus leaf, [yet] experiences suffering — such that the Supreme Lord is postulated as a bestower of grace?' Reply: <s>Rajas</s> (the quality of activity), which is the scorcher, scorches <s>sattva</s> (the quality of purity) alone, which has transformed in the form of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>). So when <s>sattva</s> is being scorched, through the superimposition upon it, the <s>Puruṣa</s> — who cognizes [himself as] non-different from it [the intellect] through the reflection of the intellect's image — is also said to be scorched. As stated by the <s>ācāryas</s> (masters):

children.text: sattvaṃ tapyaṃ buddhibhāvena vṛttaṃ bhāvā ye vā rājasās tāpakās te/
children.translated_text: '<s>Sattva</s> is what is scorched, having assumed the form of the intellect; those states that are <s>rājasic</s> are the scorchers;

children.text: tapyābhedagrāhiṇī tāmasī yā vṛttis tasyāṃ tapya ity ukta ātmā//
children.translated_text: that <s>tāmasic</s> modification which grasps [the <s>Puruṣa</s> as] non-different from the scorched — in [the context of] that [modification], the self is called "the scorched."'

children.text:
iti/ pañcaśikhenāpy uktam — apariṇāminī hi bhoktṛśaktir apratisaṃkramā ca pariṇāminy
          arthe pratisaṃkrānteva tadvṛttim anupatatīti/ bhoktṛśaktir iti cicchaktir ucyate/ sā
          cātmaiva/ pariṇāminy arthe buddhitattve pratisaṃkrānteva pratibimbiteva tadvṛttim
          anupatatīti buddhau pratibimbitā sā cicchaktir buddhicchāyāpattyā buddhivṛttyanukāravatīti
          bhāvaḥ/ tathā śuddho 'pi puruṣaḥ pratyayaṃ bauddham anupaśyati tam anupaśyann atadātmāpi
          tadātmaka iva pratibhāsata iti/ itthaṃ tapyamānasya
          puruṣasyādaranairantaryadīrghakālānubandhiyamaniyamādyaṣṭāṅgayogānu-ṣṭhānena
          parameśvarapraṇidhānena ca sattvapuruṣānyatākhyātāv anupaplavāyāṃ jātāyām avidyādayaḥ
          pañca kleśāḥ samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣitā bhavanti/ kuśalākuśalāś ca karmāśayāḥ samūlaghātaṃ hatā
          bhavanti/ tataś ca puruṣasya nirlepasya kaivalyenāvasthānaṃ kaivalyam iti siddham/
children.translated_text: Thus. <s>Pañcaśikha</s> too has stated: 'The power of the enjoyer, which is non-transforming and non-transferable, as if transferred to the transforming object, follows its modifications.' The 'power of the enjoyer' refers to the power of consciousness (<s>cicchakti</s>). And that is the self itself. 'As if transferred to the transforming object,' i.e., 'as if reflected in the intellect-principle,' 'it follows its modifications' — that is, the power of consciousness, reflected in the intellect, imitates the modifications of the intellect through the reflection of the intellect's image — this is the meaning. Thus too: 'Even though the <s>Puruṣa</s> is pure, he beholds the intellectual cognition; beholding it, though not of that nature, he appears as if of that nature.' In this way, for the <s>Puruṣa</s> who is being scorched, through the practice of the eightfold <s>yoga</s> — consisting of <s>yama</s> (restraints), <s>niyama</s> (observances), and the like — pursued with reverence, without interruption, and for a long time, and through surrender to the Supreme Lord (<s>Īśvarapraṇidhāna</s>), when the discriminative knowledge of the distinction between <s>sattva</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> (<s>sattvapuruṣānyatākhyāti</s>) has arisen without obstruction, the five <s>kleśas</s> (afflictions) beginning with <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) are uprooted completely. And the latent impressions of auspicious and inauspicious <s>karmas</s> are destroyed root and all. Thereupon, the abidance of the untouched <s>Puruṣa</s> in isolation (<s>kaivalya</s>) — that is <s>kaivalya</s> — this is established.

children.text:
tatrātha yogānuśāsanam iti prathamasūtreṇa prekṣāvatpravṛttyaṅgaṃ
          viṣayaprayojanasaṃbandhādhikārirūpam anubandhacatuṣṭayaṃ pratipādyate/
children.translated_text: Therein, by the first <s>sūtra</s> '<s>atha yogānuśāsanam</s>' (Now, the instruction of <s>Yoga</s>), the fourfold preliminary connection (<s>anubandha</s>) — which is the limb of the engagement of a discerning person — consisting of the subject-matter (<s>viṣaya</s>), purpose (<s>prayojana</s>), relation (<s>saṃbandha</s>), and qualified student (<s>adhikārin</s>) — is taught.

children.text:
atrāthaśabdo 'dhikārārthaḥ svīkriyate/ athaśabdasyānekārthatve saṃbhavati katham
          ārambhārthatvapakṣe pakṣapātaḥ saṃbhavet/ athaśabdasya maṅgalādyanekārthatvaṃ
          nāmaliṅgānuśāsanenānuśiṣṭaṃ
children.translated_text: Here, the word '<s>atha</s>' is accepted in the sense of commencement (<s>adhikāra</s>). Since the word '<s>atha</s>' has multiple meanings, how could there be a preference for the interpretation of commencement? The word '<s>atha</s>' has multiple meanings as taught by the <s>Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana</s> (the <s>Amarakośa</s>):
'<s>Atha</s> and <s>atho</s> [are used] in [the senses of] auspiciousness, succession, commencement, questioning, and totality' —

children.text:
iti/ atra praśnakārtsnyayor asaṃbhave 'pi
          ānantaryamaṅgalapūrvaprakṛtāpekṣārambhalakṣaṇānāṃ caturṇām arthānāṃ saṃbhavād
          ārambhārthatvānupapattir iti cet —
children.translated_text: thus. Here, although questioning and totality are not applicable, since four meanings — succession, auspiciousness, dependence on a prior topic, and commencement — are all possible, [one might object that] the interpretation as commencement is untenable.

children.text:
maivaṃ maṃsthāḥ/ vikalpāsahatvāt/ ānantaryam athaśabdārtha iti pakṣe yataḥ kutaścid
          ānantaryaṃ pūrvavṛttaśamādyasādhāraṇāt kāraṇād ānantaryaṃ vā/ na prathamaḥ/
children.translated_text: Do not think so — because of the inability to withstand the alternatives. If the position is that succession (<s>ānantarya</s>) is the meaning of the word '<s>atha</s>' — [then] is it succession from something or other [indeterminate], or succession from a specific cause such as the previously accomplished tranquility (<s>śama</s>) and the like? Not the first —

children.text: na hi kaścit kṣaṇam api jātu tiṣṭhaty akarmakṛt/
children.translated_text: 'For no being ever remains, even for a moment, without performing action' —

children.text:
iti nyāyena sarvo jantur avaśyaṃ kiṃcit kṛtvā kiṃcit karoty eveti tasyābhidhānam
          antareṇāpi prāptatayā tadarthāthaśabdaprayogavaiyarthyaprasakteḥ/ na caramaḥ/
          śamādyanantaraṃ yogasya pravṛttāv api tasyānuśāsanapravṛtyanubandhatvenopāttatayā śabdataḥ
          prādhānyābhāvāt/ na ca śabdataḥ pradhānabhūtasyānuśāsanasya śamādyānantaryam
          athaśabdārthaḥ kiṃ na syād iti vaditavyam/ anuśāsanam iti hi śāstram āha/ anuśiṣyate
          vyākhyāyate lakṣaṇabhedopāyaphalasahito yogo yena tad anuśāsanam iti vyutpatteḥ/
          anuśāsanasya ca tattvajñānacikhyāpayiṣānantarabhāvitvena śamadamādyānantaryaniyamābhāvāt/
          jijñāsājñānayos tu śamādyānantaryam āmnāyate — tasmāc chānto dānta uparatas titikṣuḥ
          samāhito bhūtvātmany evātmānaṃ paśyet ityādinā/
children.translated_text: by this principle, since every creature necessarily does something after doing something, [succession from just anything] is already obtained even without stating it — and thus the use of the word '<s>atha</s>' in that meaning would be pointless. Not the last [alternative] — because, even though <s>yoga</s> commences after [the attainment of] tranquility and the like, since that [tranquility] is subsumed under [the discussion of <s>yoga</s>] as a preliminary to the commencement of instruction, it lacks primacy from the standpoint of the word [<s>atha</s>]. Nor should it be said: 'Why should succession from tranquility and the like not be the meaning of <s>atha</s> for the instruction, which is primary from the standpoint of the word?' For '<s>anuśāsana</s>' (instruction) means a scripture. By the etymology: 'that by which <s>yoga</s> is instructed, i.e., explained, together with its definition, varieties, means, and results — that is <s>anuśāsana</s>.' And since instruction follows immediately upon the desire to teach the knowledge of reality, there is no fixed rule of succession from tranquility, self-restraint, and the like. For inquiry and knowledge, however, succession from tranquility and the like is proclaimed [in Śruti]: 'Therefore, having become tranquil, self-restrained, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the self in the self alone' — and so on.

children.text:
nāpi tattvajñānacikhyāpayiṣānantaryam athaśabdārthaḥ/ tasya saṃbhave 'pi
          śrotṛpratipattipravṛttyor anupayogenānabhidheyatvāt/ tavāpi niḥśreyasahetutayā
          yogānuśāsanaṃ pramitaṃ na vā/ ādye tadabhāve 'py upādeyatvaṃ bhavet/ dvitīye tadbhāve 'pi
          heyatvaṃ syāt/ pramitaṃ cāsya niḥśreyasanidānatvam/
children.translated_text: Nor is succession from the desire to teach the knowledge of reality the meaning of the word '<s>atha</s>' — because, even though that [desire] is possible, since it is not useful for the hearer's understanding or engagement, it should not be stated. For you too: is this <s>yoga</s> instruction understood as the cause of the highest good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>) or not? In the first case, even in its absence, [it] would be worth adopting. In the second case, even in its presence, [it] would be to be rejected. And [in fact,] its being the cause of the highest good is well established —

children.text: adhyātmayogādhigamena devaṃ matvā dhīro harṣaśokau jahāti/
children.translated_text: 'Having known the Lord through the attainment of the <s>yoga</s> of the self (<s>adhyātmayoga</s>), the wise one abandons joy and sorrow' —
from this <s>Śruti</s>,

children.text: samādhāv acalā buddhis tadā yogam avāpsyasi/
children.translated_text: 'When your intellect stands firm, unshaken, in <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption), then you will attain <s>yoga</s>' —

children.text:
iti smṛteś ca/ ata eva śiṣyapraśnatapaścaraṇarasāyanopayogādyānantaryaṃ parākṛtam/ athāto
